21686-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Volume one of Stevenson's works, in the Swanston Edition of 1911, opens with Andrew Lang's introduction. The set ran to twenty-five volumes, with two thousand copies for sale. This copy is number sixteen hundred and seventy-eight of the printing.

An Inland Voyage leads the contents, Stevenson's canoe trip from Antwerp toward France. Colvin's memoir tells how illness ordered the young writer south to Mentone. There the born wayfarer wrote on roads for Hamerton's Portfolio. Walter Crane designed the title page of the voyage. The volume shows Stevenson at the start of his road, a traveller before he was a romancer.
23055-the-slanderer-1901:
Anton Chekhov catches a schoolmaster in The Slanderer, his story dated 1901 here. A voice from the adjoining room calls out at a wedding feast. Vankin's cropped head soon appears in the doorway. He is the assistant instructor, and he has heard enough to start trouble. Someone has been kissing in here, Vankin announces, alone with a lady, no less.

A kiss, a witness, and a panic about reputation set Chekhov's little machine running. The slanderer of the title fears gossip so much that he manufactures it himself, begging, explaining, and spreading the story everywhere. Chekhov needs only a few pages to strip a man's dignity with perfect comic timing. The tale is a miniature of his method, funny on the surface, pitiless underneath, and done before the reader wants it to end.
a-select-bibliography-of-chemistry-1492-: A Select Bibliography of Chemistry, 1492-1897, by Henry Carrington Bolton, second series, 1901. The bibliography continues. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
abraham-lincoln-a-history-volume-01: John Nicolay and John Hay — Lincoln's own secretaries — wrote this monumental ten-volume life from unparalleled inside knowledge. This first volume covers Lincoln's origins and rise. The definitive nineteenth-century biography, it remains an essential source for understanding the man and his times.
apotelesmata-philosophica-mercvrii-trivm: Apotelesmata philosophica Mercurii triumphantis, 1601. The triumphant Mercury. This book preserves that work. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Kept for readers.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-01:
Richard F. Burton published the first volume of his Thousand Nights and a Night in 1885. His literal, unexpurgated translation of the Arabic Alf Layla wa Layla became the most famous English Arabian Nights. Shahrazad, wedded to a king who kills his brides, saves her life by telling tales that never quite end at dawn.

Volume one sets that frame and opens the early cycles of merchants, jinn, and porters. Burton kept the verse, the slang, and the frankness that earlier versions cut. His notes draw on years in the East and a scholar's appetite for custom. The full set runs to ten volumes, with six supplemental ones after. This first volume is where the great frame begins.
arabian-nights-burton-supplemental-1886-:
Burton's Supplemental Nights began in 1886, adding tales from Arabic manuscripts outside the main cycle. Volume one of the supplement is famed for holding Aladdin and Ali Baba in Burton's full rendering. Those two tales, known to every child in short forms, come here with their complete Arabic frames and details.

Aladdin's lamp and the forty thieves' cave gain depth, violence, and humor in the uncut text. Burton drew these stories from the Wortley Montague manuscript and other sources he names. The supplement was no afterthought: it rounds the Nights toward completeness. Readers who know only the famous pair will find them stranger and richer here. Six volumes carry the supplement to its end.
arxiv-2512-00101:
The classic birthday problem asks how many people are needed before two likely share a birthday. Chijul Tripathy introduces a variant in 2025, called the Bottleneck Birthday Problem. The twist limits how many birthdays may fall on any single day.

The problem asks for the largest group one can choose under that limit. No day of the year may collect more than a set number of birthdays, with probability at least one half. It is a playful question with a serious combinatorial core. Such variants sharpen probability intuition and often connect to scheduling and hashing problems in computing. Tripathy presents it as a fun problem, and the bottleneck rule gives it fresh bite.
arxiv-2512-00201:
Algebraic geometry studies shapes defined by polynomial equations, and group actions add symmetry to those shapes. Alexandre Roy studies an algebraic group action on a hybrid compactification in 2025, writing in French. The compactification was defined by J. Poineau using hybrid Berkovich spaces.

Compactifications add boundary points so that a variety's behavior at its edges can be studied cleanly. Roy considers varieties over the complex numbers whose group action is closed. The work blends Berkovich's non-Archimedean geometry with classical complex geometry, a meeting point that has become fruitful for arithmetic questions. Hybrid spaces mix archimedean and non-archimedean geometry, which is what makes them hybrid. Closed actions behave well at the boundary, so the extension is natural to ask for. The work is slow, deep math. It is meant for the small set of folks who build such spaces and need to know how groups act on them.
arxiv-2512-00601:
Reasoning models for medicine must do more than land on the right answer; their reasoning must be faithful and complete. Boyang Gu and co-authors present Clinical-R1 in 2025, training language models with a clinical objective relative policy optimization. Popular post-training methods mainly reward correctness.

Correctness alone is misaligned with multi-dimensional clinical objectives, where a lucky guess with sloppy reasoning is dangerous. The new objective rewards reasoning that is faithful to the evidence and comprehensive in coverage. Work like this pushes medical AI toward explanations a clinician can audit, not just conclusions to accept. Clinical reasoning objectives were defined with the field's real demands in mind. Faithfulness means the stated reasoning matches the evidence the model actually used. For care teams, the gain is trust. A tool that shows its work, step by step, can be checked by the staff who must sign off on the call.
arxiv-2512-01401:
Jung Hon Yip proves a claim about dense matchings in a class of graphs. A matching pairs up points in a graph with edges. The class here has independence number at most two. That means any three points hold at least one edge among them.

For large graphs in that class, Yip finds a matching of set size. He also bounds how many non-adjacent pairs the matching can leave. Dense matchings help in tasks like pairing users or jobs. A firm proof for this class adds a tool for cases where the graph is near-complete.
arxiv-2512-01501:
Hirohito Arai proposes one frame for viewing and running models in N dimensions. Tools for higher dimensions tend to split tasks. Geometry code is strong but lacks a live test space. Scholars must hop between tools to try ideas.

Arai's frame joins simulation and viewing in one place. It covers the four-dimensional case as a test. Users can tweak a model and see the result at once. That loop lowers the bar for work on higher spaces. It serves math, physics, and design teams that think in more than three dimensions.
arxiv-2512-02101:
Neutrino masses are tiny and puzzling, and one proposed explanation hides a fifth dimension where a partner particle lives. Arturo de Giorgi, Dhruv Pasari, and Jessica Turner give a 2025 overview of neutrino masses and mixing in large extra dimension scenarios, organized around that five-dimensional bulk fermion.

In a flat extra dimension curled into a circle with a twist, the bulk fermion appears in four dimensions as a tower of right-handed neutrinos, the Kaluza-Klein tower. The paper works through the phenomenological impact: what experiments would see. Such overviews help phenomenologists judge whether extra dimensions remain a live answer to the neutrino mass puzzle.
arxiv-2512-02201:
Speech recognition for South African languages lags far behind English, mostly for lack of training data. Vukosi Marivate and a large team introduce Swivuriso in 2025, a multilingual speech dataset of about three thousand hours built under the African Next Voices project.

The dataset covers seven South African languages and three topic areas: agriculture, healthcare, and general speech. It is meant both to train and to benchmark automatic speech recognition systems for these languages. Resources of this scale are the groundwork for voice technology that serves speakers whom the current market largely ignores.
arxiv-2512-03001:
Thomas Rivasseau argues that controlling large language models must reach inside their working context. Current operator control relies on preference training, prompting, and filtering of inputs and outputs. Those tools score good results, yet models stay open to abuse, and jailbreak odds grow with context length.

Long conversations give attackers more room to steer a model off course. Rivasseau's invasive context engineering seeks robust security guarantees for long context situations. Stronger in context control matters as agents take longer tasks in law, medicine, and infrastructure, where a hijacked session can do real harm. Long chats are where harm can hide in plain sight, one mild turn at a time. Guards must live in the chat, not at its gate.
arxiv-2512-03201:
A classic number in topology counts how loops link. Oleg Musin and Timur Shamazov offer a way to compute the Hopf invariant in this 2025 work. Heinz Hopf defined his map in 1931 and showed it differs from a constant map.

The authors start from Whitehead's integral formula for the invariant. They turn it into an algorithm for maps built from simple pieces. A working algorithm lets computers handle questions that are hard by hand. It may aid study of shapes in geometry, physics, and data analysis. Computing a classic invariant by algorithm brings hand proofs into the software age.
arxiv-2512-03501:
AI tutors work best when they guide rather than tell. Karthik Sunil and Aalok Thakkar present SocraticAI in this 2025 work. The system brings large language models into undergraduate computer science classes through structured constraints.

Rather than banning AI, SocraticAI enforces well-formed questions and reflective engagement. It also sets daily usage limits and gives Socratic dialogue scaffolds. Guided use could help students learn problem solving instead of copying answers. The design offers a model for schools facing generative AI in class. Scaffolds keep students active, since the tutor asks and prompts rather than solving outright.
arxiv-2512-03601:
Videos mix motion and meaning across time. Haoran Zhou and Gim Hee Lee present Motion4D in this 2025 work. Foundation models for 2D vision improved dynamic scene analysis from single-camera videos.

Those models often lack 3D consistency, a basic need for scene geometry and motion. The gap causes spatial misalignment and temporal flickering in complex scenes. Motion4D learns 3D-consistent motion and semantics for 4D scene understanding. Consistent 4D models help robotics, video editing, and virtual reality. 4D understanding joins space and time, the frame robots and editors both need.
arxiv-2601-06601:
Giacomo Vianello proves a least-area result for slices of a cone in a 2026 paper. He looks at a round cone in n plus one dims, as he puts it. A flat plane through the cone's axis cuts it in a slice.

His proof uses a gauge trick known as a calibration test. If n is four or more, the result can hold, he shows. The cone's mouth must also be wide enough for the proof to work. Then the slice has the least area of all free-edge rivals in the cone. Such tests are a clean way to prove a shape is a true least case. The paper gives a sharp rule for when the flat slice wins. It adds one more known case to a hard field of shape proofs.
arxiv-2601-06701:
Poushali Sengupta and co-authors propose the Correlation Impact Ratio for AI explainability in 2026. Complex AI systems predict better but often lack transparency, they note. That limits trustworthiness, interpretability, and safer deployments of models.

Common post-hoc explainers include LIME, SHAP, HSIC, and SAGE. They are model-agnostic but restricted in one significant regard. They tend to misrank correlated features, the authors argue. They also require costly perturbations that will not scale for high-dimensional data. A correlation-aware ratio aims to rank features more honestly instead. Correlated features are the rule in real data, not the exception. Their method could change which features doctors or bankers see first. Explainability readers get a direct answer to a known failure mode.
arxiv-2601-06801: Shujian Gao and four co-authors look at how large language models learn from rewards they can check. Their 2026 arXiv paper is called Thinking with Deltas. It deals with models that must both see an image and think about it. In past work, rewards based on text alone can push a model to skip the image and guess from words. The team sets out a new policy that ties the reward to what the model sees. The aim is to keep sight and thought linked as the model learns.
arxiv-2601-07101:
Arjun Vijaywargiya and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with inverse problems for history-enriched linear model reduction. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Standard projection-based model reduction for dynamical systems incurs closure error because it only accounts for instantaneous dependence on the resolved state.

From the Mori-Zwanzig (MZ) perspective, projecting the full dynamics onto a low-dimensional resolved subspace induces additional noise and memory terms arising. From the dynamics of the unresolved component in the orthogonal complement. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07601:
Adam Connolly, Steven Herbert, and Julien Sorci propose a quantum algorithm for estimating a key property of Markov chains. The spectral gap measures how fast a Markov chain settles to its steady state. It controls mixing times in sampling, simulation, and many algorithms. Their 2026 preprint claims performance that is quasi-optimal, meaning optimal up to small logarithmic factors.

The guarantee covers the number of vertices for all parameter settings. It also covers the reciprocal of the spectral gap itself, under a condition on the allowed relative error. That condition is that the error tolerance sits above a critical value. Near-optimal quantum algorithms matter because spectral gaps are costly to compute classically for large chains. The work speaks to quantum computing scholars building provable speedups.
arxiv-2601-07701:
Ziwen Zhuang and colleagues unite two styles of humanoid control to achieve whole-body parkour. One style, perceptive locomotion, handles terrain well but sticks to stepping gaits. The other, general motion tracking, copies complex skills but ignores the surroundings. Their 2026 preprint, Deep Whole-body Parkour, merges the two. The goal is a robot that sees terrain and still uses its whole body.

Parkour moves like jumps, climbs, and vaults need arms, torso, and legs together. Terrain awareness decides where those moves can land safely. Combining perception with full motion skills is a step toward robots that move through cluttered spaces like people do. The work should interest roboticists building humanoids for real environments. It frames parkour as a test of integrated control, not a stunt.
arxiv-2601-08001:
Qinying Chen, Arnab Roy, and Tobin A. Driscoll learn operators that model tear film breakup on the eye. Tear film breakup drives much of dry eye disease. Estimating film thickness and osmolarity from fluorescence imaging usually requires solving expensive inverse problems. The authors propose an operator learning framework to replace those solvers. Neural operators are trained on simulated tear film dynamics. Their 2026 preprint presents the approach.

A trained neural operator evaluates in a fraction of the time of a traditional solver. Fast inversion could bring quantitative tear analysis into clinics. Simulations supply the training data, so the physics stays in charge of ground truth. The method targets the two quantities clinicians most want from an image. The paper serves biomedical engineers and eye scholars. It applies a modern learning method to a small but common clinical problem.
arxiv-2601-08101: Fred Jegerlehner reviews what lepton magnetic moments tell us about fundamental physics. His 2026 arXiv paper was presented at the Matter to the Deepest conference in 2025. The Fermilab muon g-2 result matched the 2004 Brookhaven result with four times better precision. That match sharpened the challenge to the Standard Model of particle physics. On the theory side, lattice QCD calculations of hadronic vacuum polarization have advanced fast. Jegerlehner weighs experiment and theory together for readers tracking this long-running tension.
arxiv-2601-08201: Kaito Totsuka and co-authors probe nodal superconductivity in UTe2 with field-angle-resolved specific heat. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a clean single crystal with a transition temperature of 2.1 kelvin. The crystal also shows a low residual electronic specific heat, a sign of sample quality. UTe2 is a spin-triplet superconductor, a rare class with unconventional pairing. Rotating the magnetic field while measuring heat capacity reveals where gap nodes sit. Those nodes fingerprint the pairing state, helping physicists decide which theory of UTe2 is right.
arxiv-2601-08401:
Ajo Babu George, Pranav S., and Kunal Agarwal build an explainable system for pericoronitis checks on dental X-rays. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses panoramic radiographs, the wide scans dentists take of the full mouth. Diagnosing inflammation around wisdom teeth on these scans is hard for automated tools.

The pipeline runs in two stages. Stage one uses YOLOv8 to detect third molars and classify their positions and angles by Winter's classification. Later stages add pathological classification plus interpretability outputs. An explainable result lets dentists check the system's reasoning before acting. The work targets clinics that need decision support they can audit, not a bare label.
arxiv-2601-08501: Emel Altas and Bayram Tekin argue that geometry itself is wavy. Their 2026 arXiv paper shows curvature obeys a covariant quasilinear wave equation at the purely geometric level. No specific gravity theory needs to be chosen first. In Riemannian geometry with the Levi-Civita connection, the Riemann tensor satisfies such a wave equation. The right side is quadratic in the curvature itself. The authors extend the picture to generic affine connections. The result reframes curvature as a propagating field in its own right.
arxiv-2601-08801:
Pranav Agarwal and three co-authors study when a species in a chem net dies out for good. A chem net is a set of steps where stuff turns into new stuff. Such nets model cells, air, and lab tanks. To die out here means the count of a type falls to zero and stays there.

The team sets two grades of death. Weak death means the count tends to zero in time. Strong death means it hits zero in a set time span. They tie both grades to the shape of the net. Tools from smooth math, such as guide sums that can only fall, do much of the work. A reader gets firm tests for when a net must lose a type.
arxiv-2601-08901:
Yuexi Shen and three co-authors help place a new science idea in a vast field of old work. A new idea must be shown as new, yet tied to what came past. With paper counts in the millions, no one can read all near work by hand. Staff may miss the key old paper that sits close to their claim.

The team splits an idea into parts that can be placed on a map of past work. Each part can then be matched to near old ideas. Gaps on the map show where the new idea stands apart. A reader who plans or grades research gets a tool for a hard first step. It makes the place of a new claim clear at a glance.
arxiv-2601-09001:
Pedro Memoli Buffa and Luciano Del Corro hunt for a cheap sign that tells where a chat model is weak. Firms that run such models face drift. New asks come in, old skills fade, and scores slip in one zone while they hold in a next. Full tests on all zones cost much and lag the drift by weeks.

The pair test a sign that is free at run time. It is the spread, or entropy, of the model's own picks as it writes. High spread may flag a zone where the model oft errs. They test this on school science asks as traffic shifts. A reader who runs AI gets a watch tool that needs no new marks. It may point fix work to the zone that needs it most.
arxiv-2601-09101:
Pedro Henrique Barboza Rossetto, Vanessa Carvalho de Andrade, and Daniel Muller study wild paths in a class of wave shaped space times. Such spaces hold a wave that runs at light speed. A path in them acts like a bit in a two way pull field. The pull here is set by a power rule, from third to tenth power.

They look for Wada boundaries in those paths. A Wada edge is one where three or more fates meet at each point of the edge. A path near it can end in any fate with a slight nudge. A reader in chaos work gets a map of where such wild edges live in wave spaces.
arxiv-2601-09201:
Maithri K and three co-authors study key traits of items in finite fields, and of the rules that make them. A finite field is a set with a fixed count of items, yet with full add and times rules. An item can be prime like, in that its powers span the set. It can be normal, in that its shifts span the set as a base.

Traits set for items can be set for rules too. Order for a rule tells how its roots act. The team proves traits of rules that are part prime or part normal. A reader in field work gets new links in a zoo of such items, used in codes and crypto.
arxiv-2601-09301:
Geng Liu and Masahito Hayashi give a check tool for a loop method in quantum facts work. The method, called QAB, builds up a best guess step by step with no slope sums. It is strong, but its past proofs rest on needs that are hard to test for a real task. A user may run it with no proof that it will settle true in their case.

Their frame checks a run past the fact. Give it the steps the run took, and it tells if those steps prove a near best end. That turns a hope into a check. A reader who runs QAB gets a seal they can test, case by case, not a broad claim.
arxiv-2601-09401:
G. Piccinini and five co-authors show how to weigh distant companions that orbit other stars. Their 2026 arXiv paper joins radial velocity data with astrometry from the Hipparcos and Gaia missions. Radial velocity surveys find long-period companions by watching a star wobble over many years.

A wobble alone gives only a lower bound on the companion's mass. Adding proper motion anomalies, small shifts in how the star moves across the sky, pins down the orbit's tilt. With the tilt known, the true mass follows. The method sharpens the line between giant planets and brown dwarfs in long-period systems.
arxiv-2601-09501:
Yubo Yuan, Ziye Zhu, Jiaming Hu, and Wenbin Li compute how charge carriers move in a promising layered semiconductor. Their 2026 arXiv paper is an ab initio study of carrier mobility in Bi2O2Se. The material is known for strong performance and good stability.

Experiments have mapped transport in this material across many doping levels, for both electron and hole conduction. A full theory of those results has lagged behind. The authors build that theory from first principles, with no fitted parameters. Knowing what limits mobility points to ways of making faster, cooler devices from the material.
arxiv-2601-09601:
Emmanuele Barberi, Felice Sfravara, and Filippo Cucinotta align pairs of 3D point clouds with a focus on the scoring metric. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents a method called IDEM, for iterative differential entropy minimization. Point cloud registration, lining up two scans of the same scene, is a core task in computer vision.

Common methods judge alignment by Euclidean distances and minimize scores such as root mean square error. The choice of metric shapes how robust the fit is to noise and outliers. IDEM instead works with differential entropy as its guide. A better metric could steady registration for scanning, robotics, and inspection tasks.
arxiv-2601-09701:
Fahimeh Orvati Nia, Shima Salehi, and Joshua Peeples test a hybrid network for spotting odd electricity use. Their 2026 arXiv paper evaluates a GAN-LSTM model for smart meter anomaly detection. Smart meters stream fine-grained consumption data that can improve monitoring and decisions in power systems.

Spotting anomalies in that stream is hard: usage is nonlinear, nonstationary, and varies across buildings and conditions. A GAN learns what normal use looks like while an LSTM tracks its rhythm over time. The authors judge how well the pairing works in practice. Reliable anomaly flags help utilities catch faults, theft, and failing equipment early.
arxiv-2601-09901:
Joshua Perlmutter works on a shape test for groups built from graphs. In curved spaces, paths that stay near the best route have a local to global trait. Short near best bits join into long near best paths. The Morse form of this trait fits a wider set of spaces.

Perlmutter shows that graph products keep this trait. If each part group has it, the joined group has it too. His proof grows a key max step from past work on ranked groups. The groups at hand have clean bins that make the step work. The result adds a firm case to the map of these traits.
arxiv-2601-10201:
Jiarui Yao, Ruida Wang, and Tong Zhang reward each step of a model's thought, not just the end. Most past work grades the full chain at the end. That gives a weak guide for where a chain went wrong. Step grades can guide more, but past plans were slow.

Some step plans need tree search or a whole new grade model. The team made Process Reward Learning, a leaner path. It learns step grades in the train run itself. The aim is a model that reasons more well. It should also reach past its old bounds, not just match them.
arxiv-2601-10601:
Reiko Liu and Wen-Jie Ma work in celestial holography, a program that recasts gravity in flat space as a theory on the sky at infinity. Soft current algebras are known to capture the low-energy, infrared side of scattering there. But no algebra had described the finite-energy side. The authors set out to close that gap.

They uncover an infinite-dimensional hard current algebra that encodes finite-energy scattering. It implies new Ward identities, rules that any scattering result must obey. The soft algebras turn out to arise from the hard ones, not to stand apart. The work gives the holography program a single frame that covers both soft and hard physics.
arxiv-2601-10701:
Chun Hei Michael Shiu and Chih Wei Ling design a federated learning scheme that saves bandwidth and bends to privacy needs. Federated learning lets many parties train one model together without pooling raw data. That fits rules that keep data in place. Two pain points remain: the cost of constant messages, and the level of privacy each party demands.

The authors propose a mechanism that is both communication-efficient and privacy-adaptable. They back it with a convergence analysis, a proof that the training still settles to a good model. Such proofs matter when methods leave the lab. The work targets hospitals, banks, and other groups that must learn together while keeping data home.
arxiv-2601-10901:
Honglian Wang, Sijing Tu, Lutz Oettershagen, and Aristides Gionis study streaming submodular maximization with on-demand requests. The setting mirrors news recommendation sites. Users can arrive at any time. At each visit, the site must show up to k news items, chosen from a stream it cannot store whole. Picks must be diverse yet relevant, the hallmark of submodular goals.

The on-demand twist breaks the usual one-pass setup: queries come when users come, not when the stream ends. Algorithms must keep a compact summary ready at all times. The work formalizes this problem and its trade-offs. It serves platform designers who must answer instantly from endless content with bounded memory.
arxiv-2601-11201:
Jan Rosenzweig writes on finance data in this 2026 preprint. Price series move on more than one clock at once. Fast swings mix with slow drifts in the same stream. He sets out a way to split those layers apart in a clean way.

His test for the split uses two traits of the data. One is how spread out the moves are. The other is how the tails of moves behave over time. He frames both tests as eigenvalue problems, a standard math form. The split finds slow parts and fast parts in returns and prices. Tests use exchange rates, stock funds, and bond yields to show its use.
arxiv-2601-11301:
A local tool for video segmentation is the subject of this 2026 preprint. The authors are not named in the record held here. The tool is called SAMannot and builds on SAM2. It lets users mark objects in video by interaction.

Workflows for fine video masks face a three-way bind today. Hand curation is slow and eats skilled time. Paid platforms cost much and hold the data. Cloud tools raise privacy risks for raw footage. SAMannot runs on the user's own machine, fully local. It is open-source and built to use memory with care. Research teams keep their video private and their costs down. That mix serves labs that mask much video by hand.
arxiv-2601-11501:
Frederik Walter, Maria Abu-Sini, Nils Weinhardt, and Antonia Wachter-Zeh code data for torn DNA. Their 2026 preprint treats DNA decay as a torn paper channel. DNA can store data for the long term in archives. Strands decay over time, and codes must survive that decay.

The channel model has two stages of damage in sequence. First, noise flips bits by substitution at random. Then the strand breaks into unordered, noisy substrings. Coders get a bag of torn scraps, like a ripped page. Schemes must rebuild the message from those scraps alone. The team designs coding schemes for that double damage. Sound codes are a must for DNA archives to work.
arxiv-2601-11601:
Daniil Bargman, Francesca Medda, and Akash Sedai Sharma rebuild the Phillips curve. Their 2026 preprint adds latent variables to the classic model. The Phillips curve links inflation to slack in the economy. Its use for medium-term inflation forecasts is re-examined here.

The team tests a latent variable Phillips curve hypothesis. They generate 3,968 random factor combinations for the test. US core PCE inflation is the data in scope. The window runs from early 1983 to early 2025. Latent models beat traditional ones six to eight quarters out. They also stand a better chance against a univariate benchmark. Hidden factors may carry the curve's lost signal.
arxiv-2601-11701:
Abhinav Chakraborty, Yuetian Luo, and Rina Foygel Barber weigh stability against accuracy. Their 2026 preprint deals with trade-offs in statistical estimation. Algorithmic stability measures how outputs react to data changes. Small changes in training data should not swing results wildly.

Stability is central to learning theory for good reason. It shapes generalization to new data from a sample. It also shapes robustness and replicability of findings. Many notions of stability have been proposed over time. Each fits a different learning setting in the literature. The team studies the trade-off with estimation accuracy. A stabler method may pay for calm with bias. Knowing that price helps statisticians choose wisely.
arxiv-2601-11801:
Nitish Sontakke, K. Niranjan Kumar, and Sehoon Ha build a tool that designs robots with the help of vision language models. Robot design is slow work by hand. A design must meet user needs, move in the right way, and look right, all at once.

Most past tools are rule based and need a set grammar of parts. Their tool, named RobotDesignGPT in the work, uses a model that reads both text and images. Such a tool could let non-experts sketch a robot brief and get a first design fast. Human skill would then refine the result.
arxiv-2601-12301:
Mingrui Liu, Sixiao Zhang, and Cheng Long improve sequential recommendation, which predicts a user's next pick from past acts. Most systems give each item one embedding vector. Models then merge those vectors into a sequence trait for user intent.

One vector per item can hide its many facets. Their facet-aware multi-head mixture model gives items a richer form. Text-enhanced pre-training adds item sense from words. Richer items could yield picks that fit user taste with more nuance.  Facet traits may also help cold start items a lot.  One trait per item is the weak point the new model aims to fix.
arxiv-2601-12601:
Metin Can Aydemir and Muhammet Boran improve a result in analytic number theory about a divisor function. The function d3 counts ways to write a number as a product of three factors. They study how its values spread across prime arithmetic progressions on average. The key yardstick is the exponent of distribution, a measure of how far the average stays well behaved.

Their title claims an improved exponent for this function. A higher exponent means the good average holds for larger moduli. Results of this type feed sieve methods, a core engine for prime number results. Even small gains in an exponent can unlock new theorems downstream. The work states its claims in the uniform form that sieve users need.
arxiv-2601-12801: Pranali Roy Chowdhury and four co authors, based largely at the University of Alberta, study how pollutants change fish. Their focus is pigmentation, the color patterns on fish bodies. They also track spatial patterns, how fish arrange and move in their habitat. Pigment shifts can signal stress or harm from contamination in the water.
arxiv-2601-13001:
Wenrui Yu, Jaron Skovsted Gundersen, and Richard Heusdens ask when shared sums can stay private. Their focus is on systems where many nodes each hold data and a joint result must be found. They study the case where the joint step is not a plain sum but a curved, nonlinear rule.

For plain sums, good tools can often hold back leaks well. For curved rules, the authors argue, the shape of the rule itself sets hard caps. Those caps bind even when the joint result must be exact. They seek the best such caps that pure theory allows. The work maps what privacy can and cannot promise in this setting.
arxiv-2601-13501:
Youness Diouane models how a mass shooter's fate sways the fate of the next such shooter in the United States. The team uses data from 1966 to 2024. Each case is tagged by if the actor died at the scene or lived past the act.

Their tool is a bivariate Hawkes process. Such a process lets each past event lift the rate of like events to come. With two fates as two streams, the model can say if a death at the scene lifts the odds the next actor dies too. Such a fate to fate spread, if real, bears on press guides and threat work. The model gives that ask a firm form.
arxiv-2601-13601:
Zhiwen Zhou and co-authors report lab work on tiny paired states of charge in thin films in 2026. These pairs, called indirect excitons, form in a stack of two crystal sheets, molybdenum selenide and tungsten selenide. The team placed the stack in strong magnetic fields, up to eight tesla. They tracked how the pairs move across the stack.

The group found that the pairs can travel long ranges in these fields. They also found long-range spin flow carried by the pairs. Spin is a small magnetic trait of each pair. Such results matter for new devices that move spin, not just charge, to carry signals.
arxiv-2601-13701:
Frédéric Marin and a large team report new polarization data on the active galaxy MCG-05-23-16 in 2026. They used the IXPE space telescope for its third look at this object. They also took optical spectro-polarimetry with the Very Large Telescope. Older data in ultraviolet, optical, and near-infrared light join the set.

Polarization shows how light waves align, which hints at the shape of gas near a black hole. The combined data challenge the object's Seyfert-1.9 class label. Class labels guide how teams read all data on a galaxy. A wrong label can skew years of work on its core.
arxiv-2601-14001:
Niall McGuire and Yashar Moshfeghi push brain-based search a step further with heard text in 2026. Forming a query from an internal need is hard in all search paradigms. Cognitive complexity and physical impairments both block typing or speaking a query. Brain Passage Retrieval maps EEG signals straight to passage representations.

Their Auditory Brain Passage Retrieval adds cross-sensory EEG training. EEG records electric signals from the brain through the scalp. The path skips intermediate text translation on the way to results. Such tools could give people with severe impairments a direct line to information.
arxiv-2601-14101:
Emily Kim, Allen Wu, and Jessica Hodgins help action recognition work from new camera angles in 2026. Human action recognition has made significant progress in recent years. Generalizing to diverse viewpoints remains a challenge, though. Most datasets are captured from ground-level perspectives.

Models trained on ground views struggle to transfer to aerial views. The team uses curriculum-based strategies for efficient cross-domain action recognition. A curriculum orders training from easy to hard cases. Drones and security cameras need models that read actions from above. A step-by-step plan keeps the task cheap to run. It also lets small labs train strong models with less data than a brute-force run.
arxiv-2601-14201:
Amy de Castro and Hyesuk Lee split a coupled fluid and porous solid problem into parts in 2026. The Stokes-Biot system models fluid flow interacting with a poroelastic structure. Their partitioned method starts from the monolithic formulation of the system. Lagrange multipliers enforce the interface conditions between fluid and solid.

The monolithic system is discretized using finite elements, with convergence established. A Schur complement algorithm decouples the subproblems at each time step. An efficient preconditioner keeps the split solves fast. Decoupled solves let teams use their best fluid and solid codes side by side. Each part can be solved with the tool that fits it best. That is the main gain of the split for day-to-day use.
arxiv-2601-14801:
Natsuki Terano and eight co-authors study a supernova remnant and a gamma-ray binary in this 2026 paper. The remnant is G284.3-1.8. It shows a radio shell and thermal X-ray emission. Located near its center is the gamma-ray binary 1FGL J1018.6-5856. That central placement raises the question the paper sets out to test. Whether the two systems are physically associated is not clear yet.

The team ran X-ray spectroscopy with the Suzaku satellite. Their abstract states that the spectra reveal a link between the remnant and the binary, though the abstract shown here ends before the full finding is stated. Readers get an X-ray test of whether a dead star's shell and a gamma-ray pair share one origin.
arxiv-2601-15001:
Rainer Backofen and Axel Voigt study a mix of two fluids, one active and one passive. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with phase separation, where the mix splits into regions of each fluid. The pattern that forms is mostly a two-way web, called bicontinuous.

The authors run two-dimensional simulations of the mix. The web that forms is not symmetric in shape or in how it links up. They show that flows the active region makes on its own can explain the full skew. No outside force is needed to break the symmetry.
arxiv-2601-15101:
Patrick Navez, Valentina Di Meo, and a large team study a network of superconducting qubits in a shared resonator. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with these qubit networks as a device for quantum work. The resonator that holds them loses very little energy.

That setup can show collective quantum dynamics at a large scale. It can also sharpen detectors of microwave photons a great deal. The paper treats Bose condensation in the network, where many qubits act as one. It also treats Bogoliubov excitation, the sound-like ripples of that shared state.
arxiv-2601-15301:
Jivnesh Sandhan, Harshit Jaiswal, Fei Cheng, and Yugo Murawaki ask whether AI text detectors can be trusted. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the tools meant to spot machine-written text. Demand for them has grown with the rapid spread of language models.

Yet detectors often fail outside tidy benchmarks. The authors evaluate the two dominant paradigms: training-free methods and supervised ones. Both prove brittle under distribution shift. New generators and even simple style changes can fool them. The sobering results warn against leaning too hard on these brittle detector scores in court or class.
arxiv-2601-15401:
Sajjad Akherati and Xinmiao Zhang extend a basic operation of encrypted computing. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with homomorphic encryption, a tool that lets math run on locked data. The data stays sealed while the sums are done. This serves machine learning, medical tests, and finance, where raw data must stay private and safe.

In popular schemes, ciphertext multiplication is defined for two inputs only. Many applications need to multiply several inputs at once. The authors tackle multi-input ciphertext multiplication. Their work aims to make that wider product a native operation, so programs that run on locked data need fewer clumsy workarounds in the end.
arxiv-2601-15601:
Amita Malik and Rishabh Sarma extend a line of partition theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. Partitions write a number as a sum of parts. Recent work by Andrews and Bachraoui studied partitions whose smallest part repeats exactly k times. The remaining parts in those partitions are distinct. Generating functions for them turned out to be linear combinations of q-Pochhammer symbols. Polynomial coefficients in q complete those formulas.

Malik and Sarma move the idea to overpartitions. In an overpartition, the first copy of a part may be overlined. Their focus is partitions with a repeated smallest non-overlined part. Such extensions test whether neat formulas survive richer counting rules. Partition theory thrives on this pattern. A small twist in the rules often yields deep new identities.
arxiv-2601-16201:
A maths note sets out broad Bassian modules over a class of prime rings. The 2026 preprint deals with rings of the Dedekind type that are not prime in the plain sense. A module counts as broad Bassian by a test with maps in. If a map sends the module in to a part of it, a split must hold. That split means the left part is a clean part of the whole.

The note asks which modules pass that test on such rings. Tests of this kind sort modules by how they split. Clean splits ease work with sums of modules. The work sits in pure ring and module theory. It builds on the known Bassian case with a wider test.
arxiv-2601-16701:
Przemysław Berk and Łukasz Kotlewski study how paths in a math system come back or drift off. Their systems swap chunks of a line in a set dance. A weight rule then bends each step's path. Some such rules make paths come back oft. Others make paths fade and not return. Their 2026 preprint proves a split of this sort.

For a broad class of weights, the paths tend to fade. The weight blows up near the ends of the line. That blow-up drives the drift in most cases. Sharp proofs of this sort test our grip on wild systems. They also feed work on flows, waves, and chance walks.
arxiv-2601-16801:
Ben Groom and a large team of co-authors bring wild life loss into state budgets. Species keep dying off due to human acts. Yet state spend plans oft price that loss at nil. Their 2026 preprint sets out a way to price it fair. The way starts from goals a state sets for wild life.

Costs to hit those goals then set the price tag. This flips the usual path, which asks what folks would pay. Goal-based prices can slot into real spend checks. That slot may save funds for woods, seas, and fields. It also makes loss in kind show up in pounds.
arxiv-2601-17101:
Xiaodong Jiang races a beam of paired hydrogen ions in big rings. The beam holds H2+ ions, each a pair bound as one. A past run pushed such a beam in a small ring. That run reached a set speed with clear success. His 2026 preprint asks if the big RHIC ring can push it far more. The goal is one hundred GeV per unit.

The ask is time-pressed, since RHIC nears shut-down. A yes would open rare tests with such beams. A no would spare teams a vain push. Paired-ion beams act unlike lone proton beams in rings. Firm calls here guide the ring's last runs.
arxiv-2601-17401:
Dušan Dragutinović studies links between number sequences and partitions. He looks at final types, certain non-decreasing integer sequences. Each such sequence pairs with partitions in a natural way. From that link, he proves an identity for n-nacci numbers. Those numbers extend the Fibonacci rule to longer sums. The identity writes them as sums of products of binomial coefficients.

The sums run over the partitions tied to final types. The result extends a classical identity to the full family. Such identities help counters check formulas in two ways at once. They also show hidden order in fast-growing sequences. Pure counters gain a new bridge between sequences and splits.
arxiv-2601-17601:
Fangping Lan, Abdullah Aljebreen, and Eduard Dragut study why people post links on social media. Links bridge platforms and the wider web. On Twitter, now X, about one in five tweets holds at least one URL. That rate shows how central links are to information flow. The authors build an intent taxonomy for link sharing.

Knowing intent helps sort news, ads, spam, and self-promotion. Platforms can rank and moderate with more care. Researchers can track how claims spread across sites. A taxonomy turns a mass of links into named motives. That clarity aids studies of influence and misinformation. It also helps users read their own feeds with sharper eyes.
arxiv-2601-17801:
Hongfu Zhang and Hui Tang test whether quantum methods can help control the flow of fluids. Their 2026 preprint joins quantum machine learning with reinforcement learning. Flow control is hard because fluid motion is both high in dimension and strongly nonlinear. Small inputs can have large and hard-to-guess effects. Classical methods strain under that load.

Quantum computing has shown an edge over classical computing on some tasks. The authors build on that hope and train a quantum reinforcement learning setup for flow control. In such a setup, an agent learns by trial and reward which actions calm or steer the flow. The study adds a new data point on where quantum tools may pay off.
arxiv-2601-18001:
Aqsa Yousaf, Sint Sint Win, Megan Coffee, and Habeeb Olufowobi build an explainable tool for finding parasites in blood samples. Their 2026 preprint presents MorphXAI. Parasitic infections remain a heavy health burden, above all in low-resource settings. Diagnosis there leans on slow hand checks of blood smears by scarce experts. Deep learning can spot parasites well, but doctors cannot use a tool they cannot interrogate.

MorphXAI adds morphological analysis, the study of the parasite's shape and form, to the detection. Explanations tied to shape features are ones a clinician can judge. That makes the tool's calls easier to trust and to challenge. The work aims at labs where expert time is the scarcest resource.
arxiv-2601-18901:
Christopher Kissling, Elena Merdjanovska, and Alan Akbik ask if a language model knows when its own facts are firm and when they are frail. Tests of fact stock in such models grade how oft the model's first call is right. That grade skips a key trait: does the model put high trust on its right calls and low trust on its wrong ones? A model that can't tell is a risk in use, since users lean on its tone of trust.

The team grade both the calls and the trust that rides with them. They use fact pairs of the form this links to that, a clean test of stored facts. A model that knows its own gaps could flag the facts it should not be asked to state. Such self-ware tools could make fact use safer in search and in school.
arxiv-2601-19001:
Haozheng Luo and six co-authors speed up the long reasoning chains of language models. Models that think step by step often wander down paths that add words but not value. The team calls the stray steps reasoning outliers and aims to prune them with a method named FROST.

FROST reads the model's own attention weights to spot which paths count and which do not. Cutting the weak paths leaves shorter chains that the authors find more reliable as well. Shorter, cleaner reasoning saves compute and may cut the slips that long chains invite along the way.
arxiv-2601-20201:
Sherry H. F. Yan works on permutation statistics, a classic topic in enumerative combinatorics that counts patterns in arrangements. In her study of the genus zeta function, Denert found a new Mahonian statistic for permutations, later called Denert's statistic by Foata and Zeilberger. Mahonian statistics are those that share the same count distribution as inversions.

The paper gives further refinements of Euler-Mahonian statistics for multipermutations, where entries may repeat. Refined counts track several statistics at once and still match known distributions. Such results deepen the map of how permutation patterns behave, a theory with links to sorting, probability, and algebra.
arxiv-2601-20601:
Zhuonan Wang and seven colleagues present CLEAR-Mamba, a method for classifying eye angiography across multiple image sequences. Medical image classification supports early detection, treatment planning, and prognosis. In eye care, fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography reveal blood flow and lesion structure that plain fundus photos cannot capture.

Using several sequences at once is harder: the scans arrive in series and must be read together. CLEAR-Mamba aims at accuracy, adaptability, and trustworthiness in that setting. In real clinics, the two scan types are often read side by side. A tool that reads them as one case fits that habit well. Reliable classification of retinal scans could speed up diagnosis of diseases that threaten sight.
arxiv-2601-21101:
Shaheda Begum Shaik and five co-authors measure how fast a comet's tail regrows after solar storms tear it off. Their 2026 paper studies comet C/2023 P1, called Nishimura. The Solar Orbiter imager watched the comet in September 2023. In that window, the comet's ion tail shifted without pause. It suffered four tail disconnection events. Each matched the passage of a coronal mass ejection.

A disconnection event severs the ion tail from the comet's head. The tail then regrows as the solar wind reshapes it. This is the first quantitative study of that regrowth. Timing it measures how comet plasma couples to the solar wind. Such events turn comets into free probes of solar storms. The paper gives space weather science a clean, counted case.
arxiv-2601-21401:
Ferdinand Buchner, David Jobst, Annette Möller, and Claudia Czado improve forecasts of wind as a full vector. Weather services run ensembles to capture forecast uncertainty. Those raw forecasts still carry steady biases and spread errors, so statistical fixes are applied afterward.

Wind has two linked parts, speed in each compass direction, and the parts must be fixed together. New methods build the link between the parts into the model itself. A joint fix gives forecasters honest odds for both direction and strength at once. That matters for aviation, shipping, and wind power, where the pair decides the risk.
arxiv-2601-21601:
Hoyeon Chang, Bálint Mucsányi, and Seong Joon Oh test whether gradient updates keep a network's logic coherent. Networks learn by small first-order steps in their parameters. It is often assumed that a small local step spreads sensibly to all its logical consequences.

The authors name that premise the linear propagation assumption and probe its limits. Using relation algebra, they track three basic operations: negation, converse, and composition of relations. The study shows where the premise breaks down as changes propagate. Knowing those limits helps explain odd failures where a model learns a fact but misses its obvious flip side.
arxiv-2601-21801:
Jing Yang, Satoya Imai, and Luca Pezzè address a central open problem in quantum sensing. When several unknown values must be measured at once, theory gives a best possible precision, called the multiparameter quantum Cramér-Rao bound. The hard question is when that bound can actually be reached with realistic single-copy measurements.

The authors establish an equivalence. The bound can be saturated exactly under one condition. A set of traceless operators tied to the model must be made hollow at the same time. Their 2026 preprint turns a vague feasibility question into a concrete geometric test. Quantum sensors that measure several fields at once, from magnetometers to imaging devices, stand to benefit from knowing when perfection is even possible.
arxiv-2601-22201:
Gabriela Juncosa and co-authors test the wisdom of crowds in content moderation. Platforms facing misinformation have adopted community-based systems: Community Notes on X, Footnotes on TikTok, and community features on Facebook. The hope is that collective intelligence beats any single moderator or algorithm.

The team's 2026 preprint finds that benefit limited by overt political factors. When content is politically charged, the crowd's judgment bends with the politics of the raters and readers. That finding matters for platform design today: community moderation still helps. But its limits need engineering around, not wishful thinking, especially during elections and crises when accuracy carries the highest stakes.
arxiv-2601-22701:
Emilien Biré, María Santos, and Kai Yuan rank a vision-language agent's next moves with a learned value score. Such agents run web and system tasks on their own. Their 2026 preprint notes that the base models adapt poorly to fast-changing screens, and retraining for each shift is dear.

Best-of-Q scores each candidate act at run time and picks the best, with no new training. A good ranker can rescue a weak base model. It can also cut wasted clicks in live tasks. The work is a light add-on with a clear job. It steers at the moment of choice.
arxiv-2601-22801:
Ömer Veysel Çağatan and three co-authors propose a new way to train large language models with rewards. The standard methods clip, or cap, each update to keep training stable. At large scale, clipping can stall learning, invite reward hacking, and make training shaky.

Their method, CFPO, drops clipping and uses a smooth penalty based on total variation distance instead. The penalty has no hard edges, so updates stay stable but never fully flat. They test it on reasoning and alignment tasks, two core uses of reward-based training.
arxiv-2601-23001:
Afrozah Nadeem and three co-authors measure political bias in language models across many languages. These models shape public discussion worldwide, so fairness and neutrality matter. Earlier work focused mostly on rich, Western languages, leaving cross-language consistency and safe fixes little studied.

The study both evaluates ideology in multilingual models and tests ways to steer it after training. A model that leans one way in English and another way elsewhere is hard to govern. Shared measures and gentle steering tools help builders keep global systems even-handed. Cross-lingual consistency is a central test, since a fair system should not change its leanings when the language changes.
arxiv-2601-23101:
Therese Biedl and Dinis Vitorino answer a question about order among bipartite graphs. A bipartite minor relation ranks these two-sided graphs in a way akin to the classic minor relation. Chudnovsky and co-authors had asked whether that ranking is a well-order, with no endless descending chains.

The answer is no: the authors give an endless family of highly connected bipartite graphs, none comparable to another. A negative answer closes one path in graph structure theory. It also shows bipartite minors behave quite differently from ordinary minors. The counterexample family is two-connected throughout, so the failure of well-ordering cannot be blamed on fragile, barely linked graphs.
arxiv-2601-23201:
Darshan Thaker and four co-authors sharpen medical images with scale-cascaded diffusion models. Diffusion models act as strong priors for inverse problems like super-resolution, which rebuilds fine detail from coarse scans. Standard approaches train the prior at a single scale, ignoring the layered scale structure of images.

Their cascade uses several scales in sequence, so coarse anatomy guides finer detail. That ordering matches how medical images are actually structured. Sharper scans from lower-dose or faster acquisitions would help patients and clinics alike. Hierarchical scale structure is the untapped signal, since anatomy organizes itself from whole organs down to fine tissue.

arxiv-2605-08801: Forecasting traffic from data is easy to overdo: a model can memorize yesterday's jams instead of learning patterns that hold tomorrow. Peter Vanya, Katarína Šimková, and Rastislav Farkaš build data-driven transport models with built-in guards against overfitting, so the predictions stay honest on unseen days. arxiv-2605-09201: STT-MRAM stores bits in the magnetization of tiny magnets, flipped by spin-polarized currents. Afan Terko, George Lertzman-Lepofsky, Dieter Suess, and others study magnetization alignment in these memories. The 2026 paper is device physics for the next generation of RAM.

arxiv-2605-09401: Chimera states — networks where order and chaos coexist — are as beautiful as they are baffling. Rommel Tchinda Djeudjo, Riccardo Muolo, Thierry Njougouo, and others classify them with Fourier analysis and unsupervised learning. The 2026 paper taxonomizes the half-ordered world of coupled oscillators.
arxiv-2605-09501: Active nematics — swirling fluids of self-driven rods, like bacterial soups — go unstable in beautiful patterns. I.K. Joseph, A.J.H. Houston, K.N. Kowal, and N.J. Mottram study how an orienting field steers that instability and selects the modes. The 2026 paper is soft-matter physics on living liquid crystals.
arxiv-2605-09701: Self-driving cars must imagine what happens next — pedestrians stepping out, cars swerving, sudden stops. Yufeng Hong, Xiaotian Zhou, Yingyan Li, and others build DriveFuture: future-aware latent world models for autonomous driving. The 2026 paper gives robot drivers an imagination.
