Entries here handle Egypt, the Exodus, the Gospels, Israel's history, and the geography of the holy land. Long signed articles argue their cases with full notes and sources. The editors print rival views where the experts split. Together with the other volumes, this made the most advanced Bible reference of its time, still consulted for its learning.
english-act-of-settlement-1701:
Parliament passed the Act of Settlement in 1701 to decide who would inherit the English throne. The law looked past Catholic heirs and settled the crown on Sophia of Hanover and her Protestant descendants. It also set conditions that future monarchs would have to accept.

Beyond the succession, the act protects judges by letting them serve during good behavior, not royal pleasure. It limits pardons in impeachment cases and bars monarchs from leaving the realm without consent. Together, these clauses strengthened Parliament against the crown. The act still shapes the British monarchy and its rules of succession today.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-01: The first volume of Montaigne's Essays opens his famous self-portrait. The French thinker writes of habit, fear, friendship, and the self. His plain, curious style made the essay what it is. Four centuries old and still fresh.
europmc-pmc10100201: Liu and Wang review how extracellular vesicles, tiny parcels released by cells, carry messages between cells and how that traffic is regulated. The review covers how vesicles form, what cargo they load, and how target cells take them in. It shows why these parcels matter for health, disease, and new treatments.
europmc-pmc10291001:
Hu and colleagues review spinal cord injury in a 2023 paper, covering its molecular mechanisms and treatment options. A spinal cord injury can paralyze and disable for life, and full repair remains out of reach. The damage unfolds in stages, from the first crush or cut to weeks of swelling, cell death, and scarring that block regrowth.

The review explains each stage at the molecular level. It then surveys interventions in testing, from drugs and cells to implants and stimulation. The paper shows why repair is so hard and where progress is real.
europmc-pmc10719501:
Larsson, Butterworth, and Burgess explained Mendelian randomization in 2023, a method to test cause in heart research. Gene studies of the past decade found many variants tied to heart traits. The method uses those variants as a natural trial. Genes are dealt at birth much like lots in a trial, which cuts bias.

If a variant that raises a risk factor also raises disease, the factor likely plays a causal role. Larsson sets out the rules that must hold for that logic to stand. Uses span tests of new heart drugs before costly trials start. Old drugs can also be checked for fresh uses this way. The review gives the steps and the traps of the design.
europmc-pmc10758001:
Li and co-authors reviewed in 2024 how tiny carriers can deliver drug pairs for human disease. Pairing drugs can hit a disease on two paths at once. Gains include lower doses, less harm, and slower drug resistance. Pair care is now sought for cancer, heart disease, and brain decline, among others.

Nanoparticles, minute spheres of fat or plastic, can carry both drugs to one spot. Li shows they can stretch release, guard the drugs, and aim them at sick tissue. Forms in use or in tests span liposomes, polymer spheres, and nanocrystals. The review maps disease targets and the pairs matched to them. Hard parts remain: factory scale and proof in patients.
europmc-pmc10855901:
Chandrasekaran and Weiskirchen explain how excess weight drives type 2 diabetes in this 2024 overview. Type 2 diabetes is a long-term illness where blood sugar runs too high. Obesity, meaning a harmful build-up of body fat, is its strongest risk factor at all ages. Both illnesses are spreading worldwide.

Trials show that modest, lasting weight loss can improve blood sugar and insulin action, the authors note. Insulin is the hormone that moves sugar from blood into cells. Some patients then need fewer diabetes drugs. Diet, exercise, and daily habit changes form the core plan and can even help prevent the disease. The review lays out how fat and sugar control are linked inside the body. It closes with recent care plans for people who carry both conditions.
europmc-pmc10901501:
Buttenschoen, Morris, and Deane test whether AI docking tools produce shapes that could exist in the real world in this 2024 paper. Docking means predicting how a drug molecule sits in a protein pocket. New AI tools claim top accuracy and speed. The authors suspected many outputs break basic rules of chemistry and shape.

Their test suite, PoseBusters, checks bond lengths, flat rings, clashes, and other physical rules. They ran five AI tools and two classic tools through it. Judged by pose closeness alone, the AI tools looked strong. Once the physical checks were added, much of that lead vanished, the authors report. They argue that only tools passing both tests should be called state of the art.
europmc-pmc11071201:
Li and a large team uncover a self-feeding loop that drives pancreatic cancer in this 2024 study. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is a lethal cancer with fast, aggressive growth. Cancer cells often burn sugar by glycolysis, a process that makes lactate. Lactate can tag histones, the spools DNA wraps around, in a mark called lactylation.

Tumour samples showed high levels of this mark, and high levels tracked with shorter survival, the team found. Blocking glycolysis or silencing a key enzyme cut the mark and slowed tumour growth in cells and mice. Screening found the mark switches on two growth genes, TTK and BUB1B. One of those genes binds the sugar enzyme itself, closing a positive feedback loop. The authors present the loop as a driver of the cancer's onset and a possible drug target.
europmc-pmc1480401:
Kodner and Spreeuwenberg took stock of a rising buzzword in 2002: integrated care. Health services for chronic illness often come in pieces, split across many providers. Integrated care promises to join those pieces. The authors saw a young field with fuzzy terms.

They argue the idea needs clear meaning before theory or practice can grow. Their paper maps what the term could cover and what follows from each reading. At its heart, they press for a patient-centered drive. Kodner hopes the paper sparks debate on what integrated care should be. The stakes are high for people whose care spans years and many hands.
europmc-pmc1538601:
One protein sits at the heart of Alzheimer's disease. Zheng and Koo reviewed its wider life in 2006. The amyloid precursor protein, APP, is cut to make the beta-amyloid pieces that form brain plaques. Faults in its gene cause some early, inherited forms of the disease.

Yet APP does more than yield plaques. Lab studies assign it roles in cell growth, sticking, and signaling. Fly and mouse mutants, with the gene added or removed, show it matters for normal brain work. Zheng urges the field to study the whole protein, not just its toxic fragment.
europmc-pmc1618401:
Copying RNA to boost tiny samples can bend the very ratios labs want to measure. Diboun and co-authors quantified that risk in 2006 for a common amplification protocol. Boosting is unavoidable when tissue is scarce.

Distortion struck when a signal shift in one sample fell outside the scanner's range. The bend usually shrank ratios, weakening their statistical proof. Strong changes survived well: 87 percent of top genes kept their significance. Moderate changes kept it only 69 percent of the time. Diboun found the limma analysis method coped better with amplification than a rival approach.
europmc-pmc1664601:
Deaths worldwide are shifting to older ages and chronic diseases. Mathers and Loncar projected that shift in 2006, updating global forecasts from 2002 to 2030. Older projections had badly underestimated HIV/AIDS.

Their models run three scenarios, baseline, optimistic, and pessimistic, tied to economic and social trends. In all three, deaths move from infections, childbirth, and nutrition causes toward noncommunicable diseases. The risk of death for children under five falls by nearly half in the baseline case. Mathers aims the projections at health policy and priority setting worldwide.  Their findings update the widely quoted 1996 forecasts, which rested on 1990 data.
europmc-pmc1847501:
Evans and colleagues mapped the immune defenses of the honey bee in 2006 from its newly read genome. Bees are social insects that fight germs both as a colony and as individuals. The team focused on individual defenses in Apis mellifera and compared them with the fruit fly and the malaria mosquito.

They built bee models for four signaling pathways tied to immunity and found plausible matches for nearly all expected members. Yet across 17 gene families linked to insect immunity, bees carry only about one third as many genes as the fly or mosquito. The authors suggest bees can afford a leaner kit because colony behaviors block many infections. Or bees may face a narrow set of pathogens that evolved closely with them, such as the foulbrood bacterium.
europmc-pmc1939701:
Pfenninger and Schwenk asked in 2007 whether cryptic species, distinct species that look identical in effect, cluster in particular animal groups or regions. Reports of such hidden species had grown sharply over two decades. Some researchers proposed their spread was uneven, which would skew global diversity counts.

The team analyzed a literature database of cryptic animal species reports by taxon and by biogeographic region. Regression models corrected for how many species each group holds and how intensely it has been studied. After those corrections, cryptic species spread almost evenly across major animal groups and regions. That evenness suggests stasis in outward form, long-term look-alike evolution, is a constant of animal life. Hidden diversity thus inflates true species counts in a predictable way everywhere, with direct effects for biodiversity estimates and conservation planning.
europmc-pmc2125401: A medical paper on the inhibition of uranium nitrate toxicity by sodium carbonate. The uranium antidote. This article preserves that toxicology. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It retains its place in time. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2125801: A medical paper on the relation of the spinal cord to spontaneous epinephrin liberation. The cord's signal. This article preserves that physiology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2128201: A third medical paper on experimental rabbit syphilis bone affections. The rabbit bones once more. This article preserves that venereology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2128501: A medical paper with studies in agglutination, the agglutination of streptococci. The clumping strep. This article preserves that serology. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2128601: A medical paper on experimental production of pneumococcus pneumonia in mice by inhalation. The breathed pneumonia. This article preserves that research. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2131501: A medical paper with studies in the biology of metals, the influence of lead on development. The leaded growth. This article preserves that toxicology. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2140901: A biology paper on the physiological principle of minimum work applied to the angle of branching arteries. The efficient vessels. This article preserves that physiology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2169301:
Kubica and co-workers found in 2008 that Staphylococcus aureus bacteria can hide silently inside human macrophages. This bacterium is usually classed as an outside-cell pathogen, though it can invade other cells and die quickly there. In macrophages grown from human monocytes, its behaviour differed sharply. After being engulfed, the bacteria sat inside vacuoles for three to four days before escaping and bursting the host cell.

Until that escape, infected macrophages showed no signs of death and kept working. Pre-treating them with interferon-gamma let them kill the bacteria at human therapeutic doses. Survival depended on bacterial regulators called sigma factor B and agr. Mutants lacking alpha-toxin or other factors were killed efficiently. Alpha-toxin was the key survival molecule. Mobile macrophages may thus carry the infection around the body.
europmc-pmc2222601:
Deary and co-workers described the Lothian Birth Cohort 1936 in 2007, a study of cognitive ageing across a lifetime. All Scottish children born in 1936 took a general intelligence test in 1947, as part of a survey of 70,805 children. Survivors living near Edinburgh form this cohort of 1,091 people. They retook the same mental ability test at age 70, alongside medical exams, fitness tests and detailed thinking assessments.

The protocol also gathered personality, quality-of-life and food questionnaires, plus blood samples for DNA and biomarkers. Cognitive testing covered reasoning, memory, processing speed and executive function. The cohort's rare strength is a true measure of lifetime cognitive change, from age eleven to seventy and beyond. Rich accompanying data let researchers hunt for what drives differences in that change.
europmc-pmc2245901:
Zhang presented the I-TASSER server in 2008, an automated system predicting three-dimensional protein structure from amino acid sequence. The method had ranked best in the server section of the recent CASP experiment, a blind community test of prediction methods. The online server at the University of Kansas had already answered thousands of modelling requests from over 35 countries. Each query returns up to five full-length models.

A confidence measure called C-score estimates each model's accuracy from template consensus and clustering density. In large benchmark tests, C-score correlated strongly with the true structural similarity score, at 0.91 on that scale. Using a C-score cutoff gave false positive and false negative rates below 0.1 in these tests. The score reliably separates correct from incorrect overall folds. Average prediction error was just 0.08 on that similarity scale. The server is free for academic use.
europmc-pmc2361201:
Hamilton and colleagues compared survival across three aggressive womb cancers in 2006. The types were uterine papillary serous carcinoma, clear cell carcinoma, and grade 3 endometrioid carcinoma. All three are high-risk forms of cancer of the womb lining, and earlier small studies disagreed on which was worst.

Using a national US registry for 1988 to 2001, they tracked 4,180 women. Five-year disease-specific survival was 55% for the serous type, 68% for clear cell, and 77% for the grade 3 endometrioid type. The gap held for both early and advanced disease. The serous and clear cell types made up only 10% and 3% of womb cancers but caused 39% and 8% of deaths. The authors urged that these poorer outlooks shape patient advice and future trial design.
europmc-pmc2362801:
Forsyth and colleagues measured three tissue-chewing enzymes in brain tumors in 1999. The enzymes, called MMPs, cut through the protein mesh around cells. Two of them, gelatinase-A and gelatinase-B, were suspected of helping gliomas invade brain and grow new blood vessels. Gliomas are tumors of the brain's support cells.

The team measured enzyme levels in 46 tumor samples and seven healthy brain samples. Gelatinase-A ran higher in tumors than in normal tissue, even in low-grade tumors, and stayed high in the most malignant kind. Gelatinase-B rose more steeply with tumor grade and sat strongly in blood vessels at growing edges. A third enzyme, MT1-MMP, appeared in neurons, tumor cells, and vessels. The authors assigned gelatinase-B mainly to vessel remodelling, and the other two to both invasion and vessel growth.
europmc-pmc2481301:
Milano and co-authors split scleroderma into molecular subsets using skin gene activity in 2008. Scleroderma hardens and scars the skin and can damage internal organs, but patients vary wildly. The team read gene activity in 61 skin biopsies from patients with the diffuse form, the limited form, a localised form called morphea, and healthy controls.

Forearm and back skin from the same patient gave nearly identical profiles, a property they used to define each patient's intrinsic pattern. Diffuse and limited patients separated cleanly from each other and from controls. Inside the diffuse group sat three distinct subsets, and inside the limited group two. Each subset's signature pointed to a different program: cell growth, immune infiltration, or scarring. A 177-gene signature tracked how severe the skin disease was in diffuse patients. Subsets also mapped onto lung, gut, and finger complications.
europmc-pmc2577301:
Huse and colleagues validated in 2008 a shortcut for censusing microbial communities by sequencing only short variable stretches of a universal gene. Surveys of the small subunit ribosomal RNA gene identify microbes, but reading the full gene is slow and costly. Their method reads just the hypervariable tags, the stretches that differ most between species, using high-throughput pyrosequencing.

They compared tag results with full-length sequences from human gut and deep-sea vent communities. The tags gave equivalent identifications and relative abundances. This held even for tags differing from their nearest reference by up to 15 percent. The method samples communities hundreds of times deeper per dollar, exposing the rare biosphere of scarce species. It also skips the cloning step that biases older surveys. The authors offer it for projects like the Human Microbiome Project.
europmc-pmc2631701:
Donlan surveyed biofilms on medical devices in 2001, the slimy microbial communities that make device infections so hard to cure. Bacteria and yeasts stick irreversibly to surfaces such as catheters, heart valves, pacemakers, prosthetic joints, and contact lenses, then secrete polymers that encase them in a protective matrix. In that state they resist antimicrobial treatment far beyond ordinary cells.

Biofilms may start as a single species but grow multispecies with time, drawing organisms from patients' skin, staff hands, or tap water. Donlan calls for reliable sampling and measurement techniques so biofilms on devices can be compared between studies. Open questions include how much biofilms drive drug resistance and how firmly contamination of a device links to patient infection. Answering them is presented as the path to controlling device-associated infections.
europmc-pmc2662801:
Weinert and co-authors traced in 2009 the family history of Rickettsia, bacteria that live inside the cells of insects and other creatures. Some cause grave human diseases such as typhus, spread by ticks and lice. Many more live only in insects, and those were barely known. The team found 20 new strains in arthropods and built a family tree from several genes.

The tree shows Rickettsia are mainly insect partners, not mammal parasites. They do not evolve in lockstep with their hosts; instead they jump hosts often, usually to a related insect. About 150 million years ago the genus split in two, and a burst of new forms followed near 50 million years ago. Some lines gained tricks such as passing through mammals or killing male hosts. One strain proved a mix of two distant lines, a rare case of gene swapping.
europmc-pmc2695001:
Bucan and a large team scanned in 2009 the genomes of 912 families with autism, hunting rare structural variants that delete or duplicate whole gene pieces. Autism's genetics is famously tangled, and earlier work had shown such copy changes matter in a slice of cases, but too coarsely to name single genes. The team used dense typing and compared against 1,488 healthy controls.

Prioritizing changes that hit gene exons, they found over 150 spots where rare variants struck several unrelated patients but no controls. Twenty-seven held up in an independent check of 859 more cases and 1,051 controls. Known sites confirmed the method, including deletions of NRXN1 and duplications around UBE3A. New candidates emerged too: BZRAP1, a synapse protein adjuster, was hit in twelve unrelated cases and zero controls. Most variants were seen just once, a sign of how many roads lead to autism.
europmc-pmc2724101:
Gandhi and co-authors traced in 2009 how faults in PINK1, a mitochondrial kinase, make neurons prone to die from calcium stress in Parkinson's disease. PINK1 faults cause an inherited, recessive form of the disease, but what the protein normally does was unknown. Mitochondria are the cell power units, and they also handle calcium, a signal that can kill in excess.

In PINK1-deficient neurons, calcium left mitochondria too slowly through its sodium-calcium exchanger, so calcium built up inside. Overload raised reactive oxygen species, harmful oxygen forms, which blocked glucose entry and weakened respiration. That lowered the threshold for a lethal pore to open, so normal calcium pulses could trigger cell death. Feeding complex substrates partly restored respiration.
europmc-pmc2725801:
Elbasha, Dasbach, and Insinga modeled in 2007 whether a four-type HPV vaccine could cost-effectively cut cervical cancer, precancerous lesions, and genital warts in the United States. HPV, human papillomavirus, causes cervical and several other cancers and warts in both sexes. Simple cohort models cannot capture herd immunity, the indirect protection when spread falls, so policy needs a dynamic population model.

Their dynamic model tracked infection and disease across the population under several vaccination strategies added to current screening. Routine vaccination of young girls proved cost-effective in the model, and broader strategies could be judged on the same terms. The abstract frames the four-type vaccine as able to reduce cancer, precancer, and wart incidence at acceptable cost.
europmc-pmc2726301:
Seghier reviewed in 2008 the laterality index, a number used in functional MRI to state which brain half dominates a task such as language. Brain scans measure activity in each hemisphere, and the index compares left and right contributions. Small method choices can shift that number a lot, which affects both research and clinical use.

The review works through each choice: how activity is quantified, where volumes of interest sit, which statistical threshold is used, and how baseline tasks are picked. It also covers thresholding the index itself and whether values repeat well on rescan. Seghier urges that these factors be reported and kept in mind whenever index values are compared between people or studies.
europmc-pmc2727001:
Hotez and Kamath reviewed in 2009 the prevalence and burden of neglected tropical diseases among the poorest five hundred million people in sub-Saharan Africa. These diseases are chronic, disabling conditions tied to extreme poverty. Worm infections cause about eighty-five percent of the burden, they estimate.

Hookworm affects almost half of the poorest people, including tens of millions of school children and pregnant women, where it drives anemia. Schistosomiasis follows with about one hundred ninety-two million cases, then lymphatic filariasis and river blindness with tens of millions each. Together the burden may reach half that of malaria in the region. Data on many non-worm diseases are missing, so the true total is likely higher.
europmc-pmc2777001:
Hruz and co-authors described in 2008 Genevestigator V3, a web-based reference database for exploring gene expression across many biological contexts. Earlier versions let biologists query expression data, but scaling limits, single-organism storage, and missing heavy analyses held them back. The new version pairs a client-server design with large-scale manual curation and quality control of microarray data for several organisms, plus curated pathway data for mouse and Arabidopsis.

On top of better querying, V3 adds tools to study genes across many contexts at once. Users can hunt for biomarker genes, cluster genes into expression modules, and model responses inside metabolic and regulatory networks. As a reference expression database with approachable tools, it serves discovery research and the checking of new hypotheses. The system is built for meta-analysis, drawing conclusions across hundreds of experiments at once.
europmc-pmc2855701:
Rapin, Lund, Bernaschi, and Castiglione merged immune simulation with sequence-based prediction in 2010, upgrading their agent-based simulator C-ImmSim. Earlier simulators caricatured molecular binding, the step that decides whether the immune system notices an invader. The upgraded version represents germs and immune receptors by their actual amino acid sequences. It uses prediction software to forecast which fragments will bind and trigger a response, including a new scoring method built on protein binding energies.

Test runs reproduced classic vaccine studies and the growth of immune memory. Simulated people with two different tissue-type gene sets handled flu better than those with matched sets. Under chronic exposure, the highest-affinity defender clones outgrew all rivals, matching basic immune science.
europmc-pmc2883601:
Yesylevskyy, Schäfer, Sengupta, and Marrink built in 2010 a water model that adds electric responsiveness to fast, simplified computer simulations of biomolecules. Coarse-grained simulations lump atoms into beads to reach larger scales, but their usual water beads cannot polarize, so they screen electric forces wrongly. Their model packs four water molecules into three linked beads that can reorient like real water.

The new water reproduced bulk water's electric screening while keeping the density and oil-water behavior of the standard MARTINI model it extends. Two hard test cases showcased the gain: ions crossing a membrane and charged molecules in mixed environments behaved more realistically. Better water physics at coarse scale opens longer, larger simulations of membranes and proteins that finer models cannot reach.
europmc-pmc2929501:
Podhorecka, Skladanowski, and Bozko reviewed the role of the histone variant H2AX in the DNA damage response in a 2010 article. Breaks across both DNA strands are among the most harmful lesions a cell can suffer.

When such breaks form, H2AX near the damage gains a phosphate mark, creating a signal known as gamma-H2AX. The mark helps gather repair proteins at broken sites and pauses the cell cycle through checkpoint controls. Measuring the mark can reveal the harmful effects of toxic agents, track how well cancer treatment works, and hint at how sensitive a tumour may be.
europmc-pmc3003701:
Eldh and colleagues showed in 2010 that tiny vesicles shed by stressed mast cells can protect other cells from oxidative stress. Exosomes carry RNA and protein between cells, and their cargo was suspected to change with the sender's state.

Vesicles from peroxide-stressed mouse mast cells carried a different messenger RNA mix than vesicles from calm cells, and both differed from the parent cells. Receiving cells given stress vesicles lost less viability when later stressed themselves. Ultraviolet light exposure reshaped what the stressed cells loaded. The findings cast exosomal RNA as a courier of protective instructions.
europmc-pmc3087801:
Elshire and colleagues introduced in 2011 a streamlined way to genotype many individuals at once by sequencing only the DNA next to chosen cutting sites. Falling sequencing costs made reading DNA cheap, but reading whole genomes for every sample in a breeding population was still wasteful. Their method, genotyping by sequencing, uses enzymes that cut DNA at fixed spots and avoids the repetitive stretches that clog analysis.

Applied to maize and barley breeding populations, it mapped hundreds of thousands and tens of thousands of sequence tags respectively. For barley, which lacked a finished genome, the shared tags themselves served as the reference map. The approach is quick, highly repeatable, and needs no prior markers for a new species. Breeders can use it for genomic selection on fresh material, and conservation biologists can survey wild populations with no genome in hand.
europmc-pmc3097201:
Chang and colleagues calculated in 2011 how many years of life serious mental illness takes away, using a large London mental health case register covering more than thirty thousand patients. They built life tables for schizophrenia, related psychotic disorders, bipolar disorder, substance use disorders, and depression, and compared them with national figures for the same years.

Every diagnosis carried a large loss. Men lost roughly eight to fifteen years of life expectancy depending on diagnosis, and women lost roughly ten to seventeen years. The heaviest losses fell on men with schizophrenia and women with schizoaffective disorder. The authors note these gaps exceed the measured life impact of smoking, diabetes, or obesity. They call urgently for work on why these patients die early and how services can prevent it, since general healthcare gains are not reaching this group.
europmc-pmc3101201:
Zimmerman, Kiss, and Hossain opened in 2011 a journal series on migration and health by proposing that policy should follow the whole journey, not just the destination. Migrants' health is shaped long before arrival and long after, yet governments handle each phase in separate silos with clashing goals. Their framework splits migration into five phases: before departure, travel, destination, interception by authorities, and return.

Each phase carries its own health risks and its own chances to intervene, from pre travel screening and safe passage to workplace protection abroad and care on return. The authors argue mobility and health protection are fully compatible when agencies coordinate across borders and sectors. The article sets up five companion pieces, one per phase. Its aim is practical: give policy makers a shared map so migrant health stops falling between jurisdictions.
europmc-pmc3146901:
Michael Reddy and colleagues watched malaria mosquitoes bite outdoors on an island in Equatorial Guinea in a 2011 paper in Malaria Journal. Indoor spraying and bed nets had been the island's main defences, but those tools only work against mosquitoes that come inside. Volunteers collected landing mosquitoes indoors and outdoors across villages, seasons, and two years.

Outdoor biting proved surprisingly heavy all night, including early evening and morning hours when people are outside unprotected. The region's main malaria vector now sought hosts outdoors at least as much as indoors, a sharp change from its indoor-only habit recorded before control began. Roughly two fifths of bites came at hours people spend outside. The authors propose years of indoor insecticide pressure pushed the mosquitoes outdoors, and call for added outdoor measures.
europmc-pmc3215701:
M. Aleksi Kallio and colleagues introduced Chipster, analysis software for high-throughput biology data, in this 2011 paper in BMC Genomics. Microarrays and next-generation sequencing were producing data faster than most biologists could handle, and new analysis methods usually demanded programming skill. Chipster was built to put those methods within reach of non-programmers.

The software offers a graphical interface over a large collection of analysis tools for gene expression, microRNA, and genome copy-number data. Interactive charts let users click on data points and build new gene lists from their selections. Analysis steps can be saved as reusable workflows and shared with collaborators. The paper walks through the microarray tools using three case studies, and notes the platform also handles proteomics and sequencing data.
europmc-pmc3316601:
Sawyer, Krause, Guschanski, Savolainen, and Pääbo examined how DNA decays in remains that are centuries to tens of thousands of years old, reporting in 2012. DNA recovered from bones and museum specimens always arrives broken and chemically altered. The team compared mitochondrial DNA from tissues aged between eighteen and sixty thousand years, asking which kinds of damage build up steadily with time.

Fragment length, it turned out, does not shrink in a dependable way as remains age. Breaks in the DNA backbone did favor certain letters in patterns that suggest more than one decay route. One kind of chemical change, where one DNA letter masquerades as another near fragment ends, did climb reliably with age. The authors propose that pattern as a practical test for telling genuinely ancient DNA from modern contamination.
europmc-pmc3348501:
Kirilina and colleagues uncovered the bodily origin of a false signal that haunts a popular brain scanning method, in a 2012 study. The method, near infrared spectroscopy, shines light through the scalp to watch brain activity, but blood changes in the skin itself can mimic brain signals and create false alarms. During a sustained attention task, the team recorded the light signals alongside MRI scans, blood pressure, heart rate, and skin blood flow.

The fake signal sat exactly where veins drain the scalp, and it tracked the body's stress response rather than brain work. Mental effort triggered a sympathetic squeeze on scalp arteries, followed by a drop in blood held in the veins. A statistical fix that models the skin signal cleanly separated it from real brain activity. The authors warn that nearly any thinking task will stir the same bodily response, so cleanup is essential.
europmc-pmc3360701:
Sokolove and collaborators traced how the autoimmune attack in rheumatoid arthritis builds before joints ever become painful. Using stored blood from 81 people who later fell ill, some samples reaching back twelve years before diagnosis, they tracked antibodies to citrullinated proteins with a multiplex array.

The antibody response widened over time, a spread across more and more targets. Early antibodies aimed at citrullinated histones, fibrinogen, and biglycan, and as their range grew, inflammatory signals in the blood rose in step. A joint profile of antibodies and cytokines flagged whose symptoms would start within two years. The authors see this quiet phase as a chance to step in sooner.
europmc-pmc3395601:
Kamiya and a large team reported in 2012 that a single letter change in one gene decides sex in the tiger pufferfish, or fugu. The gene, Amhr2, helps build reproductive organs. By mapping the sex region and testing relatives, the team pinned down the one change that tracked perfectly with being male or female.

Females carry two copies of one version, while males carry one of each. The swap alters a single building block inside the gene's working region. The same link holds in two cousin species, and a matching defect in medaka fish also produces females. Oddly, the fugu sex chromosomes show none of the usual wear, marking them as very young proto-chromosomes.
europmc-pmc3483701:
Barrera reviewed how oxidative stress and damaged fats shape cancer growth and treatment, in ISRN Oncology in 2012. Cancer cells carry an altered chemical balance, with more reactive oxygen molecules than healthy cells. Those molecules attack the fatty walls of cells, leaving breakdown products that act as signals. One product, shortened to HNE, drew the author's focus.

At high levels, such stress can kill cancer cells, and many cancer drugs and radiation work partly by pushing it higher. Yet some tumor cells adapt to steady stress and become drug resistant. Barrera weighs both faces of the process: stress helps tumors arise, then becomes a weapon against them. Learning how resistant cells adapt could sharpen future treatments, she argues.
europmc-pmc3511201: Urine germs got a healthy-vs-germ study. This 2012 paper separates healthy urine from silent bacteriuria. The authors reveal the difference. Their work guides urology. Fouts's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped UTI diagnosis.

evelyn-diary-1901:
John Evelyn kept a diary across most of his long life, from 1620 to 1706. Evelyn was a gentleman, a gardener, and a founding member of the Royal Society. The 1901 edition prints his record in full.

He describes the Civil War years, the court of Charles II, the Plague, and the Great Fire of London. Gardens, books, and new science fill the quieter pages. Evelyn was Pepys's friend and great fellow diarist, though calmer in tone. Read together, the two diaries give the fullest picture we have of Stuart England. His notes on trees and planting reflect his other famous book, Sylva.
freeman-portion-of-labor-1901:
Harper issued The Portion of Labor in 1901, naming Mary Wilkins as author of Jerome and A New England Nun. She dedicated the book to Henry Mills Alden. Chapter one finds young Ellen, seven and a half, watching Norway spruces by her father's house.

Ellen is sure the trees mean to walk north toward their cold home land. That child's fancy opens a tale that soon leaves the village for the factory town. A strike, a love story, and the slow grind of mill life cross in its pages. The novel counts among the first American books to treat labor as a grave and central subject.
frus-1861-d101:
Writing on 18 October 1861, William H. Seward kept up his brisk exchange with Lord Lyons. The letter is document 101 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Day after day in October, the two men traded notes across a short distance in Washington. The pace shows how much of the war's fate was argued in that one city. Seward's note keeps the exchange moving on his terms as far as he could. The exchange kept a rhythm that let both men save face while holding firm. Both men prized the rhythm, since it let each claim be met on its merits.
frus-1861-d201:
Cassius Clay wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 August 1861. The dispatch is document 201 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Clay wrote in August with the news of Bull Run on its way to Russia. The czar's court did not waver in its warmth for the Union. His report gave Washington a firm point of light at a dark hour in the war. Russia's warmth held through the war and bloomed, in time, into a famous friendship. Famous friendship in time grew from these plain, dated seeds of 1861.
frus-1861-d301:
Home in Washington, Seward read a fresh report from Mr. Thayer, dated 29 June 1861. Congress received it as Document 301 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. By then, in the opening months of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d101:
By the date of 14 July 1862, Seward had new word ready for Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Congress received it as Document 101 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d201:
On 8 January 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed another note to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, printed as Document 201 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Three days of steady notes mark the reopening of normal business.

January 1862 also brought a change of war secretary in Washington and fresh Union plans for the spring. Britain watched for signs of where the war was heading. In that setting, frequent short notes between Seward and Lyons kept small disputes from growing while larger questions waited on events. Washington was a small town in 1862, and the envoys met socially as often as officially.
frus-1862-d301:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 8 August 1862 in a letter printed as Document 301 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

That week a new battle was opening in Virginia at Cedar Mountain, the first move of the campaign that ended at Bull Run. Dayton could not know it as he wrote; his concern was the French court. His reports are read today for exactly that split view: Paris gossip and policy, written in full ignorance of the week's fighting. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d401:
Dated 22 April 1862, this order from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to Horace J. Perry, secretary of the American legation in Madrid. It is Document 401 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the printed record of the year's diplomacy.

Spring 1862 brought the fall of New Orleans and fresh strain over Spain's part in the Mexican expedition. Seward's letters to Madrid balanced protest with courtesy, since Spain held Cuba and could open or close ports to Confederate ships. The dispatch belongs to that careful exchange, where each instruction tried to keep a proud old empire neutral while the Union fought for its life.
frus-1862-d501:
James Shepherd Pike sent this report from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 May 1862. It stands as Document 501 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Pike wrote as the Union's armies pressed in Virginia and the West, and Dutch opinion followed the campaigns in the papers. His reports weighed the ministry's formal correctness against the merchants' wish for an end to the fighting. He also kept Washington posted on the Dutch colonial questions that touched the war at sea. A mid-May report like this one is a typical brick in the Hague file: modest in itself, part of a wall of steady information.
frus-1862-d601:
Spain's minister of state addressed this instruction on 22 March 1862 to the commander of the Spanish expeditionary force in Mexico. It is Document 601 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, in the appended Spanish correspondence.

By March 1862 the allied front in Mexico was cracking, and Madrid's orders to its general reflect the strain. Spain soon concluded that France meant more than debt collection and pulled its troops out, a decision shaped in letters like this one. Printed in translation in an American volume, the document shows the State Department at work. It was assembling the fullest record it could of a crisis on the Union's border. The record even included papers written by governments it could not control.
frus-1862-d701: On 15 September 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to a Mr. Yrisarri for the last time in this file. The letter is document 701 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, closing a short exchange that ran from late August. The evidence names both men and the date, but it does not state Yrisarri's post, his land, or the letters' subject.
frus-1863p1-d101:
On 2 March 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams for the fifth time that day, by the volume's count. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 101 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The dozen letters of 2 March read like a table of contents for the London brief. Each took up one thread — a claim, a ship, a talk, a tone to hold. This one holds its own thread in the set. Such batch writing was desk craft of a high order, and it kept a far-off envoy fully armed for his next round of talks.
frus-1863p1-d201:
An instruction dated 18 May 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 201 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Confederate agents were buying ships and arms in Britain, and Washington wanted the trade stopped. Orders to London often carried protests, evidence, and legal arguments for Adams to use. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d301:
The State Department's mail for London dated 28 September 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 301 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

In the fall of 1863 two ironclad rams built for the Confederacy waited in a British yard. Washington's orders to Adams that season pressed hard for the ships to be held. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d401:
A formal note dated 23 February 1863 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 401 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Trade bound the countries tightly, from Southern cotton to British mills. Both sides had much to lose from a break, and the notes reflect that caution. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d501: Document 501 in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs is a letter dated 2 May 1863, from Major Turner to Mr. Hunter at the State Department.
