frus-1863p1-d601:
Document 601, dated 4 August 1863, records a letter from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the late summer of 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d101: On November 8, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Churchill, four days before sailing for the Mediterranean. The letter is Document 101 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The president's party was packing maps, staff lists, and arguments for two conferences at once. The record gives the date and the two names and no subject. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the last Washington days of the story.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d201:
Acting Secretary of State Edward Stettinius sent President Roosevelt a memorandum on 9 November 1943 about trusteeship for disputed islands in the Central Pacific. It carries two hasty enclosures and a chart, and Stettinius warns that the State Department's full studies of trusteeship were still unfinished.

The enclosure favors placing the contested islands under an international trusteeship shared by the United States, Britain, Australia, New Zealand, and China. Day-to-day rule would be split by friendly agreement, while defense would rest with the United States alone or jointly with Britain. The paper also urges Roosevelt to hear the Joint Chiefs of Staff before raising the plan with Churchill, since nearby American islands might be drawn in.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d301:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 308/7 at Cairo on 24 November 1943, on the boundaries of the Southeast Asia Command. It records Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek's objection to the boundaries set at the Quebec conference, and his counter-proposal, worked out with Mountbatten and Somervell.

Chiang backs one command under Mountbatten for the Burma campaign, but holds that Thailand and Indochina must stay in the China theater. Moving them, he argues, would wound Chinese morale, feed Japanese propaganda about British empire-building, and chill relations among the three allies. His plan has Chinese troops attack from the north and Mountbatten's from the south when the time comes, with political questions handled by a joint committee. Mountbatten accepts the boundaries but objects to the committee; the American chiefs and Roosevelt approve Chiang's proposal as it stands.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d401:
President Roosevelt wrote to the Shah of Iran from Tehran on 1 December 1943, a letter of thanks for his welcome in the Shah's country. The Shah had met him, offered his palace, an airport greeting, and a guard of honor, and sent a magnificent carpet.

Roosevelt says the circumstances of his visit made it impossible to accept those offers, much as he would have liked to. He leaves Iran with regret. He regrets not seeing more of the country and its people. The carpet, he promises, will remind him and the American people of Iranian hospitality. Iran, he writes, holds a warm spot in American hearts. It is warmer now that the two nations are brothers in arms. He hopes their wartime partnership will continue unchecked in the labors of peace. Below his signature he added, in his own hand, a hope that the Shah would visit Washington.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d501:
Harry Hopkins sent a message to President Roosevelt himself on December 6, 1943, the last day of the Second Cairo Conference. Hopkins traveled as the President's special assistant and closest adviser, yet still put matters to him in writing. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

A Hopkins note to Roosevelt is the inner circle talking on paper. Hopkins saw everything at Cairo, from the leaders' tempers to the staff's disputes, and his written word carried a weight no other aide could match. Readers interested in how Roosevelt actually made decisions will find these short staff messages among the most revealing records of the trip.
frus-1944-quebec-d101:
On August 30, 1944, Hull wrote to Lord Halifax in Washington. Halifax served as Britain's ambassador to the United States. The State Department printed the letter in its Quebec 1944 volume. Such letters kept allied channels warm between summits.

Ambassadors in Washington handled much of the alliance's daily business. A letter from Hull to Halifax joined the two foreign services directly. The Quebec Conference opened less than two weeks later. For readers, the message shows preparation running through diplomatic channels too. Not every question waited for Roosevelt and Churchill to meet. The conference opened at Quebec City on September 12.
frus-1944-quebec-d201:
An editors' note sets out the Roosevelt-Churchill agreement of September 15, 1944, on occupation zones in Germany, learned from Leahy through Morgenthau's diary. The southwestern zone went to American forces and the northwestern to British. Boundary changes moved Hessen-Nassau and Oberhessen to the American zone, and the Saarland, Palatinate, and Rheinhessen to the British.

American forces were guaranteed access through the western and northwestern seaports, with rights of passage through the British zone. The Joint Chiefs added American control of Bremen the next morning, and the Combined Chiefs' decision was approved on September 16. No evidence shows the two leaders discussed dividing Berlin's sectors, which the London protocol of September 12 had also left open.
frus-1944-quebec-d301: A joint public statement was drafted for Roosevelt and Churchill on 19 September 1944, though a draft is not a released text. The wording survives as document 301 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on the Quebec Conference. Comparing proposed language with what leaders finally said in public is one reason historians value drafts preserved in records like this one.
frus-1945-50-intel-d101:
Irwin, the interim activities director of the Strategic Services Unit, wrote to Assistant Secretary McCloy on 28 January 1946. The SSU had just passed to new interim leadership as Magruder's time ended. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A change of chief, marked by a new name on the same channel to the same patron, shows an institution outliving its founder. Irwin wrote days after the president created the Central Intelligence Group, when the SSU's remnant faced absorption into the new body. Readers can watch the handover in the paper itself: the unit's needs unchanged, the hand presenting them new. The thread continues because the work, and the danger, continued.
frus-1945-50-intel-d201:
On 2 December 1946, the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg) sent a memorandum to the President’s Special Counsel (Clifford). It is document 201 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d301:
On 1 October 1948, Acting Secretary of State Lovett sent a letter to Secretary of Defense Forrestal. It is document 301 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. While the survey team asked its questions, the CIA's covert arm was growing fast under Frank Wisner.

Between offices that did not answer to each other, a letter was the polite but firm way to press a point. The tone is formal, but the stakes were real: turf, money, and the shape of the new agencies. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d401:
Secretary of Defense Louis Johnson wrote to Secretary of State Dean Acheson on 7 October 1949. The letter is document 401 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Johnson and Acheson were the two cabinet officers whose departments used intelligence most. The armed services ran large intelligence shops of their own, and the Pentagon guarded them with care. A direct letter between the two secretaries shows how disputes and deals at the top shaped the young intelligence system below them. Both men left office within two years, but the habits their letters set outlived them.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d101:
Leo Pasvolsky pressed the same cause twice in one week. In this short note of 23 January 1945, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, he returns to the Emergency High Commission for Liberated Europe. He writes to the Secretary of State from his post working on the general world body.

Pasvolsky says agreement on the commission at the coming meeting is a need, not a wish. From his side of the work, it is the strongest answer the allies can give to fast-growing opposition at home. Critics charge that the Dumbarton Oaks plan would merely bless a system of one-sided grabbing by the great powers. A joint commission for the freed countries would prove them wrong.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d201:
The de Gaulle visit was over, and Stalin reported it to Roosevelt on 3 December 1944. His secret and personal message is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The talks, he says, allowed a friendly exchange on Franco-Soviet relations.

De Gaulle raised the two questions Stalin had forecast: the Rhine frontier and a Franco-Soviet pact. On the frontier, Stalin answered that it cannot be settled without the knowledge and consent of the main allies, whose armies are fighting on French soil. He stressed how complex the matter is. On the pact, he called for close study of its legal nature. One open point is who could ratify such a pact in France as things stand. He ends by asking the President's reply and comments.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d301:
Eden and Stettinius sat down at Malta to tie up the loose ends on Germany, and these are their agreed minutes. Printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, the record opens with Eden asking the Secretary of State what points he wished to raise. Zones of occupation come first.

Agreement exists between London and Washington on the zones, Stettinius says, but small points remain, above all the ports of Bremen and Bremerhaven. They should be settled at once. The Russians may soon be in Berlin, and might form views of their own if the negotiated protocol stays unapproved. Eden agrees the points can be cleared with the military authorities forthwith. The two also take up a zone for the French, which the President favors and which might be cut from the southern British zone.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d401:
Open items blocking the call of the United Nations conference are listed in this delegation paper of February 8, 1945. France's status came first. At Malta, the British and Americans had agreed France should be a fifth sponsoring power. Its name would join China's on the invitations.

How to consult France and China came next. The United States would do it for Britain and Russia; Grew stood ready in Washington to start at a flash from Yalta. The form of invitation followed: America could issue it for all five sponsors, and a draft was in hand. Trusteeships close the list. The paper measures how close San Francisco was.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d501:
Formal where the communiqué is warm, the Protocol of Proceedings records what the Crimea Conference actually decided. The conference of the three heads of government, it states, took place from February 4 to 11 and came to set conclusions. The first section covers the world organisation.

A United Nations conference would be summoned for Wednesday, April 25, 1945, in the United States of America. Invitations would go to the United Nations as they stood on February 8, and to Associated Nations declaring war by March 1. Ukraine and White Russia's candidacy follows. Later sections carry Poland, reparations, and the rest. Lawyers and historians cite this text, not the speeches.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d101:
General Deane reported fresh pressure on Moscow in an extract of a telegram to General Bradley dated June 26, 1945. The extract is document 101 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The omitted part of the cable sums up Vyshinsky's stiff reply of the day before, which had put off the American requests until Zhukov returned.

Deane says the importance of General Stoner's signal crews going to Berlin had been stressed when the request to enlarge Parks's group was made. On receiving Bradley's latest cable the night before, he took the matter to General Antonov again, while Harriman took it to Vyshinsky. He plans to see Antonov or his staff that day and press further. The fragment shows the daily grind of extracting approvals from the Soviet machine.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d201:
Ambassador Harriman described Molotov's first questions about the agenda in a telegram dated July 8, 1945. The message is document 201 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Harriman had handed Molotov the list of topics the President might wish to raise, sent from Washington on July 5.

Molotov asked whether reparations would be discussed. Harriman pointed out that Pauley was coming to Berlin and felt sure the President would discuss the subject if the Soviets wished to raise it. Molotov then asked whether the whole administration of Germany would be covered, and Harriman said he assumed the Germany topic covered it. Molotov would bring the list to Stalin's attention and report any comments or added topics. The exchange gave Washington its first feel for Soviet priorities.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d301:
Washington explained a deliberate silence to Ambassador Harriman on June 29, 1945. Molotov's note of March 17 had refused American requests for consultation on Rumania's political situation. The Department had left it unanswered on purpose, while the main effort went to the Polish question.

Now, the Secretary of State ad interim wrote, a detailed reply would serve no useful purpose. The subject would come up at the coming conference of heads of government, alongside the other former satellite states. The cable shows how Washington saved its Balkan complaints for the summit table at Potsdam. The Balkan questions, in short, would wait for the heads of government.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d401:
The left bank of the Rhine is treated in a briefing book paper of June 30, 1945, as a problem of military security above all. The fair needs of France, Belgium, and the Netherlands should be recognized, it says. But the problem should ultimately be solved by long-range controls over Germany, not by transfers of Rhenish territory.

While allied military government lasts in Germany, the paper adds, western Europe need not fear German aggression. So there is no need now to decide what military posts the Rhine area may require later. Its basic data describe a region of 10,598 square miles and about 6,550,000 people, including the Saar and the Palatinate.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d501:
Recognition of Poland is announced in a White House press release of July 5, 1945, carrying a statement by the President. It is with great satisfaction, Truman announces, that effective today, as of 7 p.m. Eastern War Time, the United States has established diplomatic relations with the newly formed Polish Provisional Government of National Unity, now established at Warsaw. The step fulfills the Yalta decisions on Poland.

The new government, he reports, has informed him in writing that it recognizes in their entirety the Crimea Conference decisions on the Polish question. It has thereby confirmed its intention to carry out the provisions on holding elections. Arthur Bliss Lane, chosen as ambassador to Poland, will proceed to Warsaw as soon as possible.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d601:
The United States Chiefs of Staff answered a British proposal in a top secret memo of July 10, 1945. It is document 601 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The issue was wording in the joint paper on basic objectives for the war.

The U.S. chiefs agree to write British Commonwealth in place of British Isles for one security clause. They add that the clause should no longer link security to war-making capacity. With Germany beaten, they argue, there is no case for widening pledges made for a two-front war. The commitment should be clearly tied to the war against Japan alone. The memo shows both staffs trimming grand wartime language as the conflict shrank to one foe.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d701:
A correction to the record of the Molotov-Sarper talks reached Ambassador Wilson in Ankara on July 7, 1945. His top secret wire is document 701 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The source was the Turkish foreign ministry's secretary general, Acikalin.

Acikalin said Ankara had cabled Sarper not to discuss any Soviet proposals made on behalf of the Balkan states. Sarper's reply exposed a garble in his earlier cable. No mention of the Balkan states had in fact been made on June 18. What Molotov had said was narrower and vaguer. If an alliance treaty with Turkey were in question, Ankara would have to examine certain considerations Moscow wished to formulate. No one in Ankara yet knew what those considerations might be. The correction removes a point Wilson himself had built on days before.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1001:
The Acting Secretary of State sent this telegram to the Secretary of State at Potsdam on July 31, 1945. It quotes a message Washington had sent to Stockholm five days earlier. That message answers reports that the Soviet government will ask Sweden to hand over interned German airplanes as war booty.

The Stockholm envoy is told to resist that claim, ideally with British and French support. America cannot accept the war booty theory for such property, the text says. All German assets now sit under the joint jurisdiction of the four occupying powers. None may be removed or disposed of without the consent of the Allied Control Commission.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1101:
Staff of the United States team at Potsdam drafted this working paper on 24 July 1945. Working papers were not public statements. They were the private groundwork that helped American negotiators agree on a stand before they faced the British and Soviet teams across the table.

A paper of this kind set out facts, options, and a line to take on one of the questions before the summit. Germany's future was the chief subject at Potsdam, and the first full week was spent mapping out stands. The text lets readers watch Washington sort out its own case in private. It is the homework behind the handshakes, kept in the official record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1201:
Hayter, secretary general of the British team, wrote to Cannon, a first secretary at the embassy in Portugal, on 17 July 1945. The note went out on the summit's opening day. It joined the Potsdam staff to a quiet post in a neutral land.

Portugal had stayed out of the war, but its Atlantic islands held air bases the Allies prized. Lisbon was also a crossroads of spies, trade, and quiet deals. A line from the summit's staff to the Lisbon post shows how far Potsdam's reach ran. Small posts felt the great talks too, and this note is the touch.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1301:
The Acting Secretary of State set down this memorandum on 24 July 1945. It dates from the middle of the summit, the day the Polish deputy premier sent his three papers and the talks pressed on Poland. Grew's note is the home office thinking on paper at that hour.

Memoranda from the acting chief fixed stands for the desks in Washington. They also formed the record of what the home half of the department knew and when it knew it. This one belongs to that Washington layer of the Potsdam story. It shows the department's stand-in chief at his daily work.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1401:
François Lacoste, the French chargé in Washington, wrote to the acting secretary of state on 6 August 1945. A chargé speaks for his country when the ambassador is away. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Lacoste's letter came five days after the Caffery and Bidault exchange in Paris, and it works the same tie from the other capital. While ambassadors talked in Paris, the French mission in Washington kept its own channel warm. The date also fell on the day of the Hiroshima bombing, though the letter belongs to the ordinary flow of allied business. Together, the papers show a two-ended alliance being tended at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-101: An editorial note placed after document 710 in the second Potsdam volume speaks in the editors' voice rather than a delegate's. Notes of this kind in the Foreign Relations series supply context the wartime papers assume. They can explain a missing text or point to a parallel record. The note serves readers moving through the heavy staff traffic of the conference's second week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d801:
Schoenfeld wrote from Hungary on July 18, 1945, in document 801. The representative in Budapest kept up a steady flow of reports as Potsdam began. This letter went to the Acting Secretary of State. It joined the growing Hungary file in the second Potsdam volume.

Daily reporting from a small post builds a record no summary can match. Schoenfeld tracked a country remaking itself under foreign eyes. Readers see the armistice regime from within, week by week. The document shows the value of presence: Washington knew Hungary through this man's desk. His letters let the summit's Balkan choices be judged against ground truth.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d901:
American staff prepared this undated working paper, titled simply Gold, for talks at Potsdam around July 18, 1945. A note on the copy says it served discussion with the President. The subject is the gold captured from Germany, worth about 250 million dollars in American hands.

Most of that gold, the paper says, can be traced to banks in freed nations, and pledges may bind America to return it. Calling the gold war booty might break those pledges and weaken the gold standard. The paper suggests treating the claim as a bargaining chip instead. It could trade against other nations' views on restitution and booty, and against French claims.
gao-gaoreports-b-296401: Sigmatech took its August 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Tech firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-296501: Computers Universal took its August 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Tech firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298401: Armor Group International Training took its August 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Training deals get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-309301: A recess appointment hit GAO's docket in June 2007 — was Sam Fox's install by the book? The ruling parses the constitutional fine print on presidential appointments made while Congress was away. The call is civics with teeth: who may serve, and by whose leave.
gao-gaoreports-b-310801: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by NHIC Corporation. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-b-400101: This 2008 GAO ruling is about designated Employee Agent at Jim Swistowicz. GAO's legal decisions tell agencies what federal funding law allows. Agencies follow these rulings when spending federal funds. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-101: Mad cow feed rules were better but shaky in 2005, and GAO's report says FDA's ban management improved, though oversight gaps limited the program. The review checks the feed troughs. The cattle's dinner deserved the guard. The gaps had to close.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-201: Cross-agency contracts for the wars were a mess in 2005, and GAO's report says the DOD and Interior orders had problems. The review exposes the tangled paperwork behind the military's shopping. The troops deserved cleaner deals. The problems had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-301: Major weapons programs got a GAO scorecard in 2005, and the report assesses the selected programs. The review grades the arsenal. The taxpayers' war machines deserved the honest marks. The programs were assessed. The taxpayers' war machines deserved the honest marks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-701: TANF domestic violence screening needed HHS guidance in 2005, and GAO's report says state approaches could benefit from federal direction. The findings demand the help. The report warns that the abused deserved careful screening. The guidance had to come. The abused deserved careful screening.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-801: DHS's visa security program needed stronger management in 2005, and GAO's report says actions were required. The findings demand the upgrades. The report warns that the visa gates deserved tight running. The management had to be strengthened. The visa gates deserved tight running.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-401: Federal long-term care insurance compared well in 2006, and GAO's report says the program stacked up favorably against other products. The findings give the nod. The report warns that the claims trends still deserved watching. The program had to stay sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-501: The Energy Department's small business goal needed better management in 2006, and GAO's report says improved program management could help achieve it. The findings prescribe the fix. The report warns that the atomic agency's small-firm dollars deserved care. The management had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1001: Pocket jets were coming in 2007 — and GAO's report asks what very light jets would do to crowded skies. The findings weigh the factors that could jam or smooth the national airspace. The report reads as an early weather vane for a flying revolution that partly arrived.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1101: When companies went bust in 2007, workers' pensions and health plans hung in the balance — and GAO's report maps the legal maze. Bankruptcy courts juggled retiree promises against creditor claims with murky rules. The findings show how Chapter 11 could quietly rewrite the deal workers thought they had.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-201: Trade-displaced farmers got a new lifeline in 2007, and GAO's report says the program helped some, though participation stayed limited. The findings balance the good and the gaps. The report warns that the help had to reach the hurting. The farmers needed the word out.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-301: First responders still could not talk to each other in 2007 — GAO's report says making their radios truly connect remained unfinished work. The findings demand real interoperability at last. The report's warning: the next disaster should not be met with dead air.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-401: Title insurance was a consumer blind spot in 2007 — GAO's report says the industry needed tougher watchdogs to truly protect homebuyers. The findings target the cozy deals in detail. The report's cause: the biggest purchase of a life should never hide its fees.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-301: GAO published its findings on disaster Cost Estimates: FEMA Can Improve Its Learning from Past Experience and Management of Disaster-Related Resources in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-401: GAO published its findings on US Coins: The Federal Reserve Banks Are Fulfilling Coin Demand, but Optimal Inventory Ranges Are Undefined in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gauss-disquisitiones-1801:
Carl Friedrich Gauss founds modern number theory in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, in Latin from 1801. Primes, congruences, and quadratic forms fall into one grand order. Gauss wrote the book at twenty-four, gathering two thousand years of scattered results into a new and rigorous science of whole numbers.

His proofs set a standard of rigor that math still honors today. Modular arithmetic, now basic to computing, grows from these pages in time. Few first books have ever remade a field so completely at once. The work made Gauss the prince of mathematicians in his peers' eyes, a title the centuries since have never seen fit to revoke.
godelmann-tractatus-de-magis-1601:
Johann Georg Godelmann was a Lutheran jurist at Rostock whose Tractatus de Magis, Veneficis et Lamiis appeared in 1601. The Latin title names his subjects: magicians, poisoners, and witches. The treatise is legal and theological at once, a framework for witch prosecution.

Godelmann sorts kinds of magic, weighs what proofs a court should demand, and questions confessions won by torture. He accepts witchcraft as real yet urges judges toward care that many of his peers lacked. German courts and writers on witchcraft cited his framework through the great trial years that followed. His Latin kept the argument inside the courts and universities that ran the trials.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FerrieDavidWill: A Civil Air Patrol file, numbered 301, concerns David William Ferrie of New Orleans. Ferrie piloted for the Patrol and led cadets, and he later became a figure in the Kennedy assassination story. The surviving record identifies the file by his name and its Patrol number but gives no contents or dates, so it stands as a labeled service file on Ferrie.
grotius-rights-war-peace-campbell-1901:
A C Campbell published his translation of Hugo Grotius's Rights of War and Peace in 1901. Grotius, a Dutch lawyer and scholar, wrote the work in 1625 while in exile in Paris. Europe was deep in the Thirty Years' War, and Grotius asked what law could bind even enemies.

Grotius grounded the law of nations in natural law, rules reason finds in human nature itself. He treated when war is just, what may be done in war, and how treaties and embassies bind states. Later writers built international law on his frame. Campbell's English made the founding text of international law handy for students of law, history, and diplomacy.
haeckel-riddle-of-universe-1901:
Ernst Haeckel published The Riddle of the Universe in German in 1899; this English edition followed in 1901. The book is his monist manifesto: one substance, one law, no split between matter and spirit. It sold in the hundreds of thousands and made Haeckel a world figure.

He applies evolution to everything: the cosmos, the mind, and morals alike. Soul, free will, and a personal God all dissolve into nature's single order. Churches and dualist philosophers answered with fury, and the book became the prime target of the anti-Darwinian backlash. Read today, it is the fullest statement of scientific materialism as a popular creed.
harnack-christianity-saunders-1901:
Adolf von Harnack's What Is Christianity? appears in Thomas Bailey Saunders's translation of 1901. The book prints Harnack's Berlin lectures of 1900. Harnack, a great church historian, seeks the essence of Christianity in Jesus's own teaching. The gospel, he argues, centers on God as father, the infinite worth of the soul, and the ethic of love.

Creeds, rituals, and dogmas are later shells around that kernel. This kernel-and-husk method defines liberal Protestant theology. The lectures drew crowds and stirred wide debate. Critics from several sides attacked his reduction of the faith. The book remains liberal Protestantism's manifesto in classic form. It is short, clear, and still argued over.
heartsease-or-the-brother-s-wife-pg2601: Charlotte Mary Yonge's Heartsease: the brother's wife and the moral trials of family. Tractarian fiction at its most beloved, earnest and moving. A Victorian classic of conscience. Yonge's moral earnestness never wavers, earnest and moving throughout.
herbart-outlines-educational-doctrine-19:
Herbart's Outlines of Educational Doctrine, in Alexis F Lange's translation of 1901, renders the Umriss pädagogischer Vorlesungen of 1841. The German title means an outline of his lectures on education. The book is exactly that: Johann Friedrich Herbart's concise system of teaching doctrine, set down late in his career.

Herbart compresses decades of thought on government, instruction, and discipline into a handbook for the teacher. The end is character; the means are lessons that build a many-sided interest in the pupil. Lange's version served American normal schools in the years when Herbart's method ruled them. Readers who want Herbart's whole pedagogy in brief compass start here.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume one of Carlyle's Frederick the Great: the origins, Brandenburg, and the rise of the Hohenzollerns. The foundation of the vast work, laying the ground for the hero's entrance. Carlyle's research is exhaustive, his prose already thundering. The beginning of a thirteen-year labor.
history-of-the-revolt-of-the-netherlands: Schiller opens his history of the Dutch revolt against Spain — the eighty-year struggle that created the Netherlands. This first volume sets the scene: Spanish oppression, the rise of William of Orange, and a people's awakening. Written with the passion of a lover of liberty.
hobhouse-mind-evolution-1901:
Mind in Evolution, published in 1901, is L. T. Hobhouse's study of mind, from animal instinct to human reason, told as one long growth. The British sociologist and philosopher set out to trace a single line of growth where others saw a gulf between beast and man.

He examines learning, memory, and reasoning in animals, then follows the rise of concepts, language, and self-aware thought in man. Mind, for Hobhouse, is nature becoming aware of its own ends. The book's patient natural history supported his liberal faith in progress. It stands as a founding work of its field in Britain.
jenner-origin-vaccine-inoculation-1801:
In 1801 Edward Jenner summed up his discovery in The Origin of the Vaccine Inoculation. The short London pamphlet tells how vaccination began. Jenner draws a careful line between casual cowpox, caught from cattle, and the disease raised by inoculation. That line mattered for safe practice.

He traces the vaccine from its dairy country roots to its spread among doctors. The history is concise, written by the man who made it. Doubts about where the protection came from get direct answers. The pamphlet served as his own brief account of the origin. Readers meet the discovery in its founder's words. It closes his run of tracts.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-01:
Reuben Gold Thwaites edited the Jesuit Relations in 73 volumes, issued from 1896 onward. Volume 1, from 1896, covers Acadia in the years 1610 to 1613. French priests had just reached the Atlantic shore of North America.

Their reports tell of the first missions among the Mi'kmaq people. Readers learn how the priests lived, what they ate, and how talks began. Hard winters, scarce food, and new tongues fill the letters home. The set became the base record for early North America. This opening volume shows first contact as the men on the ground saw it.
jewett-tory-lover-1901:
Jewett's Tory Lover, issued at Boston in 1901, is her lone historical novel. Chapter titles move from The Sea-Wolf and The Parting Feast to The Sailing of the Ranger. Later heads promise the coast of France and a run against wind and tide.

The scene is the New England coast during the American Revolution. A young woman finds her heart torn between a patriot officer and a dashing Loyalist, the tory lover of the title. War splits families and towns as each side must choose. Jewett's gift for place and character turns the romance into a thoughtful portrait of a community under strain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mocatta-10901:
Mocatta, an Anglo-Jewish family among the earliest resettlers of Jews in England, is traced by Joseph Jacobs, Isidore Harris, and Goodman Lipkin in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The entry's longest life is David Mocatta, a London architect born in 1806. His father Moses translated the anti-missionary classic Faith Strengthened; the son studied architecture in Italy under masters including Sir John Soane.

David Mocatta became the railway age's house architect, employed often by the London, Brighton, and South Coast Railway, and inherited fortunes from his father and his brother Benjamin. When Soane left his collection to the nation, Mocatta was made a trustee. He also helped found the West London Reform Synagogue and directed the building of its Margaret Street home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-ju:
Mordecai ben Judah Löb of Lemberg was a commentator of the later seventeenth century and rabbi of Dobri in Bohemia, given four lines by Wilhelm Bacher and S. J. Levinson in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His name rides on a single work: Ma'amar Mordekai, a commentary on the Pentateuch.

The book reached print only after his death, at Dyhernfurth in 1719, edited by his son Judah Löb, who served as shammash — beadle and factotum — of the Breslau community. The entry's sources are the standard bibliographies, Steinschneider, Fürst, Azulai, and Benjacob, which is to say the man survives as an entry in other men's catalogues and in his son's piety.
journal-of-discourses-vol-01:
Volume One of the Journal of Discourses appeared in 1854 in Liverpool and Utah's orbit. George D. Watt reported the sermons in shorthand as they were preached. Brigham Young and the apostles speak here in the Salt Lake Tabernacle.

Doctrine, prophecy, and the building of Zion fill these early discourses. The speakers teach a young church how to live, work, and endure. Their voice is urgent, plain, and sure of divine guidance throughout. No source shows Mormonism's founding generation thinking aloud quite like this. Scholars cite the Journal more than any other Mormon record of its age.
king-henry-vi-part-2-pg1501: England slides toward civil war in this edition of Shakespeare's second Henry VI play. Queen Margaret schemes, good Duke Humphrey falls, and Jack Cade's rebels storm London. Politics as blood sport, in early Shakespeare's fierce style.
kipling-kim-1901:
Rudyard Kipling published Kim in 1901, a novel set in India under British rule. Kim is an Irish orphan who grows up on the streets of Lahore. He joins a Tibetan lama on a search for a sacred river. At the same time, spies draw him into the Great Game against Russia.

Kim moves between worlds: bazaars, trains, schools, and mountain passes. He loves India in all its noise and color, yet his training pulls him toward secret work. The lama seeks freedom from the wheel of life. Their bond gives the adventure its heart. Many call Kim Kipling's finest novel.
mackenzie-voyages-montreal-1801:
Alexander Mackenzie, a Scottish fur trader in Canada, published his Voyages from Montreal in 1801. He had reached the Arctic Ocean by river in 1789 and crossed the Rockies to the Pacific in 1793. His Pacific crossing was the first across North America north of Mexico.

Mackenzie tells of canoe brigades, rapids, and tense meetings with Native nations whose help he needed. The river that bears his name carried him to the northern sea. His Pacific route crossed passes Lewis and Clark later followed in part. The book pushed Britain and America to race for the West he had opened.
maitland-english-law-renaissance-1901:
Frederic Maitland gave the Rede Lecture at Cambridge in 1901 on English Law and the Renaissance. The short work asks how the common law survived when Roman law was sweeping the Continent. Maitland called the Tudor age the law's crisis.

He shows how the Inns of Court, the Year Books, and a stubborn profession kept English law alive. Littleton and Coke become heroes of a quiet resistance. Had England taken Roman law whole, its history would differ deeply. The lecture is brief, brilliant, and quotable, the classic statement of England's legal exceptionalism by its greatest legal historian. It fits in an evening's reading.
mctaggart-hegelian-cosmology-1901:
Studies in Hegelian Cosmology, published in 1901, continues McTaggart's critical project from method to system. Having tested Hegel's dialectic, he now rebuilds its picture of the whole: the Absolute, the self, and the case for the soul's survival of death.

McTaggart argues that reality is a system of selves bound by love, and that each self is eternal, perceiving the whole from its own point. His famous argument for survival after death is developed here in Hegelian dress. The reasoning is intricate and perfectly clear at once. The book shows idealism's strangest fruit: a godless system of eternal, loving selves.
mead-apollonius-tyana-1901:

monsieur-madame-and-be-be-volume-01: The first volume of Monsieur, Madame and Bebe sketches happy married life. Droz's witty pen captures young love and new parenthood. Bright humor and warm tenderness alternate throughout. A beloved French classic of the fireside.
murray-antarctic-manual-1901:

myvyrian-archaiology-wales-1801:

plos-pbio-0020301:
Teresa A. Venezia, Akil A. Merchant, Carlos A. Ramos, and their team profiled blood stem cells in PLOS Biology in 2004. Hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow make all blood cells. Most of the time they rest quietly, a state called quiescence, then wake to divide when blood is needed.

The authors compared gene activity in resting and dividing stem cells. Each state has a clear molecular signature. Those signatures help labs tell true stem cells from their more mature offspring, a long-standing problem. They also hint at what keeps stem cells resting safely for a lifetime. Protecting that rest may matter for both aging and leukemia.
plos-pone-0000001:
Maria Almeida, Alexandre Steiner, Luiz Branco, and co-authors probed odd behavior in very sick animals for PLOS ONE in 2006. In endotoxin shock, the body's extreme response to bacterial toxin, animals seek cold instead of warmth. That cold-seeking may help survival, but the brain circuits behind it were unclear.

The team mapped the neural substrate, the brain areas that drive the behavior during shock. Knowing which regions switch an animal from fever-like warmth seeking to cooling itself matters for understanding how the brain manages body heat in crisis. The work links a survival behavior to specific brain machinery, a step toward explaining temperature control in severe infection.
plos-pone-0000101:
Mette Lundsby Jensen, Sangeeta Dave, Maarten Schim van der Loeff, and a large team studied smallpox vaccine scars in Guinea-Bissau in PLOS ONE in 2006. Vaccinia, the virus in the smallpox vaccine, leaves a lasting scar. Adults in rural areas who bore the scar lived longer than those without it, even though smallpox itself was gone.

That survival edge hints that the vaccine trains the immune system in broader ways than its target disease. Such off-target effects are now a major field of study. A cheap sign, a visible scar, made this long term follow-up possible. The finding adds weight to the idea that live vaccines can shape general health, for better or worse, beyond their named germ.
plos-pone-0000201:
Antonin Lamazière, Fabienne Burlina, Claude Wolf, and colleagues published this biophysics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Certain bioactive peptides, short protein chains with biological effects, can reshape cell membranes without being metabolized. The authors study how these peptides make membranes form tubes and become leaky.

Membrane tubulation and permeability changes sit behind many peptide actions, from killing bacteria to delivering drugs. The authors characterize the physical process in model membranes. Understanding it helps researchers design peptides that enter cells on purpose, and avoid membrane damage where it is not wanted.
plos-pone-0000301:
Ivan Laponogov, Dennis A. Veselkov, Maninder K. Sohi, and colleagues published this structural biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Topoisomerase IV is a bacterial enzyme that untangles DNA, and quinolone antibiotics attack it. The authors solved the crystal structure of its breakage-reunion domain from Streptococcus pneumoniae, at near two-angstrom resolution for the 55-kilodalton piece.

The structure is the first for a quinolone target from a gram-positive bacterium, and it shows a closed dimer shape. Seeing the drug's target in atomic detail explains how quinolones bind and how bacteria mutate to resist them. That guides the design of antibiotics that stay ahead of resistance.
plos-pone-0000401:
Joshua M. Epstein and colleagues modeled whether limiting flights could slow a flu pandemic, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Modern flu spreads worldwide on air routes, and cutting travel is one of the few levers governments can pull early. The team used computer simulation to weigh the value of international air travel restrictions.

Models like this test how much delay restrictions buy and what that delay is worth for preparing vaccines and hospital care. The results inform pandemic planning, where decisions must be made before a real outbreak shows its speed. The study is part of a wider effort to rehearse emergencies in software so that real responses rest on tested reasoning.
plos-pone-0000501:
Duygu Balcan and colleagues analyzed the wiring diagram of yeast gene control, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. In yeast, transcription factors switch genes on by binding response elements, short DNA sites near genes. The team showed that the information coded in those response elements accounts for most of the topological properties of the transcriptional regulation network.

Topology means the network's large-scale structure: which factors control many genes, which genes share controllers. If binding-site information alone explains that structure, the network's shape is written in the DNA more directly than expected. The result supports reading regulatory networks from sequence, a goal of systems biology.
plos-pone-0000601:
Karen A. Ocorr, Timothy Crawley, and Greg Gibson measured inherited differences in heart failure in fruit flies, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Genetic variation for cardiac dysfunction in Drosophila means some fly strains' hearts fail under stress while others endure, mirroring human variation in heart disease.

Flies allow large, controlled crosses that human studies cannot, so the genes behind the variation can actually be found. Heart disease genes discovered in flies have repeatedly pointed to human counterparts. The paper establishes the variation itself, the raw material every gene hunt needs first.
plos-pone-0000701:
Arndt Telschow, Matthias Flor, Yutaka Kobayashi and colleagues modeled how a bacterium can push insect populations toward splitting. Their 2007 PLOS ONE subject was Wolbachia, among the most common endosymbionts, bacteria living inside other cells, in the world. In many insects, Wolbachia causes cytoplasmic incompatibility: eggs of uninfected females fail when fertilized by infected males.

That one-way barrier is called unidirectional, and it can separate populations that meet along a mainland-island pattern. The model asks when such a barrier helps drive speciation. A microbe that blocks mating is a surprising engine of species formation, and this study maps the conditions under which it could work.
plos-pone-0000801:
Robert J. Wood, Michael D. Maynard-Smith, Victoria L. Robinson and colleagues measured the speed of a plague bacterium enzyme, in PLOS ONE in 2007. DNA adenine methylation plays an important role in several critical bacterial processes: mismatch repair, timing of DNA replication, and control of gene expression. Dependence of bacterial virulence on the enzyme Dam, DNA adenine methyltransferase, had raised interest in it as a drug target.

Their kinetic analysis used a hemimethylated molecular break light oligonucleotide, a DNA probe that lights up when cut. Kinetics describe how fast an enzyme works and what slows it. Precise rates are what drug designers need to build inhibitors against Yersinia pestis enzymes.
plos-pone-0000901:
Marc Naguib and Andrea Nemitz studied how early hunger marks male zebra finches for life, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Conditions in early growth shape many traits that decide how well an animal does. Most work stops at the youngest stages, but later youth may matter too.

Working with juvenile males, the pair tested how nutritional stress at that stage affects plumage ornaments, the feather displays males show. They also followed how attractive those males were as adults. Poor food in youth, it seems, leaves visible marks that persist. For females choosing mates, such marks may be honest news about a male's past.
plos-pone-0001001:
Li Chen, Prabhat Jha, Bridget Stirling and colleagues reviewed sixty-eight studies of sexual risk for HIV across Africa, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A common assumption says that as HIV epidemics mature, risky behaviors like many partners or paid sex matter less. Under that view, spread becomes general and early risk factors fade.

The team ran a systematic overview of epidemiological studies from early and advanced epidemics in sub-Saharan Africa. Systematic reviews pool many studies to answer what single sites cannot. Whether risk factors hold their force decides where prevention money should go. The review gives planners a firmer basis than assumption.
plos-pone-0001101:
Tanilu Grande, Andrea Bernasconi, Annette Erhart and colleagues trialed a malaria drug pair in the Peruvian Amazon, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Multi drug resistant falciparum malaria is a serious problem in that region. The standing first line treatment there was mefloquine plus artesunate.

Their randomised open label trial compared that standard with dihydroartemisinin plus piperaquine. A head to head trial in the place where resistance bites is the only way to know if a switch is warranted. Malaria drug policy turns on such regional trials, since resistance maps differ valley by valley. The results feed directly into Peruvian treatment guidance.
plos-pone-0001201:
Is beauty in art a matter of taste alone, or does the brain have built-in preferences? Cinzia Di Dio, Emiliano Macaluso, and Giacomo Rizzolatti used brain imaging to address that question in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They showed viewers with no training in art criticism images of Classical and Renaissance sculptures.

The study, sometimes discussed under the phrase the golden beauty, asked whether an objective, biological basis exists for the experience of beauty. Brain responses to the masterpieces were compared to responses to altered versions. The work is an early example of neuroaesthetics, the study of art through the brain.
plos-pone-0001301:
Cytotoxic T lymphocytes kill infected cells, but how fast they kill inside a living body has been hard to measure. Andrew Yates and colleagues revisited those estimates in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Recent experiments had made it possible to estimate in vivo killing rates by tracking target cells in the spleen.

The authors present several refinements to a method that quantifies killing using a dynamical model. Better estimates matter because killing rates feed into models of how infections are controlled and how vaccines work. Their refinements address biases that earlier estimates carried.
plos-pone-0001401:
Benoît Baras and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a flu shot tested in ferrets. A bird flu strain called H5N1 had spread wide and killed many of the people it infected. A shot that guards across strains was a clear need. The team tested a shot boosted with an added agent that lifts immune response.

Ferrets given the shot were then exposed to a lethal dose of H5N1. The authors report that the shot gave cross protection in this test. Ferrets are a close model for human flu. Proof in them is a key step before human trials of a pandemic shot can move ahead.
plos-pone-0001501:
Rick Bright and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a new kind of flu shot. Shots are a cheap, strong guard against seasonal and pandemic flu. Most shots are grown in eggs, which is slow in a crisis. The team built a virus like particle that bears parts of the H5N1 bird flu strain.

That particle drew immune replies that guarded across H5N1 branches. Cross branch guard is the hard test for a bird flu shot. A particle shot can be made fast without live virus or eggs. The work backs this route as a stockpile option for a future outbreak.
plos-pone-0001601:
Tamás Dolinay and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on lung harm from breathing machines. Ventilators save lives, but their stretch can wound the lung itself. A family of signal enzymes had been tied to that wound, yet its exact role was not firm. The team tested mice with and without key members of that family.

Mice that lacked one such enzyme bore the ventilator stretch far better. That names the enzyme as a driver, not a bystander, in the harm. Blocking it could let ventilators run with less self inflicted damage. The work gives intensive care a clear molecular lead.
plos-pone-0001701:
Christoph W. Michalski, Milena Maier, Mert Erkan, and their co-authors tested cannabis-like compounds on scar-forming pancreas cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Pancreatic stellate cells drive the fibrosis, or scarring, of chronic pancreatitis. Cannabinoids had been shown to ease liver fibrosis, but their effects on the pancreas and its stellate cells were unknown.

The team first checked the endocannabinoid system, the body's own cannabis-like signaling, in human chronic pancreatitis tissue. They then tested blocking and boosting it in cultured stellate cells, and report reduced markers of inflammation and fibrosis. The full text gives the tissue results and the cell experiments. The findings mark a possible drug direction for a disease with few treatments.
plos-pone-0001801:
Fiona Robinson, Richard J. Jackson, and Christopher W. J. Smith studied why a human splicing protein is hard to make in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Organisms differ widely in how often they use each synonymous codon, the alternative spellings for the same amino acid. Proteins with spellings rare in the host are made poorly, because the matching transfer RNAs are scarce. Codon content is often adjusted when making foreign proteins.

The team reports that expression of human nPTB, a regulator of RNA splicing, is limited by extreme suboptimal codon content in its own gene. The full text gives the sequence analysis and expression tests. A gene throttling itself through its own spelling is a neat case of regulation built into the code.
plos-pone-0001901:
Eli Zamir, Benjamin Geiger, and Zvi Kam built a sharper imaging method in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cells grip the world at adhesion sites, dense spots where many proteins crowd together. These spots shift fast and mix dozens of parts. Seeing who sits where, and when, calls for imaging at fine detail in both space and time.

Their method uses many colors at once to map the makeup of each adhesion site as it changes. Sorting the sites into true molecular domains shows how the parts sort themselves. Better maps of these grip points help explain how cells move, a key step in wound healing and in cancer spread.
plos-pone-0002001:
Martijn van den Heuvel, Rene Mandl, and Hilleke Hulshoff Pol grouped resting brain areas by shared activity, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Even at rest, far-apart brain regions can rise and fall in sync, forming resting-state networks. Finding those groups in scan data is often done by picking a seed area first, which biases the result.

The trio used normalized cut clustering, a method that splits a network into coherent groups without a seed. Applied to resting scans, it sorts regions into networks on the data's own terms. Unbiased maps of rest networks aid studies of how the brain is wired in health and illness.
plos-pone-0002101:
Benjamin Cowling and co-authors reported early results of a household flu trial in Hong Kong, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Data were sparse on whether non-pharmaceutical steps can reduce the spread of influenza. Face masks and hand hygiene are cheap and need no prescription, yet their real effect in homes was barely tested.

The team ran a cluster randomized trial among Hong Kong household members, testing the feasibility and efficacy of masks and hand hygiene at cutting transmission. Early findings guide whether such simple steps earn a place in flu plans beside vaccines and drugs.
plos-pone-0002201:
Todd Castoe and co-authors found signs of fast adaptation in the core energy proteins of snakes. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Big shifts in basic metabolic proteins are rare, and they are even more rarely tied to major turns in evolution. Snakes, though, rebuilt their bodies radically, losing limbs and evolving extreme feeding habits.

The team ran broad analyses on snake mitochondrial proteins, the machines that release energy in cells. They found several lines of evidence that these proteins underwent adaptive evolution. The finding suggests that even the most basic cell machinery can be reshaped when a lineage takes up a new way of life.
plos-pone-0002301:
Patrick Zeeuwen, Gys de Jongh, Diana Rodijk-Olthuis, and co-authors compared the skin defenses of psoriasis and eczema patients, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Both psoriasis and atopic dermatitis are chronic inflamed skin diseases. For decades both were blamed mainly on overactive T cells and their inflaming signals, a view that guided treatment.

The authors argue the skin's own host defense differs between the two diseases by genetic program. Epidermal defense proteins, the skin's built-in germ fighters, are set differently in each condition. That contrast helps explain why psoriasis patients rarely get skin infections while eczema patients often do, and it reframes both diseases.
plos-pone-0002401:
Hayashi and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Hisaki Hayashi, Tsutomu Kume, among others. Its subject is foxc Transcription Factors Directly Regulate Dll4 and Hey2 Expression by Interacting with the VEGF-Notch Signaling Pathways in Endothelial Cells. Recent studies have shown that in the developing embryo, arterial and venous identity is established by genetic mechanisms before circulation begins.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002501:
Casas and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names François Casas, Laurence Pessemesse, Stéphanie Grandemange, among others. Its subject is overexpression of the Mitochondrial T3 Receptor p43 Induces a Shift in Skeletal Muscle Fiber Types. In previous studies, we have characterized a new hormonal pathway involving a mitochondrial T3 receptor (p43) acting as a mitochondrial transcription factor.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002601:
Ohta, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Hidenobu Ohta, Shanhai Xu, Takahiro Moriya, among others. Its subject is maternal Feeding Controls Fetal Biological Clock. The daily rhythms of a fetus are widely thought to be shaped by oscillators in the mother's brain.

Those maternal rhythms are coupled to the environmental light-dark cycle. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002701:
In 2008, Angela M. Verdoni and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was defects in actin dynamics lead to an autoinflammatory condition through the upregulation of CXCL5. The catalog record names Angela M. Verdoni first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Destrin (DSTN) is a member of the ADF/cofilin family of proteins and is an important regulator of actin dynamics. A further point appears in the abstract. The primary function of destrin is to depolymerize filamentous actin into its monomeric form and promote filament severing. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002801:
In 2008, Marion Faigle and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was ATP release from vascular endothelia occurs across cx43 hemichannels and is attenuated during hypoxia. Authorship is credited in the record to Marion Faigle and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Extracellular ATP is an important signaling molecule for vascular adaptation to limited oxygen availability (hypoxia). A further point appears in the abstract. Here, we pursued the contribution of vascular endothelia to extracellular ATP release under hypoxic conditions. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002901:
Sol Efroni, Liran Carmel, Carl Schaefer and colleagues offered a new way in 2008 to judge whether a gene is on or off. They treat each gene as being in one of two states, Up or Down, based on measured activity levels. Real biology is messier, but the simple split can be useful if done with care.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors argue that a gene's state comes from stacking several transcriptional behaviors on top of each other. Their technique turns raw numbers into that call. Gene expression analysts gain a tool for sorting active from quiet genes across large datasets.
plos-pone-0003001:
Nicole Harb, Trevor Archer and Noboru Sato examined how self-renewing stem cells hold together in 2008. Embryonic stem cells grow as coherent colonies with tight cell contact. Communication between cells helps set cell identity, but the machinery of those contacts in stem cells was not fully mapped.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors identify the Rho-Rock-myosin signaling axis as the system that determines cell-cell integrity in these colonies. That axis controls tension in the cell's actin skeleton. Labs growing pluripotent stem cells can use the finding to keep colonies healthy and uniform. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003101: Fabrice Paganin, Laurent Schouler, Laurent Cuissard and colleagues reported airway and esophageal stenting in advanced esophageal cancer with pulmonary involvement in a 2008 PLOS ONE clinical article. A stent is a small tube placed to keep a blocked passage open, here in both the food pipe and the airway. The catalog record gives title, authors, and year, with an abstract snippet repeating the title. The article concerns patients whose advanced cancer affects both passages, a group facing severe breathing and swallowing problems.
plos-pone-0003201:
Maninder K. Sohi and co-authors report a hard lab case in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper, on the germ that causes most community pneumonia. Streptococcus pneumoniae also causes bronchitis, meningitis and ear and sinus infections. As drug resistance rose, labs turned to new targets in the germ, among them an enzyme called topoisomerase IV.

The team grew crystals of one part of that enzyme, ParC55, and solved its shape, a slow and tricky task. Readers see the grind behind a protein map, not just the end result. Such maps help chemists design new drugs against tough germs.
plos-pone-0003301:
Katerina V. Savelieva and co-authors breed mice that make far less serotonin in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Serotonin is a nerve signal with roles in the brain and the rest of the body. Two enzymes, TPH1 and TPH2, set the pace of its making. The team used gene targeting to knock out both enzymes in mice.

The title reports serotonin fell sharply and behaviour changed in tests that respond to antidepressant drugs. Readers see what broad serotonin loss does to a mammal. The mice help test what those drug-sensitive behaviour tests truly show about mood and nerves.
plos-pone-0003401:
Madeleine J. H. van Oppen and colleagues traced coral travel in this 2008 genetics study. The coral they studied mostly settles its young near home reefs. Such local habits should keep reef groups apart and distinct. The team read DNA from coral groups spread across wide distances.

The DNA carried signs of recent travel over long distances. Some young corals had crossed the gaps between far-apart reefs. That hidden movement links reefs into one larger network. Reef protection works better when planners know how young corals move between sites. Reef rescue plans depend on links like these between far-apart sites.
plos-pone-0003501:
Ntombizodumo B. Mkwanazi and co-authors studied HIV testing in rural South Africa in this 2008 paper. Rapid tests promise same-day results for pregnant women. Faster results should raise testing uptake and improve care. The team followed a cohort of about twelve thousand women.

They compared uptake before and after rapid testing arrived. Same-day speed did not reliably improve uptake or result collection. Counselors offered testing, yet barriers beyond speed remained. Programs may need trust and access work alongside faster kits. Pregnant women are a key group for HIV care, since treatment also guards the baby.
plos-pone-0003601:
Héla Saïdi, Marie-Thérèse Melki, and Marie-Lise Gougeon studied killer cell talks with dendritic cells in this 2008 paper. HIV exploits dendritic cells to spread and to dodge antiviral immunity. The fate of those cells depends heavily on contact with natural killer cells. How that cross-talk works was the open question.

A signal called HMGB1 proved to drive key effects. Through it, NK and dendritic cell contact triggered HIV replication and persistence. Immune teamwork can thus switch the virus back on. The finding warns vaccine designers about this double-edged interaction. Dendritic cells are also the first target of many vaccine designs.
plos-pone-0003701:
Zhen Sun, Zhi Chen, Xiaoli Hou, and colleagues published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Tests that detect many DNA targets at once save time, cost, and labor. They still need primers, short starter pieces, for each target. The team built primers meant to work universally instead.

Their primers are pentamers made of locked nucleic acid, chains just five units long. These short primers can start DNA copying across genomic DNA in PCR. The design gives labs a tool for amplifying many targets at once without crafting a primer set for each.
plos-pone-0003801:
Kathryn E. Hacker, Caroline Martz Lee, and W. Kimryn Rathmell published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Von Hippel-Lindau disease brings a family of blood-vessel-rich tumors, including kidney cancer. Different VHL mutations cause different mixes of these tumors. Loss of VHL normally breaks the cell's control of its oxygen sensor.

The team tested type 2B mutations of the VHL gene. Those mutations kept the VBC protein complex's form and function intact. Retained function of that kind helps explain why these mutations produce their particular spectrum of tumors rather than the full disease.
plos-pone-0003901:
Elizabeth Whittaker, Andrea Gordon, and Beate Kampmann asked whether a blood marker beats the standard TB test in children in 2008. Current blood tests for tuberculosis measure interferon-gamma release. Those tests cannot tell active disease from latent, silent infection. That gap makes diagnosis in children especially hard.

Their PLOS ONE article weighs a second marker called IP-10 against interferon-gamma. Both markers can be read from a blood sample. A marker that splits active from latent cases would change care for children. The study adds evidence toward a clearer test for a disease that hides well.
plos-pone-0004001:
Fabrice Lopez, Julien Textoris, Aurélie Bergon, and co-authors built a tool for mining gene data in 2008. Public microarray archives keep growing every year. Making that mass of data usable is a growing challenge. The archive they target is the Gene Expression Omnibus.

Their PLOS ONE article presents TranscriptomeBrowser for exploring that archive. They used a clustering method to pull out groups of co-regulated genes. Such groups reveal how genes work together across many experiments. The toolbox helps researchers reuse data that would otherwise sit idle. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004101:
Xueping Zhou, Michael R. Miller, Md Motaleb, and co-authors tested Lyme disease germ products on blood vessels in 2008. Borrelia burgdorferi is the spirochete behind Lyme disease. It causes inflammation across the body and in target tissues. Much of that inflammation is driven by the host's own response.

Their PLOS ONE article perfused single rat mesentery vessels directly. Fluid from virulent germ cultures raised vessel permeability. Leaky vessels help explain swelling and tissue damage in Lyme disease. The setup isolates secreted factors from the germs themselves. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004201:
Daijun Ling and colleagues published this Alzheimer's study in PLOS ONE in 2009. How neurons die across the brain in Alzheimer's disease is still not settled after two decades of work. The amyloid beta 42 peptide is believed to play a causative role in the disease.

The team expressed the human form of this peptide in fruit flies and followed the damage. They report that the resulting neurodegeneration runs through an injury of the autophagic-lysosomal system, the cell's waste-disposal route, and that the injury depends on age. The fly model ties a famous peptide to the failure of cellular housekeeping.
plos-pone-0004301:
Tsuyoshi Watanabe and colleagues published this circadian genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Screening the offspring of wild-caught mice, the team isolated a new circadian variant, an animal whose internal clock behaves abnormally. At first the variant kept weak, fading rhythms, and then lost rhythmicity after transfer from light-dark cycles to constant conditions.

The authors present a genetic and molecular analysis of these wild-derived arrhythmic mice. A clock gene variant caught from wild mice can reveal parts of the timing machinery that laboratory strains have lost. The variant came from Mus musculus castaneus, a wild subspecies.
plos-pone-0004401:
Lab tests guide care only if normal ranges fit the patients tested. Many African countries had no reference ranges of their own. Trials there often used ranges derived from other populations. Etienne Karita, Nzeera Ketter, Matt Price, and co-authors set out to fix that. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper gives blood test ranges for healthy adults. The ranges cover eastern and southern Africa.

The team followed standards from the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute. Their intervals cover hematology and biochemistry tests. Local ranges help trial teams judge side effects fairly. A value normal for local adults should not be flagged as harm. The work fills a long-standing gap for clinics and trials across the region.
plos-pone-0004501:
Two peptides cut from a hormone protein prompt white blood cells to take in calcium, report Dan Zhang, Peiman Shooshtarizadeh, Benoit-Joseph Laventie, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The source protein is chromogranin A, stored in the same glands that release adrenaline-like hormones under stress. Pieces of it act as antimicrobial peptides, part of the body's first-line defense.

The cells studied are neutrophils, the most common white blood cells and key fighters of infection. The peptides made calcium flow into them through a route controlled by calmodulin and an enzyme called calcium-independent phospholipase A2. Calcium entry is a classic wake-up signal for immune cells. The work shows stress hormones and infection defense are chemically linked at the source.
plos-pone-0004601:
Genes for catching sunlight are spread unevenly across the oceans, map Thomas Bibby, Yinan Zhang, and Min Chen in PLOS ONE in 2009. Photosynthetic light-harvesting proteins are the mechanism by which energy enters the marine ecosystem. The dominant photosynthetic bacteria in the open ocean are two cyanobacterial groups, Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus. They are defined by two distinct light-harvesting systems.

The authors study the biogeography of those genes: where each system thrives, and why. Light color and quality change with depth and with distance from shore, favoring different harvesters. A gene-level map of ocean photosynthesis helps predict how marine food webs will shift as oceans warm and stratify. Nearly all sea life runs on the energy these tiny cells capture.
plos-pone-0004701:
Guenter Albrecht-Buehler laid out a new way to read and map long stretches of genome DNA, in PLOS ONE in 2009. His method uses short runs of two DNA letters and the segments next to them. He reports that most of these runs share chains of a repeated four letter motif.

Segments rich in one letter were often found just before these runs. Blocks known as Alu elements also sat nearby, though not as part of the runs. A clear map of such landmarks could help readers move through huge genomes. It treats DNA layout itself as a guide, not just the genes.
plos-pone-0004801:
Elizabeth Gaskell and colleagues described a unique dual activity amino acid hydroxylase in Toxoplasma gondii, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The genome of this protozoan parasite contains two genes encoding tyrosine hydroxylase, an enzyme that produces L-DOPA. The encoded enzymes metabolize phenylalanine as well as tyrosine, with substrate preference for tyrosine in lab tests of their catalytic activity.

Thus the enzymes catabolize phenylalanine by hydroxylation as a second activity. Dual activity is unusual for this enzyme family. The finding matters because Toxoplasma alters host behavior and brain chemistry. Its own dopamine pathway may help to those effects. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004901:
Ariel Cohen and colleagues studied protein dynamics in single human cells combining test and theory, in PLOS ONE in 2009. A current challenge is knowledge dynamics of protein circuits in living human cells. The team addressed whether equations define dynamics and variability of a protein over time. Using accurate time lapse measurements of glowing proteins in single cells tracked for many generations under controlled conditions.

Protein levels fluctuate with surprisingly simple rules. Cell to cell variability follows predictable distributions. Theory and test converge quantitatively. Single cell biology becomes predictive science. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be.
plos-pone-0005001:
Blood platelets have no nucleus. Yet they carry a surprising variety of proteins. Karen Power and colleagues screened them at large scale in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used high-throughput proteomics. The target was alternative splicing. Splicing lets one gene produce several protein versions, called isoforms.

The screen detected novel splice isoforms in human platelets. These tiny cell fragments run a richer protein program than assumed. The catalog is a resource for platelet research. It may also matter for clotting disorders. Platelets are central to both healing and heart attacks. Knowing their full protein set sharpens both fields.
plos-pone-0005101:
The cerebellum coordinates movement and more. Its circuits were hard to trace in living people. Cristina Granziera and colleagues imaged them directly in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used diffusion spectrum imaging. That method follows water movement along nerve fibers. It reveals the wiring of the human cerebellum in vivo.

The structural wiring matched the functional circuits. That match gives the images real meaning. Many diseases, congenital and acquired, alter cerebellar function. A structural map can become a biomarker for them. Doctors could spot circuit damage before symptoms worsen. The work brings cerebellar diagnosis closer to the circuit level. It also validates the imaging method against known anatomy.
plos-pone-0005201:
Hearing depends on tiny bristles, called stereocilia, that project from hair cells in the inner ear. Those bundles move on their own and feed energy into sound sensing, which sharpens hearing. Breneman and colleagues proposed in PLOS ONE in 2009 that the bundles work as flexoelectric motors.

Flexoelectric materials turn bending into electric charge, and charge into force. The study argues this effect powers the bundle motor whose mechanism had been unknown. If right, the idea explains how the ear reaches its striking sensitivity, and it may guide designs for better hearing devices.
plos-pone-0005301:
Coenzyme Q is a fat-soluble antioxidant made inside mitochondria by a set of COQ gene products. It helps cells survive stress, including chemotherapy. Brea-Calvo and colleagues showed in PLOS ONE in 2009 what switches that production up when cells are under attack.

Survival depended on the NF-kB signal raising transcription of the coenzyme Q building pathway. Cells that could not mount that rise died more easily under treatment. For cancer therapy, the circuit is a shield worth targeting, since blocking it could make chemotherapy hit harder. A shield that helps a cell live through drug stress can help a tumor live too, so this path cuts both ways. Must be read with care in each case.
plos-pone-0005401:
Non-small cell lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in Western countries, largely because it spreads. The biology behind that metastatic capacity is not well understood. Gibbons and colleagues derived gene expression signatures of spreading in a mouse model in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The genetic mouse model of lung adenocarcinoma let the team compare tumors by their ability to metastasize. Expression signatures separated high-spreading tumors from low-spreading ones.
