Such signatures may forecast patient risk and reveal the pathways a tumor uses to travel. A mouse tumor with a known gene flaw is a clean test bed, since spread can be timed and checked. And a gene mark found there can then be sought in the tumors of men and women.
plos-pone-0005501:
Kyoung-Jae Won and colleagues built a method to find gene control regions in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Finding where control proteins bind on human DNA from the code alone is hard. Binding sites do tend to be kept similar across species, which gives one clue.

The authors combined that clue with other signs to pick out whole control modules, not just single sites. Modules are clusters of sites that work together to switch a gene on in the right tissue. Better maps of these modules help explain how genes are timed and why some changes cause disease.
plos-pone-0005601:
Elizabeth Long, Brandie Millen, and Paul Kubes compared immune triggers from bacteria in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Sensors called Toll-like receptors spot patterns that betray invading microbes. Several bacterial parts trigger one sensor, TLR2, but they plug into it in slightly different ways.

The team compared a cell wall part, lipoteichoic acid, with other TLR2 triggers. The responses it caused were distinct from the rest, not just weaker or stronger. Distinct responses mean the immune system can tell bacterial parts apart in finer detail than a simple alarm model suggests. The study also shows that one sensor can send more than one kind of message, a point drug makers must keep in mind.
plos-pone-0005701:
Anna Sandebring and co-authors studied in 2009 what goes wrong inside cells that lack a working PINK1 gene. Faults in PINK1 cause a form of Parkinson's disease that runs in families. Earlier work showed PINK1 affects both the health and the shape of mitochondria, the cell's power plants.

The team linked the shape changes to a protein called Drp1, which helps split mitochondria. A second protein, calcineurin, controls Drp1 by removing chemical tags from it. When PINK1 is missing, that control shifts and mitochondria suffer. The chain gives drug hunters new points where they might step in.
plos-pone-0005801:
Reginia Yan and co-authors measured finger length ratios across twenty inbred mouse strains in 2009. The ratio of the second to fourth finger differs by sex in many species, lower in males than females. In humans it is thought to reflect hormone exposure before birth.

Mouse strains offer a controlled way to test how much of the ratio is genetic. The team found real differences between strains, showing the trait can be mapped and bred. That opens lab studies of what the ratio truly signals. Human claims about finger ratios often outrun the evidence; mouse genetics can supply firmer ground.
plos-pone-0005901:
Jeffrey Lozier and Nicholas Mills combined habitat models with gene-flow analysis in 2009 to read the recent history of a parasitoid wasp. The wasp attacks aphids across a wide range around the Mediterranean. Its populations may have split apart in separate refuges.

Climate-based niche models pointed to where the wasp could live in the past. Genetic data on gene flow matched a pattern of recent isolation in those separate pockets. Two independent tools agreeing strengthens the story. Such wasps are used in pest control, so their population structure guides releases.
plos-pone-0006001:
Insects change form as they grow, guided by two hormones working in concert. Denisa Liszeková, Maja Polakovičová, Milan Beňo and colleagues focused on one of them, juvenile hormone, in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses a modeling method called 3D QSAR in the fruit fly Drosophila to ask which features of a molecule drive the hormone's action.

A shape-and-activity map of this kind shows which parts of a molecule matter and which can change. Such maps guide the design of compounds that mimic or block the hormone. Since pests also run on juvenile hormone, the work has a practical edge: it can inform insecticides that break a pest's growth while sparing other life.
plos-pone-0006101:
A light receptor is useless if it never reaches the cell's light-catching surface. Ines Kock, Natalia Bulgakova, Elisabeth Knust and colleagues mapped the address label on the fly's rhodopsin in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper targets Drosophila rhodopsin, the receptor at the heart of fly vision and eye development, and tests which of its parts guide its trafficking.

Helix 8, a short segment inside the cell, is required for correct targeting, while the far tail tip is not, the title reports. Human rhodopsin mutations in the same region cause blindness, so the fly map has direct medical echoes. The result sorts the receptor's true address label from dispensable parts.
plos-pone-0006201:
Jumping genes called transposons cut themselves out of one DNA spot and paste into another. Julien Bischerour and Ronald Chalmers studied the bacterial transposon Tn10 in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Its cutting enzyme uses one active site for both DNA strands, bending the DNA into a hairpin shape along the way.

The team describes an active flip and capture move, in which a DNA base flips out and is caught for the reaction. Base flipping lets the enzyme reach parts of the DNA that are normally tucked away. Knowing the steps in detail explains how jumping genes move so reliably. It also informs work on gene editing tools built from similar enzymes.
plos-pone-0006301:
Ancient grain DNA can show how crops changed as farmers moved them to new homes. Sarah Palmer and colleagues studied barley from Qasr Ibrim, an archaeological site in Nubia, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Barley there carries a two-row form unique to the region upriver of the Nile's first cataract, with distinctive side bracts.

Genetic evidence traces a shift from six-row to two-row barley over time. That local change indicates adaptation to the Nubian environment. Crops evolve under farming, not just in the wild. Ancient samples let scientists watch that evolution directly instead of guessing from modern plants.
plos-pone-0006401:
Fish show more variety in how sex is decided than any other vertebrate group. Irene Pala and colleagues characterised the sex determination cascade in the Squalius alburnoides complex in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The complex has a hybrid, polyploid genome, and knowledge of sex cascades in fish is scarce despite their diversity.

The study gives an initial characterisation of the cascade elements in that unusual genome context. Hybrids with several genome copies test how sex pathways stay stable. First maps like this enable comparisons across fish species. They also inform breeding of farmed fish.
plos-pone-0006501:
Steven Potkin and co-authors hunted genes tied to brain shrinkage in Alzheimer's disease for PLOS ONE in 2009. Apart from the APOE e4 allele, the common genetic risk factors for sporadic Alzheimer's were unknown. The team completed a genome-wide association study on several hundred subjects. They treated hippocampal atrophy, shrinkage of a memory area, as a quantitative trait.

Using a measurable brain trait can sharpen a gene hunt beyond diagnosis alone. Their study reports novel susceptibility loci linked to that trait. Each locus is a lead for understanding how Alzheimer's develops. The approach shows the value of brain imaging measures in genetic studies of dementia.
plos-pone-0006601:
Justin Wood studied how visual memory holds objects in PLOS ONE in 2009. How do people sustain a visual representation of the environment? Many researchers argue a single visual working memory system sustains non-spatial object information. Wood tests that claim directly.

His title reports distinct visual working memory systems for view-dependent and view-invariant representation. Remembering an object's appearance from one angle uses a different system than remembering its identity from any angle. Two systems explain data that one system cannot. The result refines a basic model of how we hold the visual world in mind.
plos-pone-0006701:
Yunqi Li, Ambrish Roy, and Yang Zhang built a fast tool for protein work in PLOS ONE in 2009. Half of all atoms in a protein are hydrogen atoms. Where they sit decides how bonds form in the protein. It also matters when scientists polish a protein's shape. Yet most known protein shapes leave the hydrogen atoms out.

Their tool, called HAAD, fills in the missing hydrogen atoms. It does so fast and with care. With the atoms in place, scientists can study bonds in full. Polishing a rough shape also works far better. The tool serves shapes found in the lab and shapes built by computer models.
plos-pone-0006801:
Marleen B. Schippers and colleagues scanned people's brains during a charades game in PLOS ONE in 2009. Communication lets humans coordinate behavior powerfully. At its core, it transfers mental content between brains. Spoken language is only one channel for that transfer. Gestures carry meaning without any words.

Volunteers played charades inside an fMRI scanner. The team asked whether mirror areas or mentalizing areas drive gestural communication. Mirror areas respond when we watch others act. Mentalizing areas handle thoughts about others' minds. Knowing which systems support gesture clarifies how communication began. It also informs how the brain handles sign language and pantomime.
plos-pone-0006901:
Garmay Leung and Michael B. Eisen hunted gene switches by the words in their code in PLOS ONE in 2009. Spotting switch zones in a genome is still a hard ask. Code is vast, and proven switch zones keep piling up. Most switches still hide in seas of code. The team set out a plain way to hunt them by word use.

Switch zones share a cast of code words. The hunt sets the word cast of one zone next to that of the next. A close match flags a zone as a switch in wait. A plain hunt that works is gold for genome notes. It tells labs which zones to test first with bench work.
plos-pone-0007001:
Laura Tiemann, Jutta Reidt, Lorena Esposito, and colleagues assessed brain outcomes after a neck artery procedure in PLOS ONE in 2009. Carotid angioplasty with stent placement widens a narrowed artery to the brain. Few studies had checked patients' thinking skills afterward. Results so far were partly inconsistent.

The team tested patients with high-grade narrowing before and after treatment. They also scanned brains for new ischemic lesions using diffusion weighted imaging. Then they matched cognitive changes against those lesions. Linking silent scan spots to real thinking losses matters for judging the procedure's true risks.
plos-pone-0007101:
Graham Cooke, Kirsty Little, Ruth Bland, and colleagues assessed children's HIV care in South Africa in PLOS ONE in 2009. In regions where adult HIV rates are extremely high, many infants remain at risk. Getting infected infants into care and treatment quickly is a persistent challenge. The team studied public clinics in rural South Africa.

They explored how far the primary care system reached HIV-infected children in time. Delays at this level cost lives that treatment could save. The study shows where the chain from testing to treatment breaks. Fixing those breaks is cheaper than building parallel systems.
plos-pone-0007201: Jesse L. Clark, Andres G. Lescano, Kelika A. Konda, and colleagues wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on sexually transmitted infections in urban Peru. Their subject is syndromic management, a method that treats patients based on symptom patterns. Clinics use this approach when lab testing is limited or slow. The authors connect that management style to wider STI control in city settings. Quick treatment can limit further spread. It also protects patients who may not return for test results.
plos-pone-0007301:
Partha Bhagavatula, Charles Claudianos, Michael Ibbotson, and colleagues studied how pet birds judge landing targets in 2009. Much research covers how birds navigate long distances. Far less was known about detecting targets, avoiding obstacles, and orchestrating smooth landings at close range in everyday flight.

The authors examine budgerigars as they land. They study how visual features, especially edges, guide the final approach. Their PLOS ONE paper measures landing behavior against changing visual scenes. Understanding edge detection in landing birds informs both animal vision science and small flying robot design work. The study treats the final seconds of flight as its main subject.
plos-pone-0007401:
Yong Wang and Pei-Yuan Qian improved bacterial identification primers for environmental DNA studies in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Bacterial 16S ribosomal DNA pieces are widely used to classify uncultured bacteria. Primers target conservative regions of those genes to amplify variable regions that carry taxonomic information useful for naming environmental microbes.

The authors identify conservative fragments in bacterial 16S rRNA genes. They use those fragments to design better primers for metagenomic studies. Good primers decide which bacteria a survey can even see. Their design work supports more complete censuses of microbial communities in oceans, soils, and guts.
plos-pone-0007501:
Hui Li and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how male germ cells stay immature during mouse development. In the embryo, future egg cells begin meiosis early. Future sperm cells instead pause and wait until after birth. That pause must be actively enforced. The team focused on an enzyme, Cyp26b1, made by the support cells of the developing testis.

They show Cyp26b1 expression in those Sertoli cells is required to hold male germ cells in their undifferentiated state. Without it, the careful timing of sperm development breaks down before birth. The enzyme works by clearing a signal that would otherwise push cells toward meiosis. The study explains one switch behind the different schedules of eggs and sperm. It also clarifies how the testis protects its future fertility.
plos-pone-0007601:
Danilo Menicucci and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the slow waves of deep sleep. During non-REM sleep, the brain swings between silence and bursts of activity. These slow oscillation events appear on the EEG as large waves. Each event starts at some origin site, then sweeps across the scalp. The team mapped that functional structure in sleeping humans.

Charting where waves begin and how they travel reveals the sleeping brain's organization. Origins are not random; they follow preferred routes across the cortex. Those routes likely reflect how regions are wired together. Sleep waves are thought to help consolidate memory, so their paths matter. A map of the traffic shows which neighborhoods talk during the night. The study turns a familiar EEG squiggle into geography.
plos-pone-0007701:
Mo Li and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns a protein called Bub3 and its role in mouse egg cells. When cells divide, a checkpoint system holds the process until every chromosome is attached and lined up. That pause prevents eggs from getting the wrong number of chromosomes.

The authors show that Bub3 helps run this spindle checkpoint during meiosis, the special division that makes eggs. Without proper control, chromosomes can split unevenly. Such errors are a leading cause of miscarriage and birth defects. The study clarifies one guard that keeps egg division accurate.
plos-pone-0007801:
Ferran Garcia-Pichel and Martin Wojciechowski published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It explains how some cyanobacteria came to build ropes out of themselves. These bacteria grow as long filaments that can move. Certain kinds weave or twist their filaments into thick yarns and ropes.

Those ropes can run centimeters long and grip loose ground. The authors trace the evolution of this rope-building capacity. They argue it let filamentous cyanobacteria colonize soil that erodes easily. The study links a simple act of self-assembly to a big step in land colonization by microbes.
plos-pone-0007901:
Elodie Bruel-Jungerman and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It identifies the signal chain behind exercise's boost to the adult brain. Physical exercise raises the birth of new neurons in the dentate gyrus. It also strengthens synaptic plasticity, the tuning of connections.

A kinase called Akt, which protects cells from death, switches on after voluntary exercise. The authors asked whether the PI3K-Akt pathway is required for the benefit. Blocking that signaling pathway blocked the exercise-mediated gains. New neuron growth and plasticity gains both fell. The chain links sweat to brain renewal.
plos-pone-0008001:
Onder Kartal and Oliver Ebenhoh argued that sturdy rest states are a design rule of cell signaling, in PLOS ONE in 2009. A living thing must sense change and answer it without its signals collapsing. Signal networks face steady pressure to stay reliable over ages of evolution.

The authors propose that networks settle into a ground state that shrugs off small knocks. That sturdiness, they argue, is not luck but a trait selection favors. The idea gives modelers a test to apply: a proposed network that breaks under small knocks is likely drawn wrong.
plos-pone-0008101:
Alexandre Madinier and colleagues asked whether the brain's immune cells help or harm after a stroke in rats for PLOS ONE in 2009. A blocked vessel starves brain tissue, and inflammation follows fast. Microglia, the brain's own immune cells, rush in, but their net effect was in dispute.

The team tracked the cells as the injured brain reshaped its links in the days after the stroke. Their activity lined up with changes tied to recovery of function. The answer leans toward help, with timing that matters: the same cells may harm early and heal late, a guide for when to calm them.
plos-pone-0008201:
Reiner A. Veitia and Samuel Bottani wrote a review essay in PLOS ONE in 2009 on genome size and so-called junk DNA. Genome size does not track how complex an organism is. Much DNA does not code for proteins and was long dismissed as junk. Whole genome duplications add large amounts of that DNA at once.

The authors weigh facts and hypotheses about whether junk DNA has a function. Duplications may feed the growth of non-coding DNA over time. If some of that DNA does useful work, the junk label misleads. The essay invites readers to rethink what genomes keep and why.
plos-pone-0008301:
Elia Diestra, Bastien Cayrol, and Véronique Arluison imaged a bacterial protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hfq is involved in many nucleic acid processes in bacteria. One of its best-known jobs is helping small regulatory RNAs control messenger RNA. Those interactions tune gene activity after genes are copied. Where Hfq sits inside the cell was the question.

Using cellular electron microscopy imaging, the team localized the Hfq protein. It sat close to the bacterial membrane. That position may shape which RNAs it meets and regulates. The finding refines the picture of gene control in bacteria.
plos-pone-0008401:
Mark R. Welford and Brian H. Bossak re-examined medieval plague records in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Recent studies noted many inconsistencies between the Black Death and modern plague. Modern data come mostly from Yersinia pestis outbreaks in India and China around 1900. Medieval plagues seemed to behave differently in timing and spread. Season of peak mortality was one such difference.

The authors validated an inverse seasonal peak in medieval plagues. Deaths peaked in the opposite season from modern plague. That mismatch fuels debate over whether the Black Death was truly Y. pestis. Their comparison sharpens a long-running historical question.
plos-pone-0008501:
Diego Vicente and co-authors track a meningitis germ in northern Spain in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Neisseria meningitidis causes invasive disease and changes fast. It swaps DNA at high rates, which creates new variants quickly. Two vaccine campaigns took place in the study period. One in 1997 used an A/C polysaccharide vaccine for young people. The team ask if campaigns shifted the germ's diversity.

They analyze invasive isolates collected from 1997 to 2008. They compare gene diversity before and after each campaign. Such data show if vaccines push the germ toward new types. That matters for planning future meningococcal vaccines in Spain.
plos-pone-0008601:
Huiguang Yi and co-authors read the full sequence of a plasmid in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The plasmid is called pKF3-70. It comes from Klebsiella pneumoniae, a germ that causes many hospital infections. Care of those infections is hindered by strains that resist many drugs. Resistance often spreads on plasmids, small DNA circles that move between germs. The team ask where this plasmid came from.

Their sequence analysis points to a likely origin. The plasmid seems derived from an R100-like plasmid of Escherichia coli. Tracing such origins shows how drug resistance crosses species lines. That knowledge helps track resistance in hospitals.
plos-pone-0008701:
María-Salud García-Ayllón, Iolanda Riba-Llena, Carol Serra-Basante, and colleagues measured an enzyme in the blood of Alzheimer patients. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, acetylcholinesterase, breaks down a key nerve signal chemical. Doctors want a simple blood test that flags Alzheimer disease. Past assays for this enzyme gave unclear answers.

The team used newer methods to size up enzyme levels in plasma. They compared patients with healthy controls of similar age. Levels differed between the groups in ways older tests had missed. A reliable blood marker would make diagnosis cheaper and kinder than brain scans or spinal taps.
plos-pone-0008801:
Roy Chaudhuri, Mohammed Sebaihia, Jon Hobman, and colleagues read the full genome of a diarrhea-causing germ. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The strain, known as 042, is the reference example of enteroaggregative E. coli. Such germs are a leading cause of diarrhea in poor countries. E. coli can also live harmlessly in the gut, so its harmful turn needs explaining.

Sequencing gave the strain's complete genetic blueprint. The team also profiled its metabolism in the lab. Comparing both layers shows which genes support its disease-causing lifestyle. The paired data help outbreak teams recognize close relatives quickly.
plos-pone-0008901:
Christophe Boesch, Camille Bolé, Nadin Eckhardt, and colleagues documented wild chimpanzees adopting orphaned youngsters. Their field study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Deep kindness toward unrelated group members was long called uniquely human. Lab studies of captive chimps seemed to support that claim. Captive settings, though, may hide what wild animals actually do. Forest groups in the Taï region offered years of close observation.

Chimps there adopted orphans, including infants unrelated to them. Adopters fed, carried, and protected their charges for years. Such long, costly care matches adoption in the full sense. The forest evidence dents claims that extended altruism is a human-only trait.
plos-pone-0009001:
Paul Hollenbach and co-authors ran a head-to-head contest between two similar leukaemia drugs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Azacitidine and decitabine are both used against myelodysplastic syndromes and acute myeloid leukaemia. They look alike and work in related ways, yet few studies had compared them directly. The team tested both on leukaemia cell lines grown in the lab.

Side by side, the drugs differed in how they changed gene activity and cell growth. Each one switched genes back on and slowed the cancer cells by its own route. The comparison shows the two are cousins, not twins. Doctors choosing between them gain a clearer picture of what each actually does.
plos-pone-0009101:
Daniel MacLean and David Studholme modelled a plant pathogen's weapon switchboard as a logic circuit, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pseudomonas syringae attacks many crop plants. Its key weapon is a type three secretion system, a molecular syringe. The hrp regulon is the set of genes controlling that syringe.

A Boolean model treats each gene as on or off, nothing between. The model predicted the regulon is tightly regulated, with few loose ends. Simulations showed which switches matter most for arming the system. Simple logic models can guide experiments on costlier real bacteria.
plos-pone-0009201:
Mitsutaka Kadota and colleagues published this cancer genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It uses a family of breast cell lines known as the MCF10A series. The series starts with normal-like mammary cells grown in the lab. Later lines in the series behave like pre-cancer and then cancer.

The team catalogued the genetic changes across all four lines in detail. By comparing the lines in order, they could see which changes arrive as cells step toward tumors. That step-by-step record shows how breast cancer may develop at the DNA level. It also gives other researchers a benchmark set for testing ideas about cancer progression.
plos-pone-0009301:
Morgan Sammons and co-authors published this muscular dystrophy study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Myotonic dystrophy type 2 is an inherited disease causing muscle weakness and stiffness. It shares many features with type 1, including clumps of RNA inside muscle cell nuclei. The type 2 form is caused by a repeated stretch of DNA.

The team studied a protein called ZNF9 and how it boosts production of another protein, ODC. ZNF9 normally helps ribosomes start at an internal entry point on the ODC message. That activation is decreased in type 2 disease. The finding connects the DNA repeat to a concrete failure in protein production.
plos-pone-0009401:
W. Edward Bradley and co-authors published this human genome study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Large deletions, missing chunks of DNA, are rare but can matter for health. The team searched for them in 440 families from Quebec's founder population. Those families were recruited for a study of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

Using DNA from blood, they mapped where large rare deletions fall in the genome. The deletions were not scattered evenly; they clustered in hotspots. Hotspots suggest some genome regions are fragile by their very structure. The map helps geneticists judge which new deletions are likely to be harmful.
plos-pone-0009501:
Jorge Fernandes, Jareeporn Ruangsri, and Viswanath Kiron studied natural antibiotics in Atlantic cod in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cod make small proteins called piscidins that kill germs. These proteins are part of the fish's first line of defense. The family of piscidin genes varies a lot between fish. The team asked whether natural selection has favored new forms of these genes.

Their analysis found signs of positive selection driving the family apart. In other words, new variants were kept because they helped the fish. That is the mark of an arms race with germs. The work matters for cod health, since this fish is vital to fisheries.
plos-pone-0009601:
Rahn Ilsar and colleagues tested new measures of lung blood flow in PLOS ONE in 2010. The lung's smallest vessels are the chief site where its blood flow is controlled. When those vessels are blocked, the lung suffers, yet doctors had no direct test for it. The team assessed two measures: pulmonary flow reserve and an index of microcirculatory resistance. They checked whether the measures can detect small vessel obstruction.

Both measures aim to do for the lung what like tests do for the heart. Early results support their use in spotting hidden blockage. A working test would change how several lung vessel diseases are diagnosed. It would also let doctors track whether treatments reopen the small vessels.
plos-pone-0009701:
Psoriasis makes skin grow too fast, leaving red, scaly patches. Malgorzata Romanowska and colleagues traced one possible trigger in mice and reported it in PLOS ONE in 2010. They switched on PPAR-beta/delta, a protein that helps control how skin cells grow and mature.

Mice with the switch turned on developed skin changes that looked much like human psoriasis. That gives researchers a living model of the disease to study up close. A model driven by one known switch makes it easier to test new treatments. It also helps explain how this pathway may go wrong in patients.
plos-pone-0009801:
Around deep-sea vents, whole animal communities live on chemicals instead of sunlight. Sabine Gollner and colleagues reviewed a family of small crustaceans tied to those places. Their advances appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The family is Dirivultidae, a group of copepods, tiny shrimp-like animals. The authors updated their taxonomy, ecology, and biogeography, meaning their naming, habits, and where they live. Chemosynthetic environments make their own food energy from chemicals, without the sun. The review pulls scattered knowledge about these vent animals into one account. Many of these species are known from only a few specimens.
plos-pone-0009901:
Plants use tiny RNA molecules to silence genes, including those of attacking viruses. Daniel MacLean and colleagues searched for how those small RNAs connect with each other. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Short silencing RNAs are brief RNA pieces that guide gene shutdown. The team found evidence for large complex networks linking them. Silencing can also tune the plant's own genes. A network view replaces the picture of lone RNAs acting alone. Such networks may coordinate whole defense programs in plants. The evidence came from deep scans of plant RNA.
plos-pone-0010001:
The authors were Bret Adams, Sarah Golding, Raj Rao, and others. In 2010 they asked how young human cells repair severe DNA damage. A double-strand break cuts both strands of DNA and can kill a cell or cause cancer. Early stem cells and the nerve cells that grow from them may not repair such breaks the same way.

The authors tracked two guard proteins, ATR and ATM, over time in stem cells and their neural descendants. Their focus was how reliance on each protein shifts as cells mature and change repair routes. The work matters for understanding development, nerve disease, and why young cells guard their DNA so hard.
plos-pone-0010101:
The authors were Bernhard Ross, Bruce Schneider, Joel Snyder, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study measured hearing across the human lifespan. Older adults often struggle to follow speech, partly because hearing rapid changes in sound gets harder with age. Changes in the brain's sound processing have been proposed as one cause.

The team looked for biological markers of gap detection in three age groups. Listeners were young, middle-aged, and older adults. Gap detection is the ability to hear a brief silence inside a sound. Clear markers could lead to better tests and hearing support.
plos-pone-0010201:
The authors were Oliana Carnevali, Luca Tosti, Claudia Speciale, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used zebrafish to test a common plastic chemical. The chemical, DEHP, is a phthalate that spreads widely in the environment. Phthalates have been linked to liver cancer, body malformations, and lower sperm counts in males.

Little data existed on female reproduction, so the team studied egg formation in zebrafish. They found DEHP impairs reproduction by affecting key factors in oogenesis, the making of eggs. The result adds the female side to a risk picture built mostly on male evidence.
plos-pone-0010301:
The authors were Naokazu Inoue, Tatsuya Kasahara, Masahito Ikawa, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study searched for proteins sperm need to fuse with an egg. Only one sperm protein, IZUMO1, had been proven essential for that fusion. IZUMO1 is structurally simple and carries no obvious fusion machinery, so the team assumed other proteins must help complete the process.

They identified a sperm-specific enzyme, ACE3, in mice and disrupted its gene. Testing what happens without ACE3 clarifies the fusion team. Fertility research depends on knowing each required sperm protein, step by step.
plos-pone-0010401:
Charlotte Kvennefors and colleagues surveyed bacteria living on Great Barrier Reef corals in PLOS ONE in 2010. Coral health depends partly on their bacterial partners. Changed bacterial mixes have been linked to coral disease and bleaching. Yet few surveys used enough samples to separate real patterns from noise. The team sampled two common coral species at several sites.

Both the coral species and the site shaped which bacteria were present. Some common partners appeared across most samples anyway. That mix of shared and local bacteria is the study's main picture. Knowing the normal mix is step one in spotting sick corals early. Reef managers need such baselines as oceans warm.
plos-pone-0010501:
Gábor Földes and colleagues compared innate immunity in human embryonic stem cells with adult vessel cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Stem cell therapies are nearing real clinical use. Yet little was known about how these young cells react to injury or infection. Their responses run through sensors called Toll-like receptors, first-line alarms of immunity. The team measured those responses side by side with adult endothelial cells.

If stem cells react weakly or oddly, grafts could behave unexpectedly in inflamed tissue. Knowing their immune profile helps design safe therapies. It may also reveal basic facts about how immunity matures. The study fills a gap that regulators and clinicians both care about. Young cells, it shows, are not just small adults.
plos-pone-0010601:
Kelath Murali Manoj and colleagues offered a new explanation for odd enzyme behavior, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Heme enzymes use an iron-containing group to run chemical reactions. Many of them speed up and slow down in ways that standard rules do not predict.

The authors built a fresh model around a fungal enzyme called chloroperoxidase. Their treatment linked the strange reaction rates to how electrons move during the reaction. The same logic may cover related enzymes in the human liver. A better model could improve how scientists predict drug breakdown and enzyme use in industry.
plos-pone-0010701:
Krisztian Kvell and colleagues studied aging in the thymus, the gland that trains T cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The thymus shrinks steadily after youth. With less training ground, the body makes fewer fresh T cells and fights new infections more weakly. What sets the pace of that shrinking was unclear.

Two factors stood out: a signal called Wnt4 and a nuclear protein named LAP2alpha. Their levels shifted in step with the gland's aging. The authors cast them as pacemakers of the process. If the pace can be slowed, older immune systems might keep making new defenders longer, improving vaccine responses in old age.
plos-pone-0010801:
Elina Hyppönen and colleagues studied vitamin D in the 1958 British birth cohort, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Everyone in the cohort was born in one week of 1958 and has been followed since. Low vitamin D had been proposed as a heart risk factor. The pathways were unclear, with inflammation and blood clotting as leading candidates.

Blood levels of vitamin D were compared with markers of inflammation and clotting. Higher vitamin D tracked with a calmer marker profile, even before any disease appeared. The pattern held after accounting for lifestyle and body weight. Cohort data cannot prove cause, but they show the vitamin D signal in blood long before illness.
plos-pone-0010901:
Peter Tonge, Victor Olariu, Daniel Coca and co-authors published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A uniform-looking group of stem cells can produce many different cell types, and the authors asked why. One possibility is that the cells are not truly uniform at all, but quietly divided into hidden states before any signal tells them to specialize.

They tested human embryonal carcinoma stem cells, which respond to retinoic acid by producing a mix of nerve and non-nerve descendants rather than one uniform type. Their results support the idea that interconvertible substates already exist inside the supposedly uniform population, biasing each cell's future. Tonge and colleagues call this prepatterning. If stem cells start out secretly varied, controlling that variation becomes key to making pure cell batches for research and therapy.
plos-pone-0011001:
Itaru Hayakawa and Hiroshi Kawasaki published this brain wiring study in PLOS ONE in 2010. During development, axons from the two eyes sort into separate territories in the brain's visual relay, the lateral geniculate nucleus. Whether that settled map can still rearrange was known from cats but never charted in detail, so the authors used mice.

Removing one eye after the sorting had finished still triggered rearrangement of the remaining eye's projections within five days. The reshaping ran along two axes of the relay nucleus, faster along one than the other. Hayakawa and Kawasaki provide the quantitative description the field lacked. Their result shows the young visual system keeps a window of structural plasticity after its first map hardens, relevant to treating childhood eye disorders at the right age.
plos-pone-0011101:
Scherzer-Attali, Pellarin, Convertino and colleagues reported Alzheimer research in PLOS ONE in 2010. They tested a hybrid drug built from a quinone and an amino acid in a mouse model of the disease. The drug was designed to stop harmful proteins from clumping in the brain.

In the mouse model, treatment led to a full recovery of disease traits, a striking result for this field. Protein clumps are a core feature of Alzheimer disease, so blocking them strikes at a root process. The team presents the hybrid as a strong lead for drug hunting. More work is needed before any human use can be judged.
plos-pone-0011201:
Lee, Lee, Wilusz and colleagues analyzed unstable RNA messages in muscle for PLOS ONE in 2010. Muscle cells destroy old RNA messages with great precision to keep gene use current. The team searched for short marks in those messages that mark them for decay, and for proteins that read the marks.

One protein, CUGBP1, emerged as a key regulator of message decay in muscle cells. It binds the marked messages and helps control how long they last. That timing tunes how strongly muscle genes act. Faults in such control are tied to muscle disease, so the map of marks and readers has medical value.
plos-pone-0011301:
Lin, McDonough, Sharma and colleagues studied leptospirosis germ grip in PLOS ONE in 2010. To infect, these spiral germs must attach to host tissues. Two surface proteins end in repeated tip regions. The team tested how those tips bind a host protein, fibronectin, and host cells themselves.

The tip repeats enhanced binding to a specific domain of fibronectin and to cells. That defines the germ's fingertips at molecular level. Blocking the grip is a plausible way to stop infection early. The finding aids work on a disease that floods spread worldwide yet gets little research attention.
plos-pone-0011401:
Oshrat Hershkovitz Rokah, Ofer Shpilberg, and Galit Granot reported in 2010 on an enzyme that shields a tumor-suppressing protein from destruction. Cells regularly shred proteins they no longer need, but the protector in this study, a growth-halting form of p63, must survive to do its job. The team tested whether the enzyme NQO1 guards it.

They found that NQO1 protects the p63 form from being shredded, and that this protection supports its power to arrest cell growth. When the guard is missing, the protector falls and the brake on division weakens. The result links an enzyme best known for handling toxic chemicals to direct control of cell growth. For cancer biology, it suggests that losing NQO1 could help damaged cells keep dividing when they should have stopped.
plos-pone-0011501:
Betty Tao and co-authors estimated in 2010 what type 1 diabetes costs in the United States per person. The disease requires lifelong insulin, monitoring, and care for complications, but simple comparisons overstate its cost because patients differ from others in many ways. The team used propensity score matching, pairing each patient with a statistically similar person without diabetes, so the cost gap reflects the disease itself.

Careful accounting of that kind gives policymakers a credible number for what the disease drains from families and the health system. A trusted figure shapes everything from insurance design to research funding arguments. The matching method also sets a standard: cost claims for chronic disease should survive a fair comparison, not rest on raw totals. The paper supplies both the estimate and a cleaner way to make it.
plos-pone-0011601:
Shanta Zimmer and colleagues measured how far pandemic flu had spread in Pittsburgh, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A new H1N1 flu strain emerged in 2009 and spread worldwide within months. Official case counts captured only a fraction of infections, since many sick people never saw a doctor or got tested.

After the second pandemic wave, the team tested blood samples from local residents for flu antibodies. Those antibodies mark past infection even when illness was mild or missed. Their survey gives a truer picture of the pandemic's reach in the city, which helps officials judge immunity levels and plan for later waves.
plos-pone-0011701:
Huiwen Zhao and co-authors bred fruit flies to survive extreme oxygen, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Oxygen is essential, but in excess it damages tissues through oxidative stress in mammals and flies alike. The mechanisms that make some organisms tolerate oxidants while others succumb remain poorly understood.

Through long-term selection over many generations, the team produced a fly strain able to live in very high oxygen that would kill ordinary flies. Studying what changed in the adapted flies reveals the genetic levers of oxygen tolerance. Those levers may one day inform treatments for oxygen-related injury in medicine.
plos-pone-0011801:
Sandra Kümper and Anne Ridley picked apart which grip proteins let prostate cancer cells move, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells link to each other through cadherin proteins, which join inside the cell to partners that include p120ctn. That partner was known to steady cadherins, but the partners' effects on cell movement were less clear.

In DU145 prostate cancer cells, the team tested the grip proteins one by one. Movement and invasion turned out to depend on p120ctn and on P-cadherin. E-cadherin, by contrast, played no such part. That picky result marks clear targets for drugs that aim to slow spread.
plos-pone-0011901:
Hiroki Isomura, Mark Stinski, and Takayuki Murata reported in 2010 on how one human cytomegalovirus gene controls its neighbor. This virus is usually quiet but can cause fatal lung, liver, and gut disease when immunity is suppressed, and it can harm newborns infected before birth. Its many genes switch each other on and off in a timed cascade.

The team showed that the UL76 gene regulates how strongly the UL77 gene next to it is expressed. Small control links like this run the virus's program for copying itself and spreading. Each link mapped is a possible weak point where a future antiviral drug might jam the virus's schedule.
plos-pone-0012001:
Jenia Bugaysen and co-workers recorded in 2010 the electrical behavior of neurons in a deep brain hub that helps control movement. Recordings in primates had split neurons of the globus pallidus external segment into two types: high frequency pausers and low frequency bursters. Whether those types truly reflect the cells' basic properties needed testing.

The study set out to characterize the firing traits of these pallidal neurons in detail. Cell types in this hub matter far beyond anatomy: the globus pallidus is a key station in the circuits that go wrong in Parkinson's disease, and stimulation therapies target this neighborhood. A firmer cell catalog grounds both basic and clinical work.
plos-pone-0012101:
Philip Roelandt, Karen Pauwelyn, Pau Sancho-Bru, and co-authors described a way to grow liver-like cells from stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lab-grown liver cells could help treat liver disease and test new drugs, but making cells that truly act like liver cells is hard. The team started from human embryonic stem cells and from rat adult stem cells with traits of an early gut layer.

Their method copies the steps of natural liver growth, stage by stage. First the cells become the gut layer from which the liver buds, then they mature into cells that act like liver cells. A recipe that works across species gives drug testing and cell therapy a more reliable supply of liver-like cells.
plos-pone-0012201:
Angela Devlin, Ursula Brain, Jehannine Austin, and co-authors studied newborns whose mothers had low mood in pregnancy, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A mother's depression before birth may shape her child's later behavior through chemical marks placed on the baby's genes. One gene that handles the mood chemical serotonin can carry such marks, and a common variant in a folate-processing gene may change how the marks are set.

They measured the gene's methylation in infants at birth against the mother's mood and that variant. Results at birth matter because any influence is caught before upbringing adds its own effects. Findings like these guide how doctors support depressed mothers with the child's long health in mind.
plos-pone-0012301:
Stefanie Redemann, Jacques Pecreaux, Nathan Goehring, and co-authors visualized the forces that position a dividing cell's spindle, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In the one-cell worm embryo, the spindle that splits chromosomes must sit off-center so the daughters differ. Pulling machines anchored at the cell's surface haul on the spindle's poles, stronger at the back than the front, but the pulling sites themselves are hard to see.

Watching tiny dents form in the membrane where the pulling happens made the invisible forces visible. Mapping where pulls occur tests models of how embryos set up body plans from the very first division. It is basic physics of life, measured in a worm a millimeter long.
plos-pone-0012401:
Shilpi Dasgupta, Pisapati Sirisha, Kudugunti Neelaveni and colleagues studied gene patterns in South Indian women with polycystic ovary syndrome, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. PCOS is a common hormone disorder that affects periods, fertility, and metabolism. The androgen receptor gene carries a repeating stretch whose length tunes how strongly male hormones act, and the team tested its link to PCOS.

They compared repeat lengths and X chromosome inactivation patterns between women with PCOS and controls, the first such study in this population. The patterns differed in ways that may raise androgen action. Population-specific data matter, because gene effects found in one group do not always hold in another.
plos-pone-0012501:
Daniella Bianchi-Frias, Funda Vakar-Lopez, Ilsa Coleman and colleagues examined how aging changes the tissue around the prostate, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Age is the top risk factor for prostate diseases, from benign enlargement to cancer. Most attention goes to the gland cells themselves, yet the surrounding microenvironment — the stroma — ages too and constantly talks to those cells.

The team read the molecular and cellular makeup of the aged prostate stroma. It shifts toward states that can encourage abnormal growth. That reframing matters: preventing prostate disease may require treating the neighborhood, not only the gland cells, a view gaining ground across cancer biology.
plos-pone-0012601:
Savas and co-authors searched the genomes of a well known panel of sixty cancer cell lines. The panel, called NCI60, is a standard lab tool for testing cancer drugs. Their 2010 study asked which gene variants track with resistance to selenium, a mineral linked in past surveys to lower cancer risk.

Scanning the whole genome, they found signs pointing to calcium signalling inside the cell. That link suggests selenium resistance works through paths that move calcium signals, not just through the mineral itself. The result gives cancer researchers a new lead on why some cells shrug off selenium.
plos-pone-0012801:
Gil Borlado, Moreno Lastres, Gonzalez Hoyuela and co-authors asked why the same mitochondrial fault makes some patients sicker than others. Complex III is one of the cell's energy engines, and faults in it cause serious disease. Yet the wider mitochondrial DNA background a patient carries can soften or worsen the outcome.

Their 2010 study compared how different mitochondrial backgrounds handle a complex III defect. The background itself changed how the deficiency played out in cells. That means genetic counselling for these diseases should read the whole mitochondrial line, not just the main fault.
plos-pone-0318901:
Keisuke Iida and six colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One analysis of amebiasis, a parasitic gut infection, in Japan over more than two decades of official surveillance data. Earlier work had noticed case counts falling after 2018 and during the pandemic, and the team modeled the trend in segments while profiling cases by sex, age, and prefecture.

Domestically acquired cases in men rose for years, slowed, then dropped sharply between 2018 and 2020 before leveling off. Imported cases fell mainly during the pandemic's travel restrictions. Most patients were men in their forties and fifties living in metropolitan areas. The authors conclude the pandemic dip reflects reduced social and economic activity, not only closed borders, and note case patterns resembling those of HIV in Japan.
plos-pone-0335301:
Fathi Attia, Tom Tregenza, and Ramakrishnan Vasudeva watched red flour beetles for signs that they dodge mating with close relatives. Inbreeding weakens offspring, and stored-grain beetles breed in small pockets where relatives meet often, so avoidance would pay. The team observed courtship directly, then used visible markers to tell which males fathered the young when two competed for one female.

Contrary to the expectation, males courted and mated with sisters slightly more than with strangers. Unrelated males did end up with more adult offspring, but only because inbred young died more often; once survival was counted, fertilization success showed no bias against relatives. In this beetle, the cost of inbreeding is paid in dead offspring rather than prevented by picky mating.
plos-pone-0337401:
Li Zeng and Wee-Yeap Lau built a network model of how extreme financial risk jumps between world markets, and how a country's climate performance changes that spread. They tracked daily market data from 1998 to 2024 alongside the Climate Change Performance Index, using quantile methods that focus on the worst tail events rather than average days. The model is framed around markets deemed too extreme to fail.

Climate-sensitive factors amplified system-wide vulnerability, while strong climate governance acted as a buffer during violent market swings. Risk contributions varied widely by region and era, spiking around major crises. Their nonlinear model also beat standard approaches in backtests. For regulators, the message is that climate policy is not separate from financial stability; it is part of the firewall.
plos-pone-0338001:
Clyson Mutatiri and colleagues interrogated a sacred cow of kidney care using Queensland's chronic kidney disease registry. The sacred cow is the idea that patients referred to specialists late do worse after starting dialysis. Their 2026 cohort study followed 3,775 registry patients. Late referral meant reaching dialysis within a year of first specialist contact. The team modeled deaths while handling the many patients who die before dialysis.

Among those who started treatment, about one in nine had been referred late. Late referral showed no link to dying afterward. Oddly, longer pre-dialysis specialist care carried a tiny statistical link with higher later mortality. The authors read that as an artifact more than a danger. They call for a risk-based definition of late referral instead of a calendar one.
plos-pone-0340201:
Nadia Seifi and colleagues designed a possible mRNA vaccine against HTLV-1, a virus that can cause a form of leukaemia and a paralysing nerve disease. No vaccine against it exists today. Their 2026 paper is a computer-based design study: software picked the two most promising viral proteins, hunted for fragments the immune system can recognise, and stitched those fragments into a virtual vaccine.

Modelling suggested the design has suitable physical properties and docks well with an immune receptor, and simulations kept the pairing stable. The authors stress that all of this is prediction. Only laboratory and animal experiments can show whether the candidate truly protects against the virus.
plos-pone-0341201:
Jessica V Eberle and co-authors in Germany asked a statistical question about breast scans in 2026: in small studies, how much error comes simply from having few patients? They looked at a scan measure used to tell harmless breast lumps from cancer.

They reviewed published studies, then compared the error from small samples with readings from their own hospital group of women with suspicious lumps. They also weighed a second error, the natural wobble in the scan measure itself. Knowing which error dominates tells researchers how large a study must be before its answers can be trusted in clinic decisions.
plos-pone-0342601:
Juanita Gasu and colleagues surveyed Ghanaian quantity surveyors, the cost experts of construction, about their part in reaching the United Nations development goals. Building work touches poverty, health, energy, and the environment, yet surveyors' own contribution to sustainability had been little studied. Eighty-eight professionals from firms registered with the national surveyors' institute answered the questionnaire.

Respondents rated surveyors strongest in social development and education, then in environmental care and resource management, with poverty relief and economic growth close behind. So the profession already shapes several goals through cost advice and project choices. The study also flags gaps between what surveyors could do for the twenty thirty agenda and what they do now, giving firms and trainers a map of where to build skills.
plos-pone-0344401:
Elena Silvia Gardini and seven colleagues follow Swiss children from disadvantaged families to test whether a chemical mark on a stress gene predicts thinking skills, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The mark, DNA methylation near a gene that manages stress hormones, was measured from saliva at age three. Intelligence was tested at age five, in children whose families had joined a home-visiting support programme or a control group.

Higher methylation at age three went with lower IQ at five, working through growing concentration problems. Parents' disagreement fed the same chain from the other end. Encouragingly, the support programme was tied to lower methylation levels. The authors call the evidence preliminary and ask for larger replications.
plos-pone-0345801:
McKenna P. Sperry and Thomas A. O'Neill explore how neurodivergent engineering students experience group work at a Canadian university. Such students have often been shut out of jobs, so their side of teamwork is little known. Their 2026 study interviews students who identify as neurodivergent about working through tasks and conflicts with classmates.

A wish to be understood and recognized ran through the accounts. It shaped how students spoke up, handled friction, and judged whether a team felt safe. Standard theories of social difference, the authors argue, miss these fine points. They turn the students' own ideas into advice for teachers who want team projects to welcome different minds rather than wear them down.
plos-pone-0345901:
Lei and colleagues, in a 2026 survey, measure how well the family caregivers of lung cancer patients understand cancer health information. Caregivers schedule, dose, feed, and comfort, so their grasp of health information shapes patient care. Nearly two hundred caregivers at a large hospital in Sichuan, China, answered two standard literacy scales in late 2024.

Fewer than half showed adequate cancer health literacy. Seven factors tracked with stronger scores, including younger age and more schooling; the abstract singles out age and education among them. The authors describe the study as exploratory, meant to generate ideas rather than settle them. Even so, the headline is plain: most caregivers, the people patients lean on daily, are working with a shaky grasp of the information their role demands. The team argues hospitals should teach caregivers directly, not assume families absorb what patients are told.
plos-pone-0346601:
Elena Marbán-Castro and co-workers ask people who inject drugs and their care providers how they feel about combined self-tests for three infections. One kit could check for HIV and the hepatitis B and C viruses, which spread in similar ways. Their 2026 study runs group talks and interviews in Indonesia and Kyrgyzstan, and tests instruction leaflets from four makers.

Speed, ease, low cost, and privacy topped the list of what users wanted. Testing for several infections at once also appealed strongly. Trying the leaflets led to calls for bigger print and simpler wording. The kits won early approval, but the team says training for providers and counseling for users must come with any rollout.
plos-pone-0346901:
Huakui Sun and Yang Zhou worked out the maths of sending a drone to rescue phone users stuck at the edge of a cell tower's range. Their scheme splits the cell into two zones, with the ground tower serving the inner part and the drone circling the rim to serve the edge. Because both share the same airwaves, the team modelled the interference between them and the random scatter of users.

Calculations show there is a best circling radius and a best flying height for the drone, rather than a simple higher-is-better rule. Dividing the territory sensibly lets each transmitter play to its strengths and lifts the odds that an edge user gets a usable signal. The authors offer the analysis as a planning tool for emergency networks after disasters knock out ordinary infrastructure.
plos-pone-0347301:
Lea Fortmann and Isha Rajbhandari asked whether the park near a school matters as much as the green around it. Their 2026 study used five years of test results from schools in four counties of western Washington State. They compared schools with a public park within eight hundred metres against others, while separately measuring how green each school's surroundings were.

Middle schoolers near a park scored better in both reading and maths, with a higher share meeting state standards. General greenness by itself showed no link to scores at all. Elementary and high school results showed no park effect either. The authors suggest parks offer something extra beyond green views, at least for that middle age group.
plos-pone-0348001:
Jessica Sanchez-Balandran and colleagues time how hard it is to put on and take off workplace exoskeletons, in this 2026 PLOS ONE ergonomics study. Powered or spring-loaded frames can spare industrial workers' backs, but adoption stalls on practicalities: every shift begins with assembly and fitting and ends with removal and storage.

Twenty-nine participants set up and took down exoskeletons while the team counted steps, parts, and usability problems, then linked those complexity measures to completion time and success. Fiddly setup is not a side issue; it predicts whether a device gets deployed at all. The study gives designers a checklist mentality: fewer steps and fewer snags mean the strain-saving tool actually reaches the factory floor.
plos-pone-0348201:
Luka Canton and co-workers ask whether rich and poor parts of France experienced COVID-19 differently across the pandemic's waves. Their 2026 study builds social profiles for all twenty-two large metropolitan areas from census data. It then links those profiles to testing and infection rates. The links are tracked across eight waves, from mid twenty twenty to early twenty twenty-three.

Testing lagged in poorer areas for most waves, while infections ran higher there early on. The infection pattern flipped in later waves, with richer areas recording more cases. Where vaccination coverage ran high, the testing gap between poor and rich areas narrowed. Place and wealth shaped the pandemic's course in France, and the direction of the gap changed over time.
plos-pone-0348501:
Sk Thaherbasha and co-workers work out the math of signal failure in drone-assisted wireless networks that serve several users on shared channels. Drones can lift coverage, but real gear is imperfect: parts distort signals, channel guesses err, and cleanup of overlapping signals falls short. Their 2026 study derives exact formulas for the chance a user's signal drops out under all three flaws at once.

The analysis covers the common two-user case over a fading channel type typical of line-of-sight links. Computer simulations matched the formulas, confirming the math. Knowing how each flaw eats into reliability lets engineers budget for them in advance. Drone networks planned on paper-perfect gear would otherwise promise more than the sky can deliver.
plos-pone-0348601:
Xia Sun and co-workers mine public gene data from failing hearts to guess why a newer pacing method helps some patients more than others. The method paces a natural wiring branch of the heart, but direct molecular data for it are scarce. Their 2026 study merges three heart-failure gene datasets and layers on immune cell counts, gene network maps, and drug matching.

Five genes stood out as hubs, tied to heart growth, stretch sensing, and tissue scarring. Immune cell mixes also shifted in failing hearts. Several existing drug families matched the pathways involved, offering candidates to test. The authors stress these are hypotheses built from stand-in data, to be checked in patients who actually receive the pacing treatment.
plos-pone-0348701:
Lingzhi Zhang, Changhe Yan, and Chunyong Jiang field-tested a foundation method for building railways over karst, the dissolved limestone terrain of southern China that swallows loads unpredictably. Their approach drives gravel piles stiffened with grout while also treating the fractured rock below. They instrumented a real railway embankment project. It let them watch pressures in soil and water, pile forces, and settlement as loads were applied.

Measurements revealed how grouting squeezes and strengthens the surrounding ground, how each pile picks up and sheds load along its length, and how the load splits between piles and soil. Settlement and sideways movement under the embankment stayed controlled. The authors confirm the combined method works in practice and supply the behavioural evidence engineers need to design with it confidently.
plos-pone-0348801:
Qi Liang and colleagues investigated why the cushioning cells of spinal discs age early when oxygen runs low, a key step in disc degeneration and back pain. They focused on a fat-like tag, called S-palmitoylation, placed on a channel protein where mitochondria meet another cell structure. In low-oxygen conditions the tag largely disappeared, and the contact sites between the structures broke down.

Restoring the tag changed the picture. An enzyme that adds the tag protected the channel, calmed calcium overload and harmful oxygen molecules, and kept more cushion cells alive and productive. Cells also made more of the gel-like matrix that keeps discs springy. The work points to this tagging system as a possible drug target for slowing disc aging.
plos-pone-0348901:
Shannon A H Compton, Paul F Tremblay, and co-authors asked whether the age at which gaming becomes frequent predicts problem gaming in adulthood, mirroring a well-known pattern in substance disorders. Their 2026 study modeled adults' gaming histories across childhood and adolescence and sorted them into trajectory groups with distinct shapes.

Four groups emerged. Adults who gamed heavily and consistently from early childhood showed more current problem symptoms than those who started low and rose later. Yet they did not exceed a moderate group whose members also gamed substantially in preschool. Direct analysis confirmed gaming in preschool was the single strongest predictor of adult symptoms, ahead of high school gaming. The authors suggest guidance on when children start gaming deserves the same seriousness as guidance on content.
plos-pone-0349201:
Md Farhad and colleagues hunted for wheat lines that can stand up to wheat blast, a fast spreading fungal disease that threatens harvests in South Asia. They grew more than four hundred varied wheats from Bangladesh across fourteen field trials. Each line was scored for disease and scanned across its genome for markers tied to resistance.

Most lines suffered badly when weather favoured the fungus, though a few stayed resistant in place after place. Genome scanning grouped linked markers into forty five regions tied to resistance. Some match known defence genes, while others look new. Breeders can now use those markers and the tough lines themselves to build wheats that hold up better as the disease spreads.
plos-pone-0349401:
Richard Sias and Harry Turtle revisit a puzzle in health research. People who report a strong sense of purpose tend to live longer. But is purpose itself protective, or are purposeful people simply healthier to begin with? Using a national study of nearly six thousand Americans over fifty, followed from 2006 to 2018, they reproduced the usual result and then tightened the health measurements.

With rough health measures, low-purpose adults showed well over double the death risk in the next four years. With careful, objective health measures, and after removing people already seriously ill, that link shrank sharply. The study does not claim purpose is irrelevant; it shows earlier estimates were inflated by poor health accounting. Purpose research, they argue, must measure starting health with the same care as the outcome.
plos-pone-0349601:
Tathababu Addepalli and co-authors designed a compact four element antenna for millimeter wave 5G and future 6G phones in 2026. High band service needs several antennas working together in a tiny space without spoiling each other's signals.

Starting from a plain patch, the design grew slots and serrated arrow shapes on a small board. It resonates at four bands across the high spectrum. Tests showed strong separation between elements and diversity scores well within global guidance limits. Packing four clean high band channels into a small square is a step toward phones that handle very fast links without bulky hardware.
plos-pone-0349701:
Hunaira Nasreen, Abdul Ghaffar, and Sumaira Yousaf report this 2026 PLOS One plant study on sesame seedlings sprayed with nanoparticles made from chitosan, a shellfish-derived material, loaded with ginger extract. The particles were made by a green method and verified by several instruments at about one hundred fifty nanometers across. Plants received two doses at flowering and capsule stages, alongside conventional pesticide treatments for comparison.

The stronger nanoparticle dose clearly outperformed untreated plants, raising height, leaf area, capsule number and weight, and chlorophyll, while the pesticide treatments lagged. One protective enzyme surged while two others fell, a mixed biochemical picture the authors report as measured. They present the ginger-chitosan spray as a promising, gentler growth booster for sesame farming.
plos-pone-0349801:
Nina M van den Berg and co-authors studied participatory live music with nurses in 2026, asking whether making music with patients lifts compassion satisfaction and eases compassion fatigue. Nurses' emotional wear is a retention risk, and shared music creates moments of connection ordinary care lacks.

Thirty nurses answered surveys before and after a week of the music practice, and interviews explored their own reading of any change. The mixed design pairs small numbers with rich accounts. Music is studied here not as patient therapy but as care for the carers, a framing nursing research rarely takes.
plos-pone-0349901:
Zirije Hasani and colleagues compared four artificial intelligence programs that name plant diseases from leaf photos, asking which could also run on cheap farm equipment. Their 2026 PLOS One study used a well-known leaf image collection with fifteen disease and health classes.

Each program was tested five times so the scores could be checked with statistics rather than luck. One compact model reached the highest accuracy while answering in a few thousandths of a second. The most accurate heavy model was slower, and the smallest model was fastest but notably less accurate. The authors warn the test photos were taken under tidy, controlled conditions.
plos-pone-0350101:
Octavia Pingault and colleagues ran a small pilot study in a French fertility clinic on calming patients during frozen embryo transfer. Fifty women used a virtual reality hypnosis device during the procedure. The team checked whether the device worked smoothly, how anxious women felt before and after, and how patients and staff rated the experience.

The device offers a drug-free way to ease anxiety at a stressful step of IVF care. The researchers also compared pregnancy rates with a similar group of patients who did not use the device. As a pilot, its main value is showing whether a larger trial is practical and what such a trial should measure.
plos-pone-0350201:
Yee Ran Lyu and colleagues used Korea's national health insurance records to study what happens after rotator cuff repair, a common shoulder operation. Their nationwide cohort study, published in 2026, followed patients who had the surgery between 2011 and 2021. It asked how often a second operation was needed and which patient or care factors raised that risk.

Among more than two hundred twenty thousand patients, about seven in every hundred had another operation within three and a half years. Risk was linked to sex, age, insurance type, hospital type, other illnesses, and how soon follow-up care began. The findings give surgeons and patients clearer ground for planning surgery and aftercare.
plos-pone-0350401:
Adul Saengthong and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study comparing the health of long-term shelter dogs under three management styles in Thailand. One shelter gave dogs generous space and an enrichment program, one offered medium space, and a crowded temple-based shelter packed dogs into a single communal area with no enrichment. The team measured stress hormones in feces, oxidative stress, blood metabolism, and gut microbes.

Dogs in the roomy, enriched shelter had the lowest stress hormone levels, normal metabolic readings, and the richest, most balanced gut communities. Dogs in the crowded shelter showed higher stress hormones and a blood marker suggesting strain, plus skewed gut bacteria with lower diversity. The middle shelter fell between on nearly everything. The authors conclude that space and enrichment measurably protect shelter dogs' bodies, not just their behavior.
plos-pone-0350501:
The red imported fire ant has spread northward across China since 2004, and its stings can do real harm. Huimei Chen and colleagues gathered nearly nine thousand well-described sting cases from medical reports, a search platform, and a hospital, for this 2026 PLOS One risk analysis.

Itching and pain followed most stings, and about a third produced blisters or hives. Whole-body allergy struck about one case in thirteen, while shock and death were rare but present. Combining case patterns with where people live, the authors estimate the wider threat to public health and point to southern regions, where the ant is firmly settled, as the priority.
plos-pone-0350801:
Julia Putz and colleagues asked whether probiotic supplements change what people eat, in a small sub-study of a trial on gut health and mood. Fifty-three adults, some with major depression and some healthy, took either a multi-strain probiotic or a placebo twice a day for three months. Food records at the start and at three follow-ups captured any drift in diet.

Most dietary measures barely moved, and only a few changes reached statistical significance. A handful of items, including vitamin D intake and dietary variety, shifted in the healthy group on probiotics, but the pattern was scattered rather than a broad change in appetite. As pilot data, the study mostly warns against big claims: within three months, the supplements did not remake anyone's plate, in depression or in health.
plos-pone-0351301:
Hayler Edu Ibarra Arcila and colleagues read DNA markers from over one hundred and twenty catfish of two species across sixteen hundred kilometres of Colombias Magdalena Cauca river system. Both fish face heavy human pressure. Marker patterns, selection scans, and history modelling tested whether fish form one stock or several, and what drives any split.

Each species held two coexisting genetic stocks with limited mixing. Splits tracked adaptive differences more than distance, likely shaped by the basins twin flood pulse seasons. Stocks trace back millions of years with distinct growth and decline stories. Each stock needs its own management plan, the authors urge, or fishing rules will erase local adaptation.
plos-pone-0351401:
Islamic finance apps follow religious rules while offering modern digital banking, and Ayman Abdalmajeed Alsmadi asked what keeps users in Jordan coming back. This 2026 PLOS One survey drew on about two hundred thirty active users of such services.

Feeling the app is useful, sensing that others approve, trusting the provider, and feeling confident all pushed people to keep using it. Actual use, in turn, strengthened plans to continue. The technical quality of the system changed how strongly use turned into loyalty, while service quality did not show that effect. The model explained a large share of why use continues.
plos-pone-0351501:
Tae Watanabe and colleagues watched what happens to the heart and blood pressure while people get dressed. Dressing sounds easy, yet it needs raised arms, balance shifts, and fine hand work. Groups included healthy adults, people with heart failure for the first time, and people whose heart failure had returned.

Heart rate rose during dressing and just after in all groups, but recovery paths differed. People with returning heart failure peaked later, around five minutes after dressing, and recovered more slowly. Blood pressure also set the groups apart. Counting arm movements alone did not explain the strain. For nurses, slow recovery after a simple daily task flags who needs closer support at home.
plos-pone-0351701:
Jianping Liu and six co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of pancreatic cancer. It asks how the cancer cells rewire their mitochondria, the cell's energy plants, to fuel growth. The team combined single-cell sequencing with bulk tumor data from public archives. They hunted for genes at the crossroads of cell type, mitochondrial metabolism, and patient outcomes.

Three key genes survived the screening. All three were tied to worse survival when highly active. The analysis also mapped how these genes connect to immune cells in the tumor. It found shifts in resting memory T cells and in one class of macrophages. Docking simulations nominated candidate drugs against the genes. The authors frame the trio as leads for grasping, and one day targeting, this resistant cancer.
plos-pone-0352101:
Hidehito Honda and colleagues filmed mock travel-agency consultations and decoded the dance of behaviors between clerk and customer, hunting for the moment a booking is won or lost. Thirty-minute sessions were modeled as switches among hidden interaction states built from gaze, speech, and gesture. Successful and unsuccessful consultations were compared state by state.

In winning sessions, customers typically slipped into a state of clear interest in the offer within the first ten minutes, and once there, they tended to stay. Losing sessions never settled into that state. Early engagement, in other words, behaved like a forecast of the final signature. For sales training, the advice is concrete: the first third of the meeting decides it, and a clerk who cannot spark visible interest early is unlikely to recover by talking longer.
plos-pone-0352201: Omicron COVID-19 — its primary infection’s skin manifestations. This paper documented them. The dermatological catalog distinguished Omicron’s cutaneous signatures. The findings aided diagnosis — the skin as the virus’s bulletin board.
plos-pone-0352401:
Cecilia Sánchez and six colleagues audit who gets prestigious authorship at a conservation health organisation. Their 2026 study covers EcoHealth Alliance, a nonprofit working where human, animal, and environmental health meet. Four hundred fifty-one papers from 2011 to 2022 were catalogued. First and last author spots carry the most career weight. The team recorded the gender and country base of everyone holding those positions, plus who published most prolifically.

Men and high-income-country researchers dominated the prestige slots. Male authors took sixty percent of first and last positions overall. Among the most productive authors, over nine in ten were men. Last authorships, the senior slot, skewed male by nearly three to one. Affiliations from wealthy countries crowded the same positions. Authorship inequity is not abstract: it steers hiring, grants, and promotion. A single organisation's honest mirror gives the wider One Health field numbers it cannot easily wave away.
plos-pone-0352501:
Jeong-An Gim and colleagues searched the tiny cargo of cell-made bubbles for signs of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, a fast-growing blood cancer. Cells shed these bubbles, called extracellular vesicles, loaded with small RNA molecules that can betray what the cell is doing. Working with five leukemia cell lines, including some bred to resist chemotherapy, the team collected the bubbles and read their RNA.

Thousands of small RNAs turned up, and three stood out for shifting in a consistent direction between the cell lines. Two were lower and one higher in the resistant-leaning lines. Because this was an early, exploratory pass on cell lines rather than patients, the three are candidates, not a ready test. Still, a blood test built on bubble cargo could one day spare children repeated bone marrow sampling.
plos-pone-0352701:
Huaibei Xie and three colleagues optimize a robot gripper modeled on a vulture's leg for picking cherry tomatoes, in this 2026 engineering study. Hand-picking the fruit is slow and labor-hungry, and a harvesting robot's hand must close firmly enough to hold a tomato without crushing it. Their three-finger end-effector copies the linked bone chain of a bird's foot. Using a structured experimental design, the team varied four structural dimensions and measured the grip's clearance and enclosure geometry.

A desirability analysis across the responses yielded one best configuration, balancing the space that risks bruising against the wrap that keeps fruit from slipping. Built and tested, the optimized gripper picked successfully at least eighty-eight percent of the time across the fruit sizes trialed. The authors offer the dimensions and method as a design basis for future tomato-harvesting robots.
plos-pone-0352901:
Wen-Long Mao, Ling Zhang, and Tian-Wen Wang published this 2026 laboratory study of damaged geotextile tubes, the sand-filled fabric sausages used in coastal and river works.
