When a tube's wall tears, water pressure and flow can wash its sand out. Their test rig varied tear size, sand type, flow speed, and water gradient to watch failure unfold.

Sand failed in three stages, ending in pulsing outflows, and bigger tears or faster flows sharply lowered the water pressure the fill could withstand. A widely graded sand resisted far better. Mao's results inform safer tube design.
plos-pone-0353201:
Catherine E Bowen, Konrad Pędziwiatr, Marcin Stonawski, and Vegard Skirbekk surveyed 150 Muslim religious leaders across twenty-nine countries about climate change, a constituency with unusual power to move public opinion. Their 2026 exploratory study asked imams, teachers, and seminary students what they believe about the climate, how often they raise it in religious work, and what actions they would champion.

Nearly everyone agreed the climate is changing, but only about half blamed humans mainly, and half saw substantial harm already. Most said Islamic values oblige environmental protection and that leaders should do more. Support ran high for green technology and government spending, but low for dietary change or smaller families. The gap between belief and pulpit practice is the study's headline opportunity.
plos-pone-0353301:
Sseguya and colleagues built a math model in 2026 to test how well treated bed nets hold up against malaria. Nets that kill mosquitoes are a main defense in places where malaria is common. Their power is weakening, though, because mosquitoes are growing resistant to the spray and many people do not use nets every night.

Simulations over nine years showed that how often nets are used matters most for cutting spread. Even with strong starting coverage, protection faded over time, and it faded faster when use was low. Nets with an added booster chemical killed more mosquitoes, but repeated use of plain nets sped up resistance instead.
plos-pone-0353401:
Alieva and colleagues tested gene sequencing for inherited high cholesterol in Uzbek heart patients in a 2026 study. The condition raises cholesterol sharply from birth and causes early heart disease, yet Central Asia had almost no gene data. Ninety-five patients with artery disease and suspected inherited cholesterol problems had three key genes sequenced.

Results were checked against a standard clinical scoring system that rates how likely the inherited condition is. Comparing scores with gene truth shows whether doctors can trust the score locally or miss cases it rates low. First gene data for the region can change testing policy and help families learn their risk before heart attacks strike.
plos-pone-0353701:
Abousenna and colleagues checked an emergency vaccine for foot-and-mouth disease in Egypt in a 2026 study. A virus type never before found in Egypt appeared in 2025, leaving herds guarded against older types but not this one. The team made a vaccine against the new type alone and ran quality, safety, and protection checks.

All vaccine batches passed the standard quality checks in the lab. Blood tests after vaccination measured whether animals built defenses against the virus. Calves given the vaccine were later exposed to the same virus type to test protection, and the team also checked how closely the new type matched an older vaccine type. The work supports a fast, targeted response when a new strain enters a country.
plos-pone-0353801:
Rode and colleagues, in a 2026 study, test whether camera-based pose tracking can measure elbow movement in patients as well as a doctor's eye. Clinicians judge joint range by eye because the precise tools take too long, yet eye estimates are rough. Markerless systems read body pose from a single camera, with no sensors stuck on the skin.

Forty-six patients with shoulder and elbow problems bent and straightened their elbows while two pose systems, a doctor, and a laboratory motion capture setup all measured. For bending, one pose system beat the doctor's eye, matching the lab system closely and detecting smaller real changes. For straightening, the doctor still won, and neither pose system improved on visual judgment. The authors say camera tracking is ready to help with elbow bending checks, even remotely, but not yet for extension.
plos-pone-0354301:
Xuexia Sheng and seven colleagues look closely at one shape of brain white-matter lesion, in this 2026 PLOS ONE imaging study. Bright spots on MRI scans are common with ageing and small-vessel disease, but they come in different forms. Eighty-seven people with such spots had advanced diffusion scans, and nearly a thousand lesions were sorted into dot-like, strip-shaped, and merging types.

Strip-shaped lesions lined up with the brain's fibre direction far more often than the other types, and their diffusion readings sat between the dot-like and merging groups. Fibre tracking confirmed the alignment. The authors read this as a signature of slow nerve-fibre damage from neurodegeneration, distinct from ordinary vessel wear.
plos-pone-0354601:
Nakajima and colleagues, in a 2026 study, test a whole-body MRI method for staging high-risk prostate cancer. Before treatment, doctors must know whether cancer has spread to lymph nodes or bones. Standard checks use CT scans and bone scans, which involve radiation. The MRI method suppresses background signals so spread lights up, and uses no radiation at all.

Thirty-eight men with newly diagnosed high-risk cancer had all three scans before treatment. For lymph node spread, the MRI matched CT exactly in catching cases and avoiding false alarms. For bone spread, a bone scan caught every case, while the MRI missed one in nine, though it raised no false alarms. For lung spread, chest CT saw all cases and the MRI missed one of three. The authors call the MRI acceptable overall and attractive for sparing radiation, while noting chest CT still earns its place.
plos-pone-0354701:
Syed F Javaid led a team of seven authors on this 2026 survey study of anxiety before surgery at their institute. Patients awaiting operations between late 2023 and early 2024 completed a standard anxiety scale, and the team examined how counseling about surgery and anesthesia, and the surgical technique planned, related to worry.

About two in five patients showed strong preoperative anxiety. Being female, younger, and employment details mattered, as did how counseling was delivered and which technique and anesthesia were planned. Searching the internet, notably, did not move anxiety. Javaid suggests targeting counseling to calm the patients most at risk.
plos-pone-0354801:
Katie Ridsdale and co-authors set out in 2026 a multicentre trial on whether toddlers with a common spiral shin fracture need a cast or boot at all. These stable fractures follow minor falls in children from about nine months to four years, and practice varies because both approaches seem safe. The trial will assign children at random to immobilisation or none.

The main measure is parent rated pain a week later, tested against a small allowed difference. Later checks cover pain, hospital visits, pressure sores, fracture shift, movement recovery, painkillers, costs, and family satisfaction. Families helped design the study, which aims to give clinics firm guidance.
plos-pone-0355101:
Omaymah Abulannaz and colleagues study in 2026 whether prescribed opioid exposure before birth links to how ready children are for school in Manitoba, Canada. Health records matched exposed children with similar unexposed peers, and teachers rated development at kindergarten across five areas. A separate comparison looked within families, between siblings where only one was exposed.

In the matched group, exposed children were more often rated vulnerable in every area, with higher risk when exposure came early, lasted longer, or used higher doses. Within families, the sibling gap vanished. The authors read that contrast as a sign that family circumstances, not the drug alone, may drive much of the link.
plos-pone-0355201:
Phongthana Pasookhush led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of drug-response genes in Thailand. They profiled several thousand Thai adults with a gene chip, covering eleven genes known to change how people handle common medicines, then linked the results to hospital prescription records.

Nearly everyone tested carried at least one gene result that could change prescribing. Stomach acid drugs and cholesterol drugs were the most common exposures, and many users had matching gene findings. Pasookhush argues that testing patients before prescribing, starting with those two drug pairs, would bring the largest early benefit in Thai hospitals.
plos-pone-0355301:
Asma Al Rwaily contributes a pure mathematics paper. It defines and studies a new family of operators on Hilbert spaces. Those abstract spaces are used across quantum theory and analysis. Operators are machines that transform such spaces, and named families help mathematicians sort their behavior. The new family is defined by an equation in which a repeated difference-like map, modified by a polynomial, must cancel out.

Within the paper, Al Rwaily proves basic facts about the family. She checks how it behaves under common operations. She also maps its links to better-known families, such as operators that preserve length in a broad sense. The work is theoretical, with no experiments or data. Its value lies in unifying scattered results and giving later researchers a cleaner framework for operator theory.
plos-pone-0355401:
Songyining Ding and co-authors analysed safety reports for heart assist devices used in children. Children's anatomy and blood clotting differ from adults', so adult device data cannot simply be borrowed. Their 2026 study pulled a decade of reports from the United States device reporting database and compared child and adult patterns.

Child reports numbered only a few hundred, against well over a thousand adult reports, and key fields were often missing. Because of those gaps, true complication rates cannot be calculated from the database. Ding and colleagues expose regulatory blind spots and call for a dedicated children's registry with live, multi-source monitoring to catch device risks earlier.
plos-pone-0355601:
Yasser Mohammad Al-Sharo and co-authors present a federated intrusion detector for networks of medical devices that learns without gathering private data. Hospitals cannot pool patient-linked traffic, yet shared learning catches more attack types. Heavy transformer models detect well but cost too much for small devices. Their 2026 design swaps them for state-space sequence blocks with linear cost.

Traffic features are reshaped into short token sequences for the stacked blocks. Formal privacy noise is added during training, and the merging step resists sabotage by rogue participants. Explanation tools operate at several levels so analysts can audit alerts. Al-Sharo and colleagues aim to square accuracy, privacy guarantees, and robustness in one framework.
plos-pone-0356001:
Maarten Niemantsverdriet and colleagues tested a tissue preserving method that avoids formalin, the toxic chemical standard in pathology labs. Their 2026 study used pressurised carbon dioxide to embed tissues without formalin or xylene. They then checked DNA and RNA quality in samples stored for days, two years, and seven years.

DNA from the new method was in better shape than DNA from formalin-fixed tissue. RNA quality was lower in fresher and two-year samples, but similar in the oldest ones. Even so, RNA from most samples still worked for gene sequencing, the main modern test. The results support a safer embedding route that keeps tissue usable for molecular diagnosis.
plos-pone-0356201: Symmetries of spacetime reveal deep physics. This comparative study examined homothetic symmetries of static plane symmetric spacetimes across different energy-momentum tensor representations. The mathematical classification sharpens our picture of how matter shapes geometry.
plos-pone-0356501:
Xylena Reed and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE asking whether aging leaves a permanent mark on cells that have been reprogrammed back to stem cells. DNA methylation, chemical tags on DNA, accumulates age patterns so reliably that scientists use them as aging clocks. The team took blood cells from nearly one hundred healthy adults, reprogrammed them into induced pluripotent stem cells, and compared methylation in both states.

After reprogramming, the age-related signature was largely wiped away: epigenetic clocks read the stem cells as young regardless of donor age. Each cell type also carried its own set of sites where genetic variants influenced methylation, meaning the genetic control map changes with cell state. The reset, they say, supports using donor stem cells to model disease without donor age confounding results, though such cells cannot preserve what aging did to the original tissue.
plos-pone-0356601:
Hongjuan Bai and seven colleagues scan the brains of teenagers with depression, comparing those who injure themselves with those who do not, in this 2026 study. Non-suicidal self-injury is common in this group and poorly understood at the brain level. Just over one hundred thirty adolescents, including healthy controls, lay in a scanner at rest while researchers measured spontaneous activity across brain regions.

Teenagers who self-injured showed stronger activity in a region called the left precuneus, which sits toward the back of the brain and supports self-related thought. That activity, and the region's connection to a nearby visual area, tracked closely with self-injury behavior and with the urge to escape bad feelings. Prediction checks held up well, suggesting these measures could become markers to identify at-risk teenagers and targets for more precise treatment.
plos-pone-0356801:
Alon Tomashin, Ilanit Gordon, and Sebastian Wallot studied how heart signals couple over time, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Hearts do not beat in isolation; patterns in one signal relate to patterns in another, whether within a person or between people. Two analysis tools dominate this work, and the team compared them directly.

Tomashin and his colleagues evaluated multi-dimensional recurrence analysis against cross-correlation, weighing the analytic choices each demands. Their comparison guides researchers toward the right tool for their question, and warns where choices change the answer. Subtle heart coupling is used in studies of stress, bonding, and health, so method care is not a nicety; it decides what findings can be trusted.
plos-pone-0357101:
Zhongqiu Zhang and colleagues tested whether a pharmacist-led cleanup of stroke patients' drug lists could cut waste without slowing recovery. Their 2026 study ran at a Chinese hospital. It covered 416 people with acute ischemic stroke. Care before the change was compared with care after it. The new strategy capped extra brain-related drugs and traditional Chinese medicines. Pharmacists monitored and adjusted each list.

Patients under the strategy received far fewer add-on drugs. They also spent much less on medication and hospital care overall. Their neurological recovery matched the earlier group. Harmful drug events became less common. The results make a practical case that more medicine is not better medicine after stroke. They also show that pharmacists can safely trim crowded prescriptions.
plos-pone-0357301:
Fuchao Xu, Ao Liu, Zhen Liu, and Zinan Fang published a 2026 materials study in PLOS ONE on concrete made from red mud, the caustic waste of aluminum production. The study tests its survival under sulfate attack. Sulfate-rich wetting and drying cycles crack ordinary concrete over time. They added two short fibers, a synthetic polymer fiber and basalt fiber, alone and blended, then cycled the concrete through sulfate baths and examined strength, pores, and microstructure.

Basalt fiber helped more than the polymer fiber on its own, but a specific blend of the two performed best, keeping most of the concrete's sulfate resistance after sixty cycles. Under the microscope, fibers bridged and delayed cracks, gave corrosion products room without bursting the structure, and tightened the pore network. The blend also slowed breakdown of the glue-like gel holding concrete together, pointing to a tougher use for a usually stockpiled waste.
plos-pone-0357501:
Leonie Bourauel and fellow eye surgeons compare a tiny drainage implant for glaucoma across two forms of the disease. The implant lowers eye pressure by giving fluid a new exit, and the team matched patients with the common open-angle form against patients with a flaking form that clogs drainage further. Success was judged at several pressure targets one year after surgery.

Both groups reached far lower pressure than before surgery, but the common form did better on nearly every measure. Its patients needed fewer pressure drops afterward and hit strict targets more often. The flaking form brought more complications and follow-up procedures, though none threatened sight. Bourauel and colleagues support the implant for both forms while warning clinics to watch flaking cases closer.
plos-pone-0357601:
Jinyan Zhang led a team of five authors testing plant extracts against a stubborn fungus, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Malassezia furfur, a yeast linked to dandruff and skin disease, forms biofilms that resist standard treatment. The team tested combined extracts of Angelica dahurica and Ligusticum sinense, two plants used in traditional medicine.

Zhang's group measured how well the extracts inhibit the fungus and its biofilms, and checked their safety. A natural option that works on biofilms could reduce reliance on harsh antifungal chemicals. Biofilm testing matters because microbes in biofilms can survive doses that kill them when free-floating. The study gives product developers and clinicians a careful first look at a traditional pairing.
plos-pone-0357901:
Guanyi Liu, Xuewei Li, and Rui Yang published a 2026 safety study in PLOS ONE on finding the few risk factors that matter most in railway accidents. Modern rail operations are so interconnected that traditional checklists miss how causes chain together. From more than one hundred sixty accident reports, the team extracted risk factors and their causal links, building a directed, weighted network of how one failure triggers the next.

The resulting network had the hub-heavy shape of a scale-free network, where a few nodes matter enormously. Using a combined weighting and ranking method to score node importance. They then simulated attacks that knock out key nodes in different orders. The network stayed robust, and their score identified critical nodes better than standard measures. The practical claim is targeted: fix the highest-scoring risk factors first, and accident chains lose their favorite starting points.
plos-pone-0358701:
Song Jin and three colleagues trace how institutions shape China's energy deals with neighboring countries, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their account runs in two stages: officials form choices about cooperation, and those choices then steer actual energy trade and investment. To test whether choices truly carry the influence of the formal framework, they built a Bayesian model, a statistical approach that handles tangled paths between variables while stating uncertainty honestly.

The estimates supported the chain. Policy choices carried a real share of the influence running from formal frameworks to cooperation outcomes. The indirect effect was clearly positive. The authors also ran example analyses showing how this mediation approach behaves under differing data conditions, a methods contribution in its own right. For policy analysts, the message is that formal rules matter partly by moving the choices of the people who apply them.

pmc-1664601:
Mathers and Loncar project world deaths and disease burden from 2002 to 2030. Earlier projections from the Global Burden of Disease project, based on data from 1990, were still widely quoted years later. Fresh forecasts were needed as populations aged and disease patterns shifted.

The authors update those outlooks by cause, for the world and its regions. Their projections weigh trends such as rising chronic disease and falling infections in many places. Governments and health agencies use such forecasts to plan hospitals, training, and prevention long before needs arrive.  Readers can see which causes drive the totals in each region.
pmc-2245901:
Zhang presents the I-TASSER server for predicting the three-dimensional shape of proteins from their sequences. Guessing shape from the amino acid chain alone is one of the hardest problems in computational biology. Shared contests had been set up to judge prediction methods fairly and openly.

The server threads a new sequence through known shapes, then assembles a best model of its fold. Shape hints at function, so a good model can guide drug work and basic experiments. Making the method a free server let any lab obtain careful predictions without owning specialist software.
pmc-2777001:
Hruz, Laule, Szabo, and co-authors present Genevestigator V3, a reference database for gene expression across many studies. Their web tool lets biologists explore how genes behave across a wide range of biological settings. Early versions, though, were limited by how well the system could scale.

Version three rebuilds storage and architecture to handle data from multiple organisms and growing transcriptome collections. Pooling many experiments lets users compare a gene's activity across tissues, diseases, and treatments at once. A shared reference of this kind saves each lab from rebuilding the same costly archive.
pmc-3965101:
Overbeek, Olson, Pusch, and their colleagues described the SEED and RAST systems in 2014. The SEED, started in 2004, was built to give steady, accurate labels for genes across many thousands of genomes. RAST is its rapid annotation service for microbial genomes, meaning it names genes and their roles.

The SEED links genome data with expert knowledge of cell pathways, grouped as subsystems. RAST uses that base to label a new microbe genome quickly and in a form other tools can use. Together they help labs move from raw DNA reads to a first clear map of what a microbe can do.
pmc-4993001:
Li, Severson, Pignon, and their team studied tumor immunity in 2016. A tumor does not grow alone; immune cells move in and act on it. How those two sides interact shapes how the disease will go and how drugs will work.

The team used new computing methods to count the immune cells inside tumors from gene data. They also mapped how the mix of cells forms and shifts over time. A sound count can flag which patients may gain from immunotherapy, drugs that free the immune system to attack the tumor. It can also hint at why some tumors resist drugs, and guide new cures.
pmc-535701:
Taheri, Lin, Austin, and their team studied sleep length and body weight in 2004. Short sleep had been linked to a higher body mass index in large groups of people. The team asked whether hormones that control hunger might explain that link.

They measured two hormones: leptin, which signals fullness, and ghrelin, which sparks hunger. People who slept less had lower leptin, higher ghrelin, and a higher body mass index. That hormone mix would be expected to raise appetite and drive weight gain. The study gave a clear, testable path from poor sleep to extra weight, and it is still widely cited.
pmc-5388101:
Shu and McCauley recounted GISAID in 2017, the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data. Influenza viruses change constantly, so tracking them depends on laboratories worldwide sharing virus data quickly. GISAID was created as the platform for that sharing, and the paper traces it from vision to reality.

Under GISAID, labs deposit influenza sequences and related data in a shared database with credit to the data producers. That credit system was designed to encourage sharing that pride and politics had slowed before. Fast, open virus data let scientists spot new strains and update vaccines in time. The initiative became a model for pathogen data sharing.
pmc-5908901:
Nicola Sproston and Jason Ashworth reviewed C-reactive protein at sites of inflammation and infection in 2018. This protein rises sharply in the blood when tissue is infected or inflamed. Doctors already use it as a general marker of trouble.

The review explains the protein's two forms and how the second form acts right at damaged sites. There it helps clear dead cells and can also stir further inflammation. That dual role shapes debates about whether the protein is a helper, a harm, or both. Readers get the biology behind a very common blood test.
popular-pastimes-for-amusement-and-instr: Popular Pastimes for Amusement and Instruction, 1901. The games book. This book preserves that work. Coming generations can find it. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Readers can find it here.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: The first volume opens Louis Constant's years as Napoleon's valet. He enters the emperor's service and learns the rhythms of court life. Readers see the young ruler through a servant's eyes. The private Napoleon begins to take shape.
rhys-celtic-folklore-1901:
John Rhys, the Oxford Celtic scholar, gathered this two part set of Welsh and Manx folk lore, printed in 1901. He drew on tales told to him and on notes sent from Wales and the Isle of Man. His aim was to save folk belief before it faded.

The pages hold fairy tales, ghost lore, well rites, and tales of folk heroes. Rhys traced marks of the old Celtic faith in what the folk still did and said. The set is a rich store for any reader drawn to Wales and Man.
rob-roy-volume-01: Walter Scott opens his beloved Highland tale with young Frank Osbaldistone, cast off by his father and bound for the North. There he meets the gallant outlaw Rob Roy and the high-spirited Diana Vernon. This first volume sets one of literature's great adventures in motion.
royce-world-individual-vol-2-1901:
Josiah Royce published The World and the Individual, Volume 2, in 1901, completing his Gifford Lectures. This volume turns from metaphysics to nature, man, and the moral order. Royce studies how the Absolute expresses itself in the natural world. He also treats evil, individuality, and the hope of immortality.

Nature, for Royce, is the outer sign of an inner spiritual order. Human selves matter as unique members of a divine community. The supplementary essay on the one, the many, and the infinite is a technical high point. Together the two volumes state his system whole. They remain a peak of American idealist thought.
scheible-das-kloster-vol01:
Johann Scheible, a Stuttgart publisher, began Das Kloster in 1845 as a vast storehouse of older German print. The title means the cloister, worldly and spiritual, and band one holds the first four cells, or Zelle, of the set. Scheible reprinted rare and half-lost texts whole, rather than in scraps.

Readers find grimoires, Faust books, and the stern spell books called Höllenzwänge side by side with folk charms. Cheap chapbooks and popular tales fill out the shelf. Few readers of the day could have found these works at all without Scheible's press. The set grew into the central source book for the German grimoire world.
schiller-maid-of-orleans-1801:
Schiller's Maid of Orleans, his tragedy of Joan of Arc, appeared in 1801 in Anna Swanwick's English translation. Joan, a shepherd girl, hears voices calling her to save France from English invasion. Schiller makes her a figure of pure faith and martial fire.

Crowned by her victory at Orleans, Joan falters when love and doubt touch her mission. Schiller departs from history, giving her a death in battle rather than at the stake. The play fixed Joan's image for much of the nineteenth century. Verdi and Tchaikovsky both later drew operas from Schiller's version. Its verse and pageantry show Schiller's Romantic side at full stretch.
sebillot-folk-lore-pecheurs-1901:
Paul Sebillot, a French hoarder of folk lore, wrote this book on the lore of fishermen in French in 1901. He spent years on the coasts of Brittany and Normandy, where he heard the tales at first hand. No book of his day knew the French sea folk so well.

Sirens, morgans, and the freaks of the sea fill his pages from the tales of the coast. He tells how fish folk read winds, wrecks, saints, and strange lights on the waves. In French, the book is the lead word on the sea lore of France.
serge-panine-volume-01: The first volume of Ohnet's Serge Panine introduces the charming villain. A polished Polish adventurer dazzles gullible Parisian society. His cold designs on a rich heiress slowly unfold. The making of a famous and heartless scoundrel.
serviss-other-worlds-1901:
Garrett P. Serviss made star science a joy for the plain reader in the United States. His Other Worlds came out in 1901. The full title deals with the nature and chances of life on the planets. Serviss tests each world with the best facts then known.

The Moon, Mars, Venus, and the far gas worlds each get a test. He weighs air, heat, and water, and asks who might live there. Serviss writes with warmth and a clear love of the sky. The book was the States' match to Proctor's famed work on the worlds.
shiel-purple-cloud-1901:
One man wakes to a dead world in M. P. Shiel's novel The Purple Cloud, from 1901. A strange cloud from a burst peak has killed all life on earth. He sails and walks through still towns. Grief and pride warp his mind year by year.

For much of the tale he is the last man alive. Then a sign of hope tests all he has built. Shiel set the mold for last-man tales. His rich prose makes ruin feel grand, sad, and oddly bright. He burns dead towns, mints coins, and builds a vast tomb for the world. Those mad acts show pride and grief at war in one soul.
sidonia-the-sorceress-the-supposed-destr: This edition of Meinhold's haunting novel brings the story of Sidonia von Bork — the Pomeranian noblewoman tried as a witch — to English readers. Dark pacts, doomed dukes, and sixteenth-century superstition fill its pages. A landmark of gothic literature, as chilling now as when it first appeared.
spr-proceedings-vol15-1900-1901:
Volume fifteen gathers parts thirty six through forty, spanning 1900 and 1901. Five parts in one volume mark a burst of society business. The new century finds the SPR testing telepathy with card and drawing trials. Apparition reports continue, now sorted by standards set in the census years.

Trance mediumship holds the center, with Piper sittings reported in detail. Physical phenomena surface now and then, handled with visible caution. The journal of record keeps its promise: print the evidence, print the doubts. Volume fifteen bridges the society's Victorian and Edwardian phases. Its cases entered the standard literature of the field. It is a rich year book of psychical research.
spr-proceedings-vol16-1901:
Part forty one alone forms volume sixteen of the Proceedings, dated 1901. A single part can still run long when the Society for Psychical Research has much to report. Telepathy experiments and their statistics take a leading place. The society by now weighs chance results with practiced care.

Sittings with trance mediums supply the human drama of the volume. Named sitters, verbatim notes, and cross references fill the reports. Apparitions and kindred experiences arrive in smaller, well checked batches. Volume sixteen shows the enterprise in its mature routine. The evidential debate of 1882 to 1930 rests on files like these. Readers get method and mystery in equal share.
strindberg-easter-1901:
August Strindberg wrote Easter in 1901, a three-act drama, here in Edith and Warner Oland's translation. The Easter drama of guilt and forgiveness marks the turning point toward reconciliation in Strindberg's art after Inferno. Its quiet close shocked readers who knew only the Strindberg of the battle of the sexes plays.

The Heyst family waits in dread for a creditor who holds their father's fraud over their heads. Elis, the son, nurses grievances against the world, his fiancée, and the asylum-kept daughter's strange return home. Lindkvist, the feared creditor, arrives and proves gentle, forgiving the debt in the spirit of the season. Maundy Thursday to Easter Saturday frames a slow thaw from resentment toward a chastened, communal grace in the house. The Olands' translation brought this gentler Strindberg to English readers who had missed the turn.
tesla-talking-planets-1901:
Nikola Tesla told Collier's Weekly in February 1901 that he had caught signs from Mars. The piece, Talking with Planets, set out his claim in his own words. Tesla said odd beats in his gear in Colorado matched no earthly source. He thought wise beings on Mars might be at work.

He goes on to muse on how men might hail other worlds one day. Plans for vast power and clear signs fill the last pages. No proof came, and most star men doubt the claim. The piece stays the most famed tale of its kind from the dawn of radio.
the-adventures-of-ferdinand-count-fathom: Tobias Smollett's dark comic novel follows Ferdinand Count Fathom — gambler, swindler, and one of fiction's great villains — through his early career of roguery. This first volume launches his adventures across Europe. Smollett's savage humor and vivid lowlife scenes make it a landmark of the eighteenth-century novel.
the-antiquary-volume-01: Walter Scott's Antiquary opens with Jonathan Oldbuck — the lovable, blustering student of ruins — and the coastal mysteries of northeast Scotland. This first volume sets one of Scott's most warmly human novels in motion, introducing the beggar Edie Ochiltree and a tangle of secrets. Antiquarian charm and romantic intrigue.
the-captives-pg3601: Plautus's comedy The Captives turns war into laughter on the Roman stage. Two prisoners swap identities and fool their captors with clever tricks. The ancient farce moves at a brisk and merry pace. A classic comedy that still earns its laughs today.
the-complete-works-of-brann-the-iconocla: Volume one of the collected works of William Cowper Brann, the Texas "Iconoclast" whose savage editorials made him famous and got him killed. Brann lashed Baptists, politicians, and humbugs with unmatched fury. The most fearless and funniest journalism of the 1890s Southwest.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau: The first volume of Rousseau's Confessions opens his incomparable autobiography. The Genevan writer recalls his childhood with total and startling candor. Deep shame and deep tenderness mix in the telling. The most honest memoir ever written by any man.
the-magus-or-celestial-intelligencer-bei: The Magus, or Celestial Intelligencer, 1801. The complete occult system. This book preserves that classic. It waits for future eyes. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
the-prince-of-india-or-why-constantinopl: Lew Wallace — author of Ben-Hur — opens his epic of the fall of Constantinople in 1453. The mysterious Prince of India, a Wandering Jew figure, moves through the doomed city's last days. This first volume sets the stage for one of the great historical novels of the nineteenth century.
the-red-lily-volume-01: The first volume of Anatole France's The Red Lily opens between Florence and Paris. The beautiful Therese drifts restlessly between love and boredom. Gilded Parisian society shimmers all around her. Fine irony and desire in perfect balance.
the-science-of-palmistry-and-its-relatio: The Science of Palmistry, 1901. Palmistry and phrenology. This book preserves that manual. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
the-thirty-years-war-volume-01: Friedrich Schiller — better known as Germany's great dramatist — was also a historian of power, and this opening volume begins his account of Europe's devastating Thirty Years War. The Bohemian revolt and the war's early campaigns unfold with a playwright's sense of drama. History written by a poet.
the-wandering-jew-volume-01: Eugène Sue's Wandering Jew, volume one: the great serial begins. The Rennepont heirs and the curse. Melodrama's grand opening. The 19th century's bestseller, sue's great serial opens, the curse begins, melodrama's grand start, Eugène Sue.
thomasius-de-crimine-magia-latin-1701:
Christian Thomasius, professor at Halle, defended his theses on the crime of magic in 1701. The Latin dissertation is a juridical demolition of witchcraft prosecution. Thomasius argues that the crime, as the courts defined it, rests on a pact no evidence can prove and no law should punish.

With this work the Enlightenment enters the courtroom in robes and wig. Thomasius traces the trials to torture, bad metaphysics, and borrowed Roman law. His students carried the argument across German courts. Within a generation, prosecutions withered in the lands his influence reached. The dissertation is brief, dry, and devastating. Reason here performs the executioner's last service, ending the trials for good.
thomson-bible-1808-vol-01:
Charles Thomson, secretary of the Continental Congress, spent his retirement translating the Greek Septuagint into English. His version, printed at Philadelphia in 1808, was the first English Bible translation published in America. This first volume runs from Genesis through the second book of Samuel.

Thomson worked straight from the Greek, not from the Hebrew or the Latin, so his Old Testament often reads fresh against the King James text. The volume gives the creation, the patriarchs, the exodus, and the rise of Israel's kings. Jane Aitken, the printer, was the first woman to print a Bible in America. The work is a landmark of the young republic.
tob-0101:
Five books of Solomonic magic make up the Lemegeton, called the Lesser Key of Solomon. Mathers edited the famous English text. Its first book, the Goetia, lists seventy-two demons with their ranks, seals, and powers, and tells the magician how to call and bind them.

Later books cover spirits of the air, planetary angels, and the Ars Notoria, prayers said to grant learning and memory. The set reads like a court directory for an unseen world. No grimoire name is better known to modern occultists. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-10501:
Three classic English renderings of the Quran stand side by side here, verse by verse: those of Abdullah Yusuf Ali, Marmaduke Pickthall, and Mohammad Habib Shakir. A compiled edition like this serves comparison rather than devotion alone. Readers can watch three translators handle the same Arabic line in real time.

Where the three agree, the sense is likely clear; where they differ, readers see genuine choices about tone, theology, and English idiom. Yusuf Ali's poetic notes, Pickthall's plain formality, and Shakir's directness contrast sharply at times. For students without Arabic, parallel translation is an invaluable tool for reading the Quran carefully and honestly.
tob-10801:
Matthew Arnold delivered the lectures published as On the Study of Celtic Literature in 1867, asking what Welsh and Irish poetry in translation contributed to English letters. Arnold was a poet and critic concerned with the cultural balance of Britain. The Celts, he argued, supplied qualities the Saxon temper lacked.

In Celtic writing he finds natural magic, melancholy, and a joyful wildness, set against English steadiness and common sense. Part literary criticism and part cultural politics, the lectures helped invent the modern idea of Celticism. Scholars now question his racial categories, but the essays remain a landmark in how English readers learned to value Celtic literature.
tob-9101:
Griffith translated the Atharva Veda, the fourth and most earthly of the Vedas, in the edition verified from the 1919 scan. Where the Rig Veda soars, the Atharva works at ground level: spells against fever and worms, charms to win love, keep a king safe, or curse a rival.

Healers, lovers, and householders speak in its verses more than priests at great sacrifices do. Hymns to time, breath, and the earth show its reach upward as well. Scholars call it the everyday religion of ancient India, and the description fits. Griffith's flowing English keeps the charms brisk, strange, and very human.
tolstoy-anna-karenina-garnett-1901:
Leo Tolstoy wrote Anna Karenina in Russian, and Constance Garnett made it English in 1901. Garnett's was the first major English version, and it made Tolstoy's novel an English classic. The book pairs a doomed love affair with a search for faith and meaningful work.

Anna leaves her cold husband Karenin for Count Vronsky and loses her son and rank. Levin, the other lead, seeks truth in farming, marriage, and God on his estate. Anna's passion curdles into jealousy and despair as society shuts its doors to her. Her death under a train closes one of fiction's most famous arcs of love. Tolstoy renders balls, races, harvests, and inner thought with equal, unmatched vivid force.
ueber-kunst-und-kunstler-1901: Ueber Kunst und Künstler, 1901. The art essay. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. The library keeps the document safe for everyone.
un-ga-res-63-301:
A coup in Honduras in the summer of 2009 drew swift rebuke in Resolution 63/301 of the General Assembly. Troops had seized President Jose Manuel Zelaya Rosales on 28 June 2009 and forced him from the land. The text voices deep worry at the break in the state's lawful and free order. It also faults acts of force against envoys and their staffs, in breach of the 1961 Vienna pact on such ties.

The coup is condemned in plain words. It broke the free and lawful order of Honduras and cut short the rule of a president the people had picked. The Assembly demands the instant and full return of the lawful state, headed by Zelaya. The record's catalog year of 1961 is wrong; the vote is of 2009.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly resolution 63/301 responds to the military coup of 28 June 2009 in Honduras. In that coup, the elected president was detained and expelled, and a de facto government installed. Adopted at the sixty-third session, the text treats the overthrow as a serious attack on democratic order and constitutional rule.

The resolution condemns the coup and the detention and expulsion of President Manuel Zelaya Rosales. It demands his immediate and unconditional restoration, together with the government he headed. It calls on all states to recognize no Honduran government other than his. It backs regional efforts under the United Nations Charter to settle the crisis. It asks the Secretary-General to report as the situation develops. The vote signaled that the Assembly would not treat a military takeover as a fait accompli.
un-sc-res-101:
An Israeli raid on the Jordanian village of Qibya brought the Council's strongest censure in 1953. Armed Israeli forces had attacked the village on the night of 14 October. Dozens of civilians died in the assault. Truce officials reported on the attack twice that autumn. On 24 November 1953 the Council found the raid broke the ceasefire rules of 1948. It also broke the armistice duties both sides owed.

The Council expressed its strongest censure of the action. Such raids, it said, hurt the chances of the peace both parties had to seek. Israel had to take real steps to stop them for good. Jordan, for its part, had to keep blocking armed crossings of the line. The Qibya case became a byword for reprisal raids.
un-sc-res-1301:
Morocco and the Polisario Front remained deadlocked over Western Sahara in 2000. On 31 May 2000 the Security Council extended MINURSO for two months. The mission's task was to run a referendum on self-determination. The Secretary-General's envoy had just toured the region. His report saw the same old split over the Settlement Plan's main terms.

The mandate now ran until 31 July 2000. In that time the parties were expected to bring the envoy concrete proposals. The Council wanted ideas that both sides could accept. It hoped that would open a path to an early and lasting settlement. A fresh assessment had to reach the Council before the term expired.
un-sc-res-1401: Numbered 1401 in the Council's sequence, this resolution is catalogued as a 2001 entry in the United Nations official record. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1501: Crossing into the 1500s sequence, Resolution 1501 was adopted by the Security Council in 2003. The text here follows the official record as transcribed on English Wikisource. Readers will find the Council speaking in its two registers: weighing language in the preamble, and direct orders, authorizations, or demands in the paragraphs that follow.
un-sc-res-1601:
Haiti's stabilization mission received a short bridge in May 2005. On 31 May 2005 the Security Council extended MINUSTAH until 24 June 2005. The Council said it meant to renew the mission for further periods. A Council team had visited Haiti in April. Its report, and the Secretary-General's May report, informed the decision. The situation still threatened peace in the region. The mission acted under Chapter VII of the Charter.

The brief term covered the gap before a fuller renewal. Haiti's transitional government was preparing elections for that year. The mission guarded security while the vote was organized. The Council stayed seized of the matter. A longer extension followed within the month.
un-sc-res-1701:
Resolution 1701 ended the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon. After a month of fighting, the Council adopted the text in August 2006, with both sides accepting a halt. It remains the basic settlement document for southern Lebanon.

The text calls for a full stop to attacks, Israel's withdrawal as a strengthened UNIFIL deploys, and no armed groups south of the Litani River except Lebanon's army and UN troops. It also demands respect for the Blue Line border. Nearly every later crisis on that border has been argued in this resolution's language.
un-sc-res-1901:
Rwanda tribunal judges gained room to finish their trials on 16 December 2009. The tribunal's president had written in October and November about the bench. Its completion strategy report admitted that not all work could end in 2010, as the Council had ordered. Terms of judges had already been extended to the end of 2010.

The Council said it meant to extend the appeals judges' terms by 30 June 2010, in light of progress. To let the tribunal finish trials already running, it raised the number of ad litem judges who may serve at one time. Judge Erik Møse was allowed to complete the Setako case, which he had begun before his term ran out. Judgment in that trial was expected by February 2010. The Council stayed seized of the matter, as the tribunal's slow wind-down became a standing item on its agenda.
un-sc-res-2001:
Resolution 2001 extended the United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq once more in 2011. American forces were preparing to leave the country by year's end. The Council kept UNAMI in place to advise Iraq's government through the transition.

Its tasks in the text include election support, help with disputed internal borders such as Kirkuk, and work on refugees and human rights. The Secretary-General is asked to report every few months. The resolution shows the UN becoming the main outside presence in Iraq just as the military chapter closed. It stands in a long series of yearly UNAMI renewals preserved in this record.
un-sc-res-201:
The military situation in Cyprus stayed mostly quiet in the first months of 1965, and the Secretary-General credited the peacekeeping force for much of that calm. His report recommended keeping the force in place. Cyprus's government wanted it to stay beyond 26 March 1965. Resolution 201 was adopted unanimously on 19 March 1965.

The Council thanked the states that supplied troops, police, supplies, and money. The parties were told to show restraint and to cooperate with the force. The earlier Cyprus resolutions were reaffirmed. The force's stationing was extended for three months, ending on 26 June 1965. The renewal was routine in form, but it rested on a clear judgment. Without the force on the ground, the quiet on the island might not have held.
un-sc-res-301:
With Resolution 301, adopted on 20 October 1971, the Council turned to Namibia. South Africa ruled the territory in defiance of the United Nations, which claimed direct duty for it. France and the United Kingdom abstained, while thirteen members voted in favor.

The Council backs the World Court's advisory opinion of 21 June 1971 in full. That opinion held South Africa's presence in Namibia to be illegal. South Africa must pull its administration out at once. Member states must treat the occupation as unlawful and give it no support. The text also condemns South Africa's plan to split Namibia into tribal Bantustans.
un-sc-res-401:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was extended once more on 14 December 1976. The Secretary-General's report of 9 December held that the force's presence remained essential. It kept quiet on the island and supported the search for a settlement. The force's freedom of movement in the north was still restricted, though talks on its stationing were moving. Both communities had agreed to the extension.

The Council restated resolution 186 (1964), which had created the force. It also restated its backing of the General Assembly's call for a settlement respecting Cyprus's sovereignty and unity. The parties were urged to show the utmost restraint and avoid any act that could spoil the talks. The stationing of the force in Cyprus was extended for six months, to 15 June 1977. The Secretary-General would continue his good offices mission and keep the Council informed of progress.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
A night raid on a Jordanian town shocked the world in 1953. Israeli troops hit Qibya on 14 and 15 October. Homes fell. Scores of folk died. Truce staff sent word on 27 October and 9 November. Both Jordan and Israel spoke their case. Resolution 101 passed on 24 November 1953 by nine votes to none. Lebanon and the Soviet team held back.

The raid was found to break the 1948 ceasefire text. It broke the armistice pact with Jordan as well. The Council gave the act its strongest blame. Israel had to bar all such raids to come. Jordan, in turn, had to firm its watch on wild crossings of the line. Those crossings fed the cycle of raid and counter-raid. More staff for the truce team were pledged. Its chief owed a report in three months.

Two months, and a pointed wish, mark this Sahara text of 2000. On 31 May, the Council adopted Resolution 1301. The Secretary-General's May report lay before it. His Personal Envoy's mission won the Council's backing. The vote mission, MINURSO, had been blocked for years. The parties read the vote plan's core rules in opposed ways.

The text extends the mandate just to 31 July 2000. It sets a clear hope for those two months. The parties should bring the envoy firm, concrete offers that both can accept. All paths to an early, lasting deal should be tried. The Secretary-General must assess the state of play before the term ends. The deadline kept pressure on both sides.

A new United Nations mission for Afghanistan, UNAMA, is created on 28 March 2002. The Bonn Agreement had set the country's interim path, and an Afghan Interim Authority had taken office in December 2001. The Secretary-General's report of 18 March 2002 laid out the new mission's shape.

UNAMA is set up for an initial 12 months, with the tasks and structure the report proposed. Its work covers political support for the Bonn process, human rights, relief, and recovery across the country. All Afghan parties are called on to cooperate with the mission and protect its staff, and progress reports are due every four months.

Bunia, in Congo's Ituri district, changes hands in this text of 26 August 2003. A French-led Interim Emergency Multinational Force had stabilized the town. Its authority was to pass to the United Nations mission, MONUC, on 1 September, and the Council wanted no security gap in between.

States in the departing force are authorized to help the MONUC contingent in and around Bunia if the mission asks and exceptional circumstances require it. That backup applies only to force elements still present before 1 September and only during the pullout, which was to end by 15 September at the latest. The aim was a smooth transfer.

Haiti's peace force won a stay of just three weeks in 2005. The force, MINUSTAH, had run the land's guard since 2004. A Council team had toured Haiti in mid-April. Its tale, plus the chief's report, sat on the table. Resolution 1601 passed on 31 May 2005.

The mandate ran to 24 June 2005, and no more for now. The text says the Council means to renew it for more terms. The short span let members weigh the state of play first. Haiti's strife was named a risk to peace in the area. The force drew its teeth from a 2004 text. That text let it act with force to keep the peace. Brief stays like this one marked the Council's watchful, month-to-month grip on Haiti.

The 2006 war between Israel and Hizbollah in Lebanon is ended by this text of 11 August 2006. A month of fighting had killed and injured hundreds on both sides, wrecked much civilian infrastructure, and displaced hundreds of thousands. A full cessation of hostilities and the release of the abducted Israeli soldiers are called for.

A permanent ceasefire is backed, built on Hizbollah ending all attacks and Israel ending offensive operations, followed by Israel's withdrawal as a strengthened UNIFIL deployed. UNIFIL is greatly expanded, up to 15,000 troops, with a stronger mandate to help Lebanon's army hold the south. An arms embargo on weapons to Lebanon outside state authority is also called for, along with urgent world aid for Lebanon's recovery.

Resolution 1901, adopted on 16 December 2009, extends the terms of the Rwanda tribunal's judges. Letters from the Secretary-General in November passed on the tribunal president's requests. The completion strategy report for 2009 conceded the tribunal would not finish all work in 2010 as once ordered. A July resolution had already stretched trial judges' terms to the end of 2010.

The Council extended the terms of the permanent and temporary judges sitting in the trial chambers to 31 December 2010, or until their assigned cases finished, if sooner. It also signaled it would review the appeals judges' extensions before mid-2010. The genocide trials' slow tail, not new policy, is what this administrative text protects.

Iraq's security had improved after years of war, but attacks and sectarian violence continued. On 28 July 2011 the Council adopted Resolution 2001. It extended the United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq, known as UNAMI. National unity in Iraq remained fragile at the time.

The Council extended UNAMI's mandate for twelve more months. The mission advises and assists Iraq's government and people. Its work covers elected bodies, broad political talks, and national unity. It also helps with regional dialogue and talks on disputed internal borders. Aid for refugees and displaced people is part of the job, along with human rights work and reform of the courts and laws. The Council said it would review the mandate again in a year.

Spring 1965 brought another Cyprus renewal in New York. On 19 March, the Council adopted Resolution 201 without dissent. The Secretary-General advised keeping the peace force three more months. The Cyprus government said it wanted the force past its March end date.

His report noted a mostly quiet island. The force itself deserved much of the credit. Yet the calm stayed uneasy in several spots. A fresh round of fighting was a real danger there. Such a clash would bring harsh results. The Council renewed the mission and thanked its backers again. The text shows why the force stayed: few trusted the calm to hold without it.

Namibia's illegal occupation by South Africa is condemned in Resolution 301, adopted on 20 October 1971 by 13 votes to none, with France and the United Kingdom abstaining. The General Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate in 1966, making the UN responsible for the territory. The International Court of Justice advised in June 1971 that the presence was illegal.

The Council agrees with the Court: South Africa must withdraw its administration now. Member states must treat the presence as illegal, South Africa's acts for Namibia as invalid, and give it no support. It condemns moves to destroy Namibia's unity, such as the Bantustans, and calls again on South Africa to leave. States must not sign treaties with South Africa for Namibia, send consular agents there, or strike economic deals that entrench its rule. Contracts granted by South Africa after 1966 get no protection against a lawful Namibian government.

Resolution 401, adopted on 14 December 1976 by thirteen votes to none, renews the Cyprus peacekeeping force for six months. The Secretary-General's report of 9 December said the force was essential both to keep the island quiet and to help the search for a settlement. Talks between the two communities' representatives offered the best hope, he judged, if both sides showed flexibility.

The Council extended UNFICYP's stationing to June 1977. It noted that the force's freedom of movement, and that of its civilian police, was still restricted in the north, though talks on deployment were inching forward. Concern was voiced about actions raising tension between the communities, and the parties were reminded to honor the agreements reached in earlier rounds of talks.

Czechoslovakia split in two at midnight on New Year's Day 1993. The Czech Republic and Slovakia parted without violence. Both needed fresh UN seats, since the old federation's membership lapsed. Resolution 801, adopted without a vote on 8 January 1993, handled the Czech application, filed as document S/25045.

The Council recommended the Czech Republic's admission to the General Assembly. The Assembly acted on 19 January. Prague's diplomats took their places within weeks of independence. The speed showed how orderly the divorce had been. Unlike Yugoslavia's violent breakup, this split needed no peacekeepers. The resolution is a brief, calm record of a negotiated separation entering international law.
voltaire-philosophical-dictionary-flemin:
Voltaire built an arsenal in dictionary form, and William F. Fleming's 1901 translation gives the Philosophical Dictionary complete in ten volumes merged. Entries run from angels to zeal, each a small essay with a sting. Superstition and intolerance take the blows, in the cool voice of a man who trusts reason.

Short pieces suit quoting, which made the dictionary the Enlightenment's most handy reference of dissent. Some entries argue, some mock, some simply define a word until its misuse shows. Readers can open anywhere and find Voltaire thinking aloud, the eighteenth century's sharpest pen at work on faith and power.
voyages-of-samuel-de-champlain-volume-01: Samuel de Champlain, the founder of Quebec, recorded his explorations of northeastern North America in these famous journals. This first volume covers his early voyages along the Atlantic coast and into the interior he would claim for France. A foundational document of Canadian history, written by the man who lived it.
wells-first-men-in-the-moon-1901:
H. G. Wells sent two men to the Moon in The First Men in the Moon in 1901. A broke man of trade, Bedford, meets a sage, Cavor, with a great find. Cavor has made a stuff, cavorite, that shuts off the pull of Earth. They seal it in a sphere and ride it to the Moon.

In the Moon they find air in deep caves and a race of ant-like Selenites. Chains, strange beasts, and a vast brain at the core fill their tale. Bedford wins back to Earth, while Cavor's fate comes by faint signs. The book is a key text of the first space age tales.
weston-legend-sir-lancelot-du-lac-1901:
Jessie Weston, the scholar who translated Parzival and retold Gawain, turned to Lancelot in this study of 1901. She asked who the famous knight was before the great French romances made him the queen's lover. Her book traces the character across centuries of story.

Weston follows Lancelot from early folk tale roots through the poems of Chrétien de Troyes. She ends with Malory, who gave the knight his lasting English shape. Her work was bold research for its day and still reads well. Anyone who loves the Arthur tales will find here the life story of a legend in the making.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol01:
Sermons preached in Utah's first settlements fill Volume I of the Journal of Discourses, printed at Liverpool in 1854. Reporters took down the talks in shorthand as Brigham Young, his counsellors, and the Twelve Apostles spoke. The result is a running doctrinal record of the Latter-day Saints in their founding decades.

Doctrine, counsel, and daily building orders share these pages, since the speakers led both church and colony. Historians read the Journal to hear early Mormon teaching in the speakers' own words, unedited by later hands. Volume I opens a set that would run to twenty-six volumes.
